The United States is delaying the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles already paid for under a NATO-coordinated weapons purchasing initiative, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with Bloomberg on Oct. 18.

Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which allows NATO allies to finance the purchase of U.S.-made weapons for Ukraine, Zelensky said, according to Bloomberg.

"The American side approved the delivery of only some of them, but not the rest. And this is not a technical issue," Zelensky said.

The Ukrainian president said the U.S. is currently supplying just 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, approximately one-quarter of the number provided under former President Joe Biden's administration.

Unlike the military aid provided under Biden, Ukraine must now purchase the missiles, Zelensky said.

The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian ballistic missile attacks and increasingly severe shortages of the interceptors needed to defend against them.

Ukraine's Patriot interceptor stocks had again reached critically low levels by mid-October, with a Ukrainian official telling the Washington Post that only a handful remained. CNN separately reported that Kyiv's available missiles had been exhausted.

Patriot systems are among Ukraine's most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to intercept using other systems.

Russia launched ballistic missile attacks against Kyiv on consecutive nights, Oct. 18 and 19, killing at least one person in the first attack and damaging residential buildings and infrastructure.

Zelensky also told Bloomberg that he had proposed suspending Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure in exchange for additional Patriot missiles.

"My latest model was: We don't target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel," Zelensky said.

The proposal comes at a time of growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington over U.S. President Donald Trump's demands that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.

The Trump administration has threatened to restrict military and intelligence support unless Ukraine ends the campaign, even as Russia continues targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Trump previously appeared to support expanding Ukraine's access to Patriot missiles. On July 8, he told Zelensky that Ukraine could produce the missiles domestically.

But Trump walked back that promise on July 31, saying Washington had not agreed to grant the licenses and describing the technology as difficult to share.

In September, Zelensky said Trump had made a final decision to grant Ukraine licenses to manufacture Patriot missiles, although domestic production has yet to begin.

Zelensky has appealed to Washington repeatedly, making the case for additional Patriot missiles as Russia intensifies strikes against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.

The U.S. government has not publicly confirmed Zelensky's latest figures or explained the reported delays in approving deliveries.

By Brittany Carter

Topic:Netball

The long arms of Kelly Jackson was a nightmare for Australia's shooters. (Getty: Hannah Peters)

A five-year hoodoo continues to hinder the Diamonds in New Zealand.

Since 2021, the team has been unable to beat their old foes across the ditch.

That unwelcome stat remains after tonight's shellacking in Auckland, where the hosts outplayed their shiny counterparts in every position on court.

The final score read 56-50 after a late challenge from Australia, but the margin was as great as 15 goals at one point, and that felt like a truer reflection of the game.

With a significant lead at half-time, Silver Ferns head coach Noeline Taurua rung the changes, offering opportunity to her bench players and allowing the Diamonds to work their way back into the contest.

Both teams will use the series to prepare for the 2027 Netball World Cup and have to strike the balance between winning and talent rotation.

The New Zealand Silver Ferns were very happy with their performance in game one. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

Leading into Sunday's Constellation Cup opener, the world number two ranked side was in much better shape.

Just a month ago, they stood on top of the Commonwealth Games podium in Glasgow, undefeated, to claim gold.

They'd gone through the major netball tournament without needing to face the Australians, who were on the opposite side of the draw and lost their semi-final to Jamaica, and may well have come into the series opener with some unanswered questions.

Are we as good as we think?

Would it have been a different story had we met the Diamonds in the finals?

After the way they played they should sleep well.

As their heads hit the pillow, they now know that on their day, at full strength, they are the best side right now.

Even if the official standings don't show it.

New Zealand celebrate gold in Glasgow. (Getty: Mattia Ozbot)

Their campaign at the Commonwealth Games closed the gap in the global ratings.

If they win all four Tests of the Constellation Cup, they'll dethrone the Diamonds for the first time since 2013.

"Any day to beat Australia is definitely satisfying because it doesn't come often," a pleased Silver Ferns head coach Noeline Taurua told the media.

"When we get rhythm, when we get flow and when we create, we get the speed on and we play some beautiful netball."

A lot of that hinges on the strength of Kiwi powerhouse Grace Nweke.

Nweke was still able to take the ball despite being sandwiched by Diamonds defenders. (Getty: Hannah Peters)

The 193cm tall goal shooter is only 24 years old and with the right feed from her teammates, is extremely difficult to stop.

Tonight she shot 40 goals at 98 per cent.

Nweke was ruled out midway through the last World Cup due to a knee injury, and New Zealand struggled without her up front.

They still haven't found another player that can fill Nweke's shoes. But if she's in the team, they don't need to worry.

The speed at which the ball was delivered to her in Auckland had the Diamonds' heads spinning.

Australian coaches Stacey Marinkovich and Nicole Richardson were left scratching their heads after the loss. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

Then there's the wingspan of defenders Kelly Jackson (192cm) and Karin Burger (184cm).

With 11 gains between them, they spooked the Australian shooters and held them tightly together in a pack, making it hard to break free and find space in the goal circle.

The Silver Ferns midcourt is also growing in confidence after Maddy Gordon and Kate Heffernan spent a season overseas playing Super Netball in Australia.

The Diamonds miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time after a shock semifinal loss to Jamaica.

Brimming with confidence, the Kiwis worked seamlessly as a team to blow their visiting opponents out of the water.

It doesn't help that the Diamonds are dealing with a lot of head noise at the moment.

A difficult campaign in Glasgow followed a tough season of Super Netball for many players.

There have been shaky and inconsistent performances from the attackers.

Add in the hoodoo of playing in New Zealand, and it all fell apart. The miscommunication was rife and the team were in chase mode from the get go.

The Diamonds still made sure to celebrate Bruce's milestone with a guard of honour. (Getty: Hannah Peters)

There was no fairytale for Courtney Bruce, whose 100th cap was one she'll be hoping to forget.

Both she and captain Liz Watson — the two centurions in the current group — ended up being pulled off to finish the game.

"That never happens, aye," Tarurua remarked.

The one positive was the debut of 23-year-old South Australian Jessie Grenvold after a phenomenal domestic season.

Injected in the second quarter, Grenvold finished the game with more gains (three) than any other Diamond.

Still, head coach Stacey Marinkovich defended her veterans, insisting the changes that saw them head to the bench were about connections rather than individual performances.

Jessie Grenvold finished with three gains, more than any other Diamonds player in her debut. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

"At the end of the day we were looking at different combinations and what could other people do," Marinkovich said.

"Jessie's here for a reason and we only have four games before the World Cup so if I don't get players out there I'm not going to know what they can do against international opposition.

"We switched things around, it's not to discredit our senior players we just need to trial other things."

Marinkovich highlighted the need to improve now there were more New Zealand imports than ever before playing in the Australian competition.

Nine Kiwi players will feature in Super Netball for 2026, after the New Zealand governing body relaxed its national selection policy. But just like the green fruit, their influx has left a sour taste in the mouth of rusted-on Australian Diamonds fans.

"There's not doubt Super Netball has shown them what to do in pressured moments on a regular basis ... That is the reality of it now."

"I don't know if we were a bit tense coming in but that's the thing coming to New Zealand off the loss of the Commonwealth Games.

"We need to process that and work our way through what that experience was and how do we get our connection out on court."

A game review will likely find that 15 substitutions in the middle quarters was too many for the losing team.

Although substitutions were definitely needed, whether the right ones were made at the right moments is the finesse that was probably lacking in the game plan. As was the fortitude to beat at team at the peak of their powers.

The Diamonds were missing Kate Moloney in the centre position and are hoping the vice captain will be available for the second Test after suffering a finger laceration at training.

The next game takes place on Wednesday night in Christchurch.

Legal education experts explain what losing federal recognition could mean for student loans, state-level accreditation, and the path to becoming a lawyer as the Trump administration weighs the American Bar Association's future.

The Trump administration is expected to decide by late December whether to strip the American Bar Association’s (ABA) law school accrediting arm of federal recognition, a move that would not automatically end the ABA’s accreditation of law schools or change state bar-admission rules but could accelerate states’ efforts to approve alternative paths to becoming a lawyer.

Two legal education experts told Fox News Digital that while most law students would be unlikely to lose access to federal loans if the ABA's accrediting arm loses recognition, the decision could accelerate a broader shift away from the organization's longstanding dominance over legal education, with states increasingly exploring alternative accreditation pathways that could change how law schools operate and who qualifies to practice law.

"I think the biggest thing is, everyone should know that the federal recognition of the ABA is just the first step," Adam Biggs, general counsel of the University of Austin, told Fox News Digital. "If they get knocked off their perch, that's going to supercharge the conversations of these state supreme courts to create alternative pathways that are not just the ABA."

The looming decision follows a September vote by the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI), the federal panel that advises the Education Department on accreditation matters, which remained deadlocked over whether to recommend renewing the ABA's federal accreditation recognition. Education Department staff have already recommended denying renewal, and now the decision rests in the hands of Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent to rule on whether the ABA's accrediting arm can retain its federally recognized status, which it has held since 1952.

AI BACKLASH REACHES MAJOR UNIVERSITY WITH BOLD BAN ON LAPTOPS AND PHONES FOR LAW STUDENTS

TKTK (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

The ABA has long served as the primary gatekeeper for legal education in the United States, with most states requiring graduates to have attended an ABA-accredited law school to qualify for the bar exam. Although losing federal recognition would not automatically end that arrangement, critics argue it could accelerate efforts already underway in some states to recognize alternative law school approval systems, potentially allowing institutions to experiment with cheaper, shorter programs outside the ABA’s traditional accreditation model.

One such alternative is taking shape in Texas, where Biggs is helping develop a new law school at the University of Austin (UATX) that would operate without ABA accreditation. The university is considering a two-year law program or a model that combines undergraduate and legal studies. It plans to make tuition free and avoid federal funding altogether. The proposed school could also depart from traditional law school staffing models by relying more heavily on practicing attorneys and federal judges as adjunct instructors, rather than maintaining the extensive full-time faculty structure that Biggs says ABA accreditation standards require and that can pose a high bar for institutions.

Biggs argued that the ABA's longstanding influence over legal education has discouraged such experimentation by imposing what he described as a "one size fits all elitist model of education," which he said drives up costs and limits schools' ability to offer alternative approaches to training future lawyers.

DUKE LAW'S ALLEGED RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT RULING: DOJ

Adam Biggs is the General Counsel and Chief Compliance Officer at the University of Austin. (Fox News Digital)

"Right now, the model they force makes it impossible to cut overhead, and it's going to be an expensive product," Biggs said, criticizing the ABA's accreditation requirements. "That makes the decision for you. Because you need to live in a big city to go work at a firm to pay off your massive amount of debt."

Biggs added that reducing the cost of legal education could help address attorney shortages in rural and underserved communities, where graduates carrying substantial student debt may struggle to pursue lower-paying legal work. Allowing law schools to operate with less overhead, he said, could give new attorneys greater flexibility to serve those communities and potentially make legal services more affordable.

Students take the bar exam. (shu.edu)

The ABA faculty requirements criticized by Biggs are also facing scrutiny from the Justice Department, which has threatened an antitrust investigation over restrictions on adjunct professors teaching core law school courses. In an Oct. 7 letter, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward gave the ABA 15 days to revise or justify its rules, arguing that the requirements restrict competition and contribute to higher tuition costs, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The emergence of alternative accreditation pathways could offer aspiring lawyers new opportunities, but also introduce complications for graduates hoping to practice in states other than where they attended law school.

While the federal government determines which accrediting agencies it recognizes for federal purposes, state supreme courts generally set their own bar-admission requirements. Many states currently require graduation from an ABA-accredited law school, a requirement that would not automatically disappear if the ABA loses its federal recognition.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ACCUSES PRESTIGIOUS LAW SCHOOL OF FAVORING BLACK APPLICANTS OVER WHITE, ASIAN PEERS

That means graduates of schools approved through alternative state-level processes, such as the one UATX hopes to pursue in Texas, could qualify for the bar in their home state but face additional hurdles elsewhere. Biggs predicted that as more states adopt alternative pathways, others could face pressure to reconsider their requirements.

"Eventually there's gonna be a very large group of states that are not ABA or nothing," Biggs said, predicting that states such as New York and Illinois would eventually have to confront the issue. "They're gonna have to come to the table and try to figure out how portability is gonna work."

Several states have already begun loosening the ABA's longstanding hold over legal education. In January, Texas became the first state to end its exclusive reliance on ABA accreditation for bar eligibility, with the state Supreme Court assuming authority to approve qualifying law schools. Florida followed nine days later, adopting its own approach to recognizing law schools outside the traditional ABA system.

The movement has since extended to other states. Ohio's Supreme Court proposed changes in May to establish a state-run law school approval process, while courts in Tennessee, Alabama and Washington have also taken steps toward reducing their reliance on the ABA, as Fox News Digital previously reported.

Langdell Hall Library on the campus of Harvard Law School in Cambridge, Mass. (Brooks Kraft LLC/Corbis via Getty Images)

ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TUITION PERKS PUT 4 STATES IN TRUMP DOJ CROSSHAIRS

The potential consequences for federal student loans, meanwhile, may be far more limited. Biggs explained that most law schools are affiliated with larger universities that maintain their own institutional accreditation, allowing students to access federal aid without relying exclusively on the ABA's recognition.

"So unless you are a freestanding law school that only relies on the ABA, your students are gonna be fine," Biggs said.

Sarah Parshall Perry, attorney and vice president of nonprofit Defending Education, similarly told Fox News Digital that the more immediate federal-aid concerns would fall on standalone law schools that rely on the ABA's federal recognition rather than a parent university's institutional accreditation. Perry estimated that roughly 15 standalone law schools could potentially face federal funding complications if the ABA loses its recognition.

Beyond the immediate financial implications, Perry argued that loosening the ABA's grip on legal education could bring more fundamental changes to what law schools teach and how they prepare students for the profession.

TRUMP'S JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUES NEW YORK, OTHER BLUE STATES OVER TUITION FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

"These law students are actually going to get a better education," Perry argued. "Because we get the ABA meddling away from curricular inclusions, and we get them away from race mandates in admissions and in hiring and promotions, we get back to ground zero on making excellent lawyers."

"I don't care what color my attorney is if I get in a car crash. I am very concerned that he recognizes principles of contract law and insurance liability. That's what matters most," she added.

Sarah Parshall Perry, attorney and vice president of the nonprofit Defending Education (Fox News DigitL)

The ABA's accrediting council has already moved to roll back some of its DEI requirements amid concern the federal government could strip its accrediting status. In September, the council voted 10-6 to repeal Standard 206, which had required law schools to demonstrate a commitment to diversity and inclusion among students, faculty and staff.

Fox News Digital got an up-close look at autonomous and counter-drone technology at the Army's annual AUSA conference.

A four-legged robot dog prowled the floor of the Army's largest annual conference in Washington, D.C., this week. Nearby a handheld weapon promised to knock drones from the sky without firing a shot, and a new interceptor was built to chase down the faster, deadlier versions coming next.

The displays offered a glimpse of a battlefield changing at a pace that is forcing the U.S. military and defense industry to race not only to develop new weapons, but to keep them from becoming outdated as quickly as they arrive.

"It's always a cat and mouse game, and we do have to be looking down the field," Eric Brock, CEO of defense technology company Ondas, told Fox News Digital in an interview at the Association of the United States Army's (AUSA) annual meeting.

That race was hard to miss at the AUSA expo this week, where drones, counter-drone weapons and autonomous systems crowded the show floor as the Army looks to rapidly incorporate lessons from conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East into its battleplan.

Iran coordinates mass drone warfare campaign across Middle East targeting Western sites. (Getty Images)

PENTAGON JUMPS FROM $225M TO $55B ON DRONES AS CHEAP ATTACKS OVERWHELM US DEFENSES

"If you walk around the hall at AUSA, it'll give you a good indication of the Army's priorities. Our priorities are reflected in what we're procuring," Army Under Secretary Mike Obadal said ahead of the conference.

On the ground, Ondas demonstrated a huge piece of that shift: Scout, a four-legged robotic system designed to move ahead of troops into buildings, tunnels and other potentially dangerous areas while sending imagery back to an operator.

"The whole concept is that if the Scout takes fire, it's better than the soldier," Brock told Fox News Digital during the demonstration.

The Army's new autonomous systems command is part of a wider Pentagon effort to organize around unmanned warfare, while War Secretary Pete Hegseth said at AUSA this week that the department is working toward a four-star-led Autonomous Warfare Command.

Obadal predicted an "immense number" of drones and counter-UAS systems at the show, saying their prevalence reflected procurement and budget priorities across the Pentagon. Ukraine, he said, had "cemented" counter-UAS as a critical part of modern operations.

The Army is reorganizing around that reality. This month it announced a new Futures and Autonomous Systems Command tasked with accelerating autonomous capabilities across formations including aviation, armor, fires, sustainment and reconnaissance. At AUSA, the service also expanded drone and counter-drone marketplaces designed to allow the U.S. and its allies to purchase pre-approved systems in days rather than months.

(iStock ) (iStock)

US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING

For Brock, one of the clearest lessons from the recent war with Iran was the sheer number of threats defenses could be forced to confront.

"It's more about mass," he said. "So we have to make these affordable, low cost, returnable systems, and we have to produce this to scale."

Ondas has rapidly expanded its own role in that push. Its Mistral subsidiary has secured more than $240 million in orders under the Army's $982 million Lethal Unmanned Systems contract, including an additional order worth more than $50 million announced in August.

The company also acquired DZYNE Technologies this summer in a deal valued at roughly $875 million, adding a portfolio of drones and counter-drone weapons that includes the IonStrike kinetic interceptor and handheld Dronebuster demonstrated for Fox News Digital at AUSA.

INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH

IonStrike is designed to physically intercept incoming drones, including Shahed-class one-way attack drones. Brock said newer versions of the threat are becoming faster and increasingly difficult for defenses built around earlier, slower drones to defeat.

"The faster moving [Shaheds] now need more autonomous systems," Brock said during a demonstration of the interceptor. "So this system is designed to be very fast."

The system uses onboard guidance to pursue a detected threat and is designed to be deployed in numbers when multiple drones are approaching.

But no single weapon can address the growing range of unmanned threats.

Ondas also demonstrated its handheld Dronebuster, which uses electronic warfare to jam or spoof communications and navigation links rather than physically destroying an incoming drone. The company recently unveiled a longer-range version under contract for delivery to the Office of Naval Research for testing and evaluation.

Those tools illustrate the increasingly layered approach to counter-drone warfare: electronic attack may be enough against one type of drone, while another operating without a vulnerable radio link could require a physical interceptor.

And each adaptation can prompt another.

Brock pointed to Ukraine, where defenders have developed increasingly effective ways to counter the Shahed-type drones Russia has used in attacks across the country. Russia and its suppliers, in turn, have worked to make those weapons faster and harder to stop.

That rapid cycle is putting pressure on a Pentagon acquisition system historically accustomed to developing major weapons over years or decades. The Army used AUSA itself to hunt for more affordable interceptor technology, offering up to $20 million through a competition focused on defeating air and missile threats at a more sustainable cost.

The challenge is also moving beyond individual drones and interceptors.

AI predicts which restaurants are likely to get orders, allowing Flytrex drones to wait nearby before food is ready for pickup. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Ondas has partnered with Palantir on software aimed at connecting sensors, drones, robotic platforms and command systems so they can operate as part of a larger autonomous network. Its SkyWeaver system uses Palantir-powered AI as part of an architecture designed to link intelligence, mission planning and autonomous operations across multiple domains.

"We're moving from each platform being individually autonomous platforms to mission autonomy," Brock said.

That could mean connecting intelligence gathered by high-altitude balloons and long-endurance unmanned aircraft with smaller drones, ground systems and other sensors closer to the fight, including in environments where traditional communications are degraded.

For Brock, keeping pace will increasingly depend on whether the U.S. can manufacture autonomous weapons and defenses in the numbers a future conflict could demand.

"I think that's the bigger challenge," Brock said. "Technology is not really a challenge. We can build fast interceptors. We can build autonomy. That technology is there. It's ready."

Senator Tim Scott joins anchor John Roberts to break down the battle for Senate control as the midterm elections approach. They analyze the latest power rankings, key toss-up races, and top economic issues like the cost of living. Scott discusses Republican strategies to win the majority with nineteen days left before voters head to the polls.

Democrats have expanded their once-narrow path to reclaiming the Senate majority with just over two weeks until Election Day, but they'll need to win several competitive races to take control of the chamber.

If Democrats ride a massive blue wave in the midterm elections, they could end up with 52 or even 53 seats in the next Senate. But if Republicans out-perform the polls, they could hold their majority, which currently stands at 53-47.

Here's a look at the current battlefield and both parties' routes to securing a Senate majority in the midterms.

The latest Power Rankings point to Democrats and Republicans each taking 47 seats in the midterms, leaving six races rated as true toss-ups. Additionally, three races are rated as leaners — one step shy of a toss-up. These nine showdowns will likely determine whether the Democrats make a net gain of four seats to win control of the Senate or if the GOP holds the majority.

DEMS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP SENATE SEATS BUT GOP'S MASSIVE CASH ADVANTAGE AN OBSTACLE

Fox News Power Rankings Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

"Nine races will determine control of the Senate, and on the polling alone, you could call any of them toss-ups," said Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the network's Power Rankings.

The GOP is fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. Republicans also face a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and President Donald Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings.

With Republicans controlling the seats in six of the nine competitive races in the Power Rankings, the GOP is playing more defense than the Democrats.

The six toss-up states are Alaska, where Sen. Dan Sullivan is seeking re-election against Democratic challenger and former Rep. Mary Peltola; Iowa, where Rep. Ashley Hinson is trying to keep retiring Sen. Joni Ernst's seat in GOP hands against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek; and Maine, where longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins is running for re-election against former state Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic challenger.

DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT

Fox News Power Rankings Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

Also on the list is Ohio, where appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted is running to serve the final two years of the term won in 2022 by now-Vice President JD Vance. He's facing former longtime Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. And in Texas, state Attorney General Ken Paxton is battling Democratic state Rep. James Talarico in the race to succeed longtime GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who was ousted by Paxton in a bitter Republican primary.

Democrats are playing defense in Michigan, the sixth toss-up, where nominee Abdul El-Sayed is trying to keep party control of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters' seat, as he faces former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks at the Michigan Democratic Party convention, on August 29, 2026 in Lansing, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Democrats are also on defense in New Hampshire, where Rep. Chris Pappas is aiming to keep retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen's seat blue against former GOP Sen. John E. Sununu. The Power Rankings rate the race "Lean Democrat."

It's a similar story in Minnesota, where Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan is trying to keep retiring Sen. Tina Smith's seat in party hands.

But the Power Rankings this past week shifted the race in the blue-leaning state toward the GOP, from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat, as Republican nominee Michele Tafoya appears to gain traction.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Meanwhile, the GOP is on defense in red-leaning Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces a difficult re-election fight against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton, a pastor. The Power Rankings rate the race Lean Republican.

Numa, pointing to Kansas, Minnesota and New Hampshire, said that "the voter profiles and histories of those states are keeping them at 'Lean D' and 'Lean R' on the forecast, but this map has expanded, and with the exception of the North Star State, mostly into red territory."

Meanwhile, two states are now pretty much off the table for the GOP.

Georgia was a top Republican target when the 2026 cycle began, but Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff holds a solid lead over GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins in the southeastern battleground. Republican outside groups have cut their spending significantly in Georgia, and the Fox News Power Rankings rate the race as Likely Democrat.

In neighboring North Carolina, Republicans appear to have conceded the seat held by retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis. Republican groups have pulled the plug on spending on behalf of GOP nominee Mike Whatley, who trails former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee, in polling. The Fox News Power Rankings also rate this race as Likely Democrat.

The Democrats win the majority if they run the table by holding Georgia, Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire, and flip North Carolina as well as at least three of the five GOP-controlled toss-up states.

"Senate Democrats are in the strongest position yet to win the majority – with multiple paths to flip GOP-held seats and growing momentum across the map," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, touted in a recent statement.

Conversely, Republicans would keep control of the chamber by holding at least three of the toss-ups where they're playing defense. A 50-50 Senate would remain in GOP hands, thanks to the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance.

Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at Tyler Pounds Regional Airport on Oct. 13, 2026, in Tyler, Texas. Vance is campaigning across the country for Republican candidates on the November midterm ballot. (Saul Loeb-Pool/Getty Images)

Gillibrand's counterpart, National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, remains optimistic.

"I think it's going very well for us," Scott said Thursday in an interview on Fox News "America Reports." "The momentum, frankly, is with us, not against us."

The GOP majority could be bolstered if the party goes on offense. While chances of Sununu flipping New Hampshire appear to be receding, Republicans are optimistic Rogers can top El-Sayed in Michigan. Trump is expected to hold a rally with Rogers in the Great Lakes battleground later this month.

Meanwhile, Scott has his eyes on a flip in Minnesota.

"Michele Tafoya is running a very independent campaign, lots of traction," he told Fox News. "I think we close that gap. And if there's an October surprise, Minnesota goes Republican."

A family text message on her sister’s phone is what triggered the raid on embattled “Squad” Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-Minn.) Washington, DC, home, according to a bombshell report.

Federal investigators seized the phone of Omar’s sister, Sahra Noor, earlier this year, as they began looking into whether Somalia-born Omar conspired to commit immigration fraud when she came to the US, three people familiar with the matter told the New York Times.

The text messages were used to secure a federal judge’s approval for Department of Homeland Security agents to raid Omar’s home Monday, when they seized the congresswoman’s phone, passport, notebooks and personal computers.

Noor, who currently lives in Kenya, skipped a scheduled event in Rochester, Thursday, to promote her new book, “Salt in the Snow: A Somali Immigrant Story,” citing a “family emergency” amid the fallout from the raid.

Federal agents also went dumpster diving to collect DNA from Omar’s trash before the raid, sources told NewsNation.

“To me, if they are obviously trying to obtain DNA, then, yes, that is a very easy get, especially if it was discarded even in a trash can,” former FBI special agent Tracy Walder told the outlet.

The evidence is expected to go before a federal grand jury in Minnesota, to determine whether Omar and her family lied when they immigrated to the US in 1995.

The feds have issued subpoenas to several members of Omar’s family.

Omar and her family were admitted to the US as refugees after Somalia’s civil war, even though Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, was a high-ranking colonel for the brutal dictator who killed an estimated 200,000 people before was overturned. Sources previously told The Post he misrepresented his identity when he came to the US.

The Minnesota lawmaker has claimed she became naturalized in 2000 at 17, through her father.

When asked about the seizure of Noor’s phone, a spokeswoman for Omar declined to comment directly, instead alleging a personal vendetta.

“Trump has spread lie after lie about the congresswoman in a desperate attempt to justify his extraordinary abuse of power,” Jackie Rogers told the NYT in a statement.

“This is politically motivated and an escalation of Trump’s personal vendetta against her lasting over a decade.”

Defender Sarah Klau was still named in Australia’s Constellation Cup squad despite being fined $5,000 by Netball Australia and handed a two-match ban for breaching the sport’s code of conduct and bringing the game into disrepute.

Klau plead guilty in a Sydney court to common assault after kicking a bouncer in the back when she was denied entry to a pub back in June. The matter came to light after Klau played in the team at the Commonwealth Games and an investigation was launched into the timeline of events to determine whether the athlete knew they were being summoned to court prior to leaving the country for Scotland.

Ultimately, the sanction has been suspended by Netball Australia for 12 months pending good behaviour. The dress that caused a stir in Glasgow for potentially being too short made by Commonwealth Games Australia uniform provider Valour Sport will not be used for this series. This actually has nothing to do with the controversy surrounding the major tournament as that dress was specifically made for the Games and would not have been used beyond that event anyway.

However, it was important following that drama that Netball Australia ensure its next kit would be fit for purpose, taking on athlete feedback and midcourter Jamie-Lee Price worked closely with new provider ASICS to design a dress for this series that hopefully won’t hitch up while the team is in action. There is reportedly a different one in the works with ASICS for next year’s Netball World Cup in Sydney.

“Athletes come in all shapes and sizes and you want to make sure that they all feel comfortable in the dress, so that’s probably been the priority for us as players is to have something that is functional and doesn’t just look great when you’re standing still, so far it’s been awesome,” Amy Parmenter told ABC Sport.

By Brittany Carter

It'll be interesting to see how each team fares after so much exposure to each other in the domestic Super Netball season. With unlimited imports allowed in the Australian league and New Zealand's competition struggling in recent years, there has been a big influx of Kiwi talent that now get to train alongside and play against the Diamonds every week.

Next season there has been even more New Zealand players signed and once this Constellation Cup wraps up Diamond Sophie Dwyer and Silver Fern Grace Nweke will link up for pre-season training as new teammates at the Sydney Sirens. Dwyer told ABC Sport that Nweke was a huge threat in this series.

"That’s the beauty of Super Netball we have so many people that are our rivals one day and teammates the next.”

By Brittany Carter

This series is REALLY important when it comes to world rankings.

After an unbeaten run at the Commonwealth Games, New Zealand closed the gap in the ratings, while Australia’s semi-final loss to Jamaica proved very costly.

The opportunity to leapfrog Australia and take the world number one ranking is apparently something the Silver Ferns had spoken about.

"We've put it out there on day one [in camp],"head coach Noeline Taurua told the media.

"There is the opportunity, we have to win all four games to be in the number one position, if we win three then we're even."

Since 2014, with both nations eager to hold an equal number of Tests, the Constellation Cup has been a four-game series decided by goal aggregate. This has been an ongoing bug bear for fans, who would prefer to see three of five games played with hosting duties switched each year to make it fair across the countries.

Instead in 2024, a series decider was added by organisers to the format to try and make it more exciting. It wasn’t required that year, with New Zealand winning 3-1, but was required in 2025 with the series locked at 2-all in Christchurch.

At the end of the game, a 12-minute break was held before two seven-minute halves were played as a tiebreaker. Australia won the series outright in this period but lost defender Sunday Aryang to a devastating ACL injury in the dying seconds. Kiwi stars Maddy Gordon and Kate Heffernan both dealt with cramps and were forced to come off during the additional time period.

The decider has now been ditched for the 2026 series. Organisers insist it had nothing to do with Aryang’s injury. Even so, Diamonds midcourter Amy Parmenter told ABC Sport it was the right choice:

“We do as much prep as we can but to play that many games across two weeks and then to add an unlimited amount of time depending on the game result, I think the priority is to make sure we’re not overdoing it.

"Seeing what did come out of last year with Sunday, I’m not saying that’s the reason, but in October we’re not fresh off the back of the domestic season and it is quite a demand on the body to play 60 plus minutes, so I support the decision.”

New Zealand has only won the Constellation Cup three times (2012, 2012 and 2024) but comes into the series in better shape, off the back of winning gold at the Commonwealth Games. However, neither of these teams met at the major tournament, starting in opposite pools.

This opening Test in Christchurch will mark the first time Noeline Taurua has coached the Silver Ferns on home soil in two years, after copping a controversial suspension in 2025 that caused a massive rift in the sport.

“We know that Netball World Cup [next year] is in August in Sydney so I'd like to think maybe the pressure is on them at the moment,” Taurua told Radio New Zealand.

“It's an opportunity for us to consolidate from Commonwealth Games but also possibly to see what we can do to give others an opportunity. So it's a fine line we're going to tread, but definitely working ourselves towards Netball World Cup."

You can read more about that here from Bridget Tunnicliffe.

Australian shooter Sophie Dwyer hasn't had much time to get over the team's devastating loss in the semi-finals of the Commonwealth Games. Brought on very late in the game, Dwyer missed the Diamonds' last shot at goal to tie the match against Jamaica and send it into extra-time. Dwyer didn't make it on court during the bronze medal match the next day. Tonight she's been named on the bench.

“I reflect on Comm Games and it was probably the highest of highs and lowest of lows in one week,” Dwyer told ABC Sport earlier this month.

“I’ve had to do a lot of mental work on that, it was the hardest couple of days I’ve experienced in my career, but the girls and Stacey Marinkovich were amazing.

"I felt the whole netball community get behind me ... There was so much disappointment with how we finished but the way that we bounced back in less than 24 hours and came together to win bronze is something that we’re really proud of.

"Not everyone leaves with a Commonwealth Games medal. At the same time our expectations of ourselves and what other people expect of us is gold and we want to keep being that number one team in the world, so we have done a lot of reflection and that’s why I think it’s so exciting that we’re about to test ourselves against the team that did get gold and we haven’t played them in a year."

This will be the 16th edition of the Constellation Cup, which has been contested annually since 2010 (except for 2020 when the series was cancelled due to the COVID-19 pandemic). Australia is the current title holder and has been the more dominant side throughout history, winning the series 12 times overall.

But in recent years, they've struggled with form in New Zealand — last winning a game there in 2021. Interestingly enough, according to Netball Scoop, that match was Liz Watson's first-ever game as Australian captain and Stacey Marinkovich's second game as head coach. Neither has tasted success across the ditch since.

The team comes into this series off the back of its lowest-ever finish at a Commonwealth Games, claiming bronze after facing an upset from Jamaica in the semi-finals. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) said during an appearance at the University of Chicago on Tuesday that she wants planned prosecutions of Trump administration figures to deter young people from taking jobs in the administration.

historic_day_in_college_football_sees_5_:
College football has never experienced a Saturday like this.

Five of the top seven teams in the AP Top 25 lost on the same day in the regular season for the first time in history. The last time anything even remotely close happened was on January 2, 1989, according to Sportradar, when five of the top eight teams lost.

Shakeup Saturday was driven by the Southeastern Conference, with No. 1 Georgia, No. 6 Alabama and No. 7 Texas going down as touchdown or more favorites.

AUBURN SHOCKS NO. 1 GEORGIA 🤯@AuburnFootball x 📺 ESPN pic.twitter.com/OUYjFx1ywj

No. 2 Notre Dame (at No. 8 BYU) and fifth-ranked Indiana (against No. 4 Ohio State) also lost, although those were less shocking.

It’s the first time Nos. 1 and 2 lost on the same day in the regular season since Oregon (to Stanford) and Kansas State (to Baylor) in 2012.

The chaos, which is sure to shuffle the poll and College Football Playoff seeding forecasts, cleared a path for No. 3 Miami to take over the top poll spot after beating rival Florida State 43-35 in a double-overtime classic that ended in controversy.

The Hurricanes can only hope to do better than the No. 1 team has the last two weeks; Texas and Georgia lost to unranked teams, the first time that’s happened in consecutive weeks since Notre Dame (to Stanford) and Michigan (to Michigan State) in 1990.

The last time five of the top eight teams in the AP poll lost on the same day was when No. 3 West Virginia, No. 5 USC, No. 6 Nebraska, No. 7 Auburn and eighth-ranked Arkansas stumbled in bowl games. It had never happened in the regular season — until Saturday,

It was nearly as rare for heavyweights Georgia, Alabama and Texas to lose on the same Saturday, which hadn’t happened since Oct. 26, 1996, according to the SEC.

It showed why SEC coaches were so hesitant to give in to playing a nine-game league slate. And it might be fitting that the bloody Saturday came on the same week the SEC capitulated to the Big Ten to move closer to finalizing a 24-team playoff.

The Bulldogs (6-1, 4-1 SEC) had been the league’s last remaining team without a loss, but Gunner Stockton threw two interceptions and fumbled with less than a minute to play in a 27-24 stunner to unranked Auburn (4-2, 2-2). Georgia, which had won 53 in a row against unranked teams, was a 20 1/2 -point favorite in the game known as “the Deep South’s Oldest Rivalry.”

Alex McPherson’s 34-yard field goal on the final play sent the visiting sideline into a frenzy. It was Auburn’s first win in Athens since 2005 and the program’s first road win against the nation’s No. 1 team since winning at Florida in 1994.

“We’re just continuing to plug,” said Auburn coach Alex Golesh, whose team scored on a trick play and an amazing, one-catch. “We’re going to build Auburn back to where everybody wants it, one game at a time. Just hang with us.”

Auburn’s win meant the team ranked No. 1 in the AP Top 25 lost in consecutive weeks to unranked teams for the first time since Notre Dame and Michigan in October 1990, according to Sportradar. Then-No. 1 Texas lost last week to Oklahoma in the Red River Rivalry.

That setback seemed to have a carryover effect for the Longhorns.

Arch Manning had more late-game woes against Florida. He fumbled with less than two minutes to play — a week after throwing an interception that helped Oklahoma win a week ago — and the Longhorns (4-2, 1-2) lost 27-24 at home to the Gators (5-2, 3-2). Texas was a 10 1/2-point favorite.

‘A uniquely American job’: What it takes to be a big-time college quarterback

Manning completed 14 of 20 passes for 173 yards and a touchdown. He was sacked five times as Texas lost consecutive regular-season games for the first time since 2021.

Like Auburn and Florida, No. 14 Tennessee delivered a defensive gem in the rivalry known as the “The Third Saturday in October.” The Volunteers (6-1, 3-1) held Alabama to 201 yards in a 26-10 win in Knoxville, shutting down dynamic quarterback Keelon Russell and breaking out cigars for the third consecutive year.

The Vols finished with five sacks and four takeaways.

“Phenomenal performance,” Tennessee coach Josh Heupel said.

Alabama (5-2, 3-2) was a 7 1/2-point favorite and played without leading receiver Ryan Coleman-Williams. Fans rushed the field afterward, and the Vols will gladly pay the SEC fine.

Tennessee won despite without quarterback Faizon Brandon (shoulder). George MacIntyre filled in and got plenty of help from DeSean Bishop, who ran for 159 yards and two touchdowns.

It was Alabama’s second straight loss.

In other ranked SEC action, Lane Kiffin’s former and current teams rolled. Kiffin and No. 22 LSU overwhelmed 16th-ranked Mississippi State 31-3. And No. 9 Ole Miss thumped 13th-ranked Missouri 31-3.

And No. 15 Kentucky beat Oklahoma 21-13 on the road, making first-year coach Will Stein the first Wildcats coach to win six of his first seven games in more than a century.

Indiana’s 22-game winning streak ended in gut-wrenching fashion against No. 4 Ohio State.

The defending national champion and fifth-ranked Hoosiers looked like they were going to rally to beat the Buckeyes, but standout receiver Nick Marsh stepped out of bounds in the end zone and negated what would have been a 27-yard touchdown reception on a fourth-and-4 play in the final minute.

Indiana’s first loss in almost 2 years shows Hoosiers a new, painful side to being in college football’s top tier

Ohio State (6-1, 4-0 Big Ten) ran out the clock from there, escaping with a 19-15 victory despite losing quarterback Julian Sayin to a right shoulder injury. Sayin left in the fourth quarter returned with his throwing arm in a sling. Coach Ryan Day said Sayin would miss “several weeks.”

It was Indiana’s first loss since falling at Notre Dame in the 2024 College Football Playoff and ended a 19-game winning streak at home.

The Hoosiers (6-1, 3-1) turned the ball over twice and missed two field goals, the first one after quarterback Josh Hoover missed seeing a wide-open receiver streaking toward the end zone.

Jeremiah Smith delivered another highlight catch, this one resulting in a 38‑yard touchdown on a fourth-down play against Indiana. Smith tracked the pass from Julian Sayin and outjumped two defenders in the end zone for his 12th TD catch of the season and the 39th of his three-year college career.

JEREMIAH SMITH IS INEVITABLE ‼️@OhioStateFB converts on 4th down to extend their lead pic.twitter.com/XVjQFppOxg

Smith’s latest one matched former Michigan standout Braylon Edwards for the record for most receiving touchdowns in a Big Ten career. Smith accomplished the feat in nine fewer games than Edwards.

By

Ava Berger

Demonstrators march through the Country Club Plaza shopping district during a "No Kings" protest Saturday, March 28, 2026, in Kansas City, Mo.
                
                    
                    Charlie Riedel/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

No Kings, the coalition known for organizing anti-Trump protests, is trying a different democratic tactic: increasing voter turnout.

On Saturday, grassroot groups across the country will hold over 3,000 "No Kings: Vote Early" marches and other events. Organizers say these events are a nonpartisan effort to promote early voting in the midterm elections, and will involve helping people check their voter registration, make a plan to cast their ballot and understand their voting rights.

The voting push effort marks a pivot for the No Kings coalition, which comprises hundreds of partner organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union and Black Voters Matter.

No Kings has previously held three days of nationwide protests since the start of Trump's second term because organizers say Trump's actions in office are more akin to those of a monarch than a democratically elected head of state. Trump has previously rejected the idea that he is behaving like a monarch.

"The first three No Kings were designed to send a message," says Ezra Levin, the co-founder of Indivisible — one of the major organizations within the No Kings network. "We're done sending a message."

Now, he says, they want people to vote.

There are two main goals for the event, says Levin, the first is to help facilitate what he hopes will be the largest number of midterm early voting numbers in the country's history.

The second goal is No Kings groups getting volunteers trained as poll watchers, an endeavor Levin says is in response to efforts by the Trump administration that he views as threats to election integrity. Levin points to the failed SAVE America Act that would have required voters to show a document proving their U.S. citizenship, such as a passport or a birth certificate, when registering to vote. He also raises concerns that federal immigration officers will be sent to the polls, and President Trump's attempted restrictions on voting by mail.

Saturday's events vary widely across the country, from block parties to cookouts to rallies. In Golden, Colo., a "Paws to the Polls" event invites people to bring their dogs on a march. Organizers in Everett, Wash., planned a "concert for democracy," featuring an environmental troubadour.

All events will share similar restrictions, Levin says, including a rule against political endorsements and inviting current candidates to speak.

Superhero capes and masks will be a staple of Cammy Dunford's event in Frisco, Texas. Dunford, a co-leader of Indivisible Frisco, plans to hold a "voting is your superpower" gathering. She will be wearing a red and blue cape (to embrace the political spectrum of voters) and will give away other superhero capes and masks.

"I don't care if you're an independent, first-time voter, Democrat, Republican," Dunford says, "if you are eligible to vote, you need to get out there and vote. Because without everybody voting, we don't have a democracy."

Early voting in Texas does not start until Oct. 19, but Dunford and a group of her neighbors put together 500 mini goodie bags to hand out — filled with QR codes linking to voting information and voting resources. They will also wave bright signs with superhero-shaped images urging people in passing cars to vote.

Dunford says that her group has two people already trained as poll monitors and is hoping to recruit more on Saturday. She says poll monitors are trained by Common Cause, a government watchdog group that equips them to answer questions from voters. They have T-shirts that identify them at the polls, she says, so voters can find them and ask questions.

At a Wyandotte, Mich., event, Christy McGillivray, the executive director of Voters Not Politicians, a nonpartisan advocacy organization, is scheduled to speak to a No Kings crowd about the history of fighting for democracy in the U.S. She says the organization of grassroots events across the country is inspiring.

"It makes people feel like they're a part of something bigger than themselves," she says. "And that's what democracy is. Democracy is about working with each other and for each other."

White House reporters were stunned by the brief tenure of President Donald Trump's press secretary Katie Zacharia after just five days on the job.

"Brutal," one White House correspondent reacted to Fox News Digital.

Zacharia, who first took to the podium Tuesday after the August departure of her predecessor Karoline Leavitt, did not receive the warmest reception among critics who pointed to her nervous demeanor and how she only called on three reporters during her debut.

"I knew she was out two minutes into her prepared remarks on Tuesday," a second White House reporter told Fox News Digital. "It was just too drastically different from Karoline. We were all shocked after.

"Karoline was beautiful and hardcore MAGA ... and dignified and professional and substantive. She set a new standard for press secretaries. You can't just be hot and good on TV."

A third White House correspondent expressed surprise Trump offered her the job in the first place, saying, "Usually, he’s spot on about who has 'it' and who doesn’t.

"There is no excuse for Katie’s first briefing performance," the reporter said. "In that role, you have to be the best communicator because your job is speaking to the American people on the president’s behalf. No one expected her to have all the answers or even most of them. "She probably could have been better than Karine Jean-Pierre if she had more time to prepare. But it was a brutal start," a fourth White House reporter told Fox News Digital.

KATIE ZACHARIA ADDRESSES BREVITY OF FIRST PRESS BRIEFING, DEFENDS LEGAL CREDENTIALS AFTER CRITICISM

While Zacharia's shaky performance in the briefing room drew a lot of attention, it was her repeated claims of having been a lawyer that may have been more lethal to her future in the Trump administration.

The fourth White House reporter suggested that was a "bigger threat" than her first and only day at the podium.

A fifth White House correspondent who spoke with Fox News Digital was of two minds. On one hand, the reporter said Zacharia deserves no sympathy since she accepted the job she was "manifestly unqualified for," noting her embellished resumé she knew would eventually be exposed.

"On the other hand, shame on the president," the correspondent said. "He was clearly getting antsy and impulsive. He wanted his new press secretary now, and he wasn't going to let mean old Susie Wiles tell him to wait while she convinced someone more competent and more prepared for one of the hardest jobs in government to actually take that job."

The correspondent pointed to current staffers in the White House communications shop like Anna Kelly and Lauren Bis as individuals who can handle the job but aren't "central casting" in Trump's eyes.

"He took someone who seemed like a nice young woman who was defending him on TV, doing an OK job of that, and subjected her to a massive amount of humiliation and made her a national laughingstock because he didn't want to be told no," the reporter said of Zacharia.

"I don't want to say he ruined her life, but she's gonna be a punchline for a very long time. And that's not fair."

JEN PSAKI MOCKS TRUMP’S NEW PRESS SECRETARY, QUESTIONS IF SHE’S A 'POTENTIALLY FAKE LAWYER'

As the search continues for Zacharia's replacement, a sixth White House correspondent insisted it "doesn't matter" who serves as press secretary during the current administration.

People Have Been Tracked and Killed in Cases Involving AirTags, Yet One Company Tried to Make the Devices Nearly Impossible to Detect

Elevation Lab is no longer selling a device designed to silence Apple’s AirTags after critics warned that the tool could make stalking harder to detect. The backlash over the AirTag Silencer has brought renewed attention to a frightening reality. The small tracking devices have already been connected to cases of harassment, domestic violence, and even murder.

The company introduced the AirTag Silencer on September 30, 2026, promoting it as a way to prevent AirTags from making sounds that could alert someone to their location. According to Elevation Lab’s original product announcement, the device was intended to help people recover stolen bicycles, camera bags, electronics, and other valuables without tipping off thieves.

The $9.99 accessory permanently disabled an AirTag’s built-in speaker while leaving its tracking capabilities functional. That meant an AirTag could continue reporting its location without making the audible warnings Apple designed to discourage unwanted tracking.

For stalking victims, that missing sound could be a critical safety concern.

Following criticism, Elevation Lab published an apology on October 13, acknowledging that the product could be misused.

“We have always made products we want for ourselves, and this was no different – we wanted it for AirTags on our bikes,” the company explained.

It also acknowledged the potential danger, stating, “In retrospect though, this also has the side effect of aiding someone with bad intentions to track someone that wouldn’t get phone notifications.”

Elevation Lab confirmed its decision to withdraw the product, adding, “We have removed the product and will use our patent on it to prevent anyone else from making one in the future.”

The response followed criticism from technology journalist Glenn Fleishman, who described the device as “appalling” in an October 1 article for Six Colors. Fleishman argued that making it easier to silence AirTags also made it easier for stalkers and domestic abusers to conceal their surveillance.

Importantly, the AirTag Silencer did not disable smartphone tracking notifications. Apple’s software can still identify an unfamiliar AirTag moving with someone. However, removing its speaker eliminates a separate warning and makes the tracker more difficult to locate by sound, particularly when someone does not receive a phone notification.

According to Apple’s official safety documentation, AirTags are designed to produce audible warnings when separated from their owners. Compatible iPhones and Android devices can also notify users about unfamiliar trackers traveling with them.

Those safeguards exist because unwanted AirTag tracking has already had devastating consequences.

In January 2022, Heidi Moon, a 43-year-old mother from Akron, Ohio, was killed by her former boyfriend hours after discovering that someone had been monitoring her movements.

According to News 5 Cleveland, Moon contacted a private investigator after her ex-boyfriend, Nick Mima, sent messages indicating he knew where she had been staying. Investigators discovered an Apple AirTag hidden inside her vehicle.

Approximately four hours later, Mima fatally shot Moon outside her home before shooting himself. Her death demonstrated how technology-enabled surveillance can become part of a much larger pattern of threatening behavior.

Another devastating case unfolded in July 2023, when 21-year-old Jailene Flores was fatally shot at a Mariano’s grocery store in Evergreen Park, Illinois.

According to FOX 32 Chicago’s reporting on court documents, Flores’ brother discovered an AirTag hidden in her car. Investigators said the device was connected to Armoni Henry, a man Flores had previously dated.

Prosecutors alleged that Henry confronted Flores after the AirTag was removed. On the morning of her death, he reportedly sent her 124 text messages, including threats against her life.

Henry was subsequently charged with first-degree murder. The case illustrated how discovering and removing a tracking device does not necessarily end the danger when an abusive person is determined to maintain control.

AirTag tracking was also involved in the June 2022 killing of 26-year-old Andre Smith in Indianapolis.

According to WRTV’s court reporting, Gaylyn Morris used a tracking device to locate Smith at a bar after suspecting he was seeing another woman.

Following a confrontation, Morris repeatedly struck Smith with her vehicle, killing him. She was convicted of voluntary manslaughter in August 2023 and sentenced to 18 years in prison that September.

The risks extend beyond fatal incidents.

In Miami, a police officer was arrested in 2022 after allegedly using AirTags to track his former girlfriend. According to Local 10 News, investigators accused Javier Magarin of secretly placing tracking devices in her vehicle following their breakup.

The woman reportedly discovered the surveillance after receiving warnings and later found another concealed tracker. Police said the alleged harassment included threatening behavior and unauthorized interference with her travel plans. Magarin was charged with stalking and illegal use of a tracking device.

More recently, the Miami Herald reported that Steven Colon Sr. received supervised probation in 2026 after pleading no contest to illegally tracking a woman’s vehicle with an AirTag in Florida.

These incidents explain why the AirTag Silencer controversy has generated such concern. Tracking technology can provide someone with information about another person’s movements, including locations that person may be trying to keep private.

Apple has continued strengthening its safeguards. In January 2026, the company introduced its second-generation AirTag with a speaker 50 percent louder than the original. Apple also maintains cross-platform unwanted tracking alerts.

For anyone who receives an unfamiliar AirTag notification, Apple’s safety guidance recommends reviewing the tracking alert, attempting to locate the device, and following instructions to disable it. Anyone who feels threatened should consider contacting law enforcement and preserving relevant evidence.

Elevation Lab’s decision to pull the AirTag Silencer removes one commercially marketed tool for disabling those audible protections, although other methods of tampering still exist.

The larger concern remains unchanged. A product intended to help someone recover a stolen bike could also make it easier for an abuser to follow a person who is desperately trying to stay safe.

black-homeownership-gop-selling-point:
Conservative values, National renewal

On Oct. 7, Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner opened an investigation into Wells Fargo over its pledges to increase black homeownership. He said the bank’s conduct was “immoral, unethical and un-American” even if it broke no law.

Raising black homeownership is a Republican goal, and a Republican administration is investigating a bank for pursuing it, weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Black Republicans call that a mistake in private. Few will say it on the record, so I will.

Unlimited access to in-depth reporting, expert analysis, and the stories that shape our country.

Already a member? Log in

Start with what is at stake. President Donald Trump doubled his share of black voters in 2024, from 8% to 16%. Public safety and immigration will not hold them this year or in 2028. An economic message could, and the administration has not written one.

Guy Benson made the same case about energy in these pages this month: Republicans, starting with the president, should have been “consistently seeding the message.” With black voters, the message is sitting in plain sight.

That message is ownership: property and capital in private hands, not dependence on government. Republicans have a claim to it that goes back to President Richard Nixon, who created the federal minority business office in 1969. Former President George W. Bush set a goal of 5.5 million new minority homeowners. Trump’s own 2020 Platinum Plan promised to advance homeownership in black communities, and Wells Fargo made its $60 billion pledge in his first year in office.

Candidates have numbers to work with. Black household income rose 4.8% last year after falling 3.3% in 2024. Black homeownership was 45.4% this spring, up from 43.9% a year earlier, and the black Conservative Federation’s new report sets a goal of a 5-point gain within a decade.

Not every number flatters. Black unemployment rose to 7% in September, a statistically significant jump. Good or bad, numbers like these are how Washington measures progress. It rarely writes black-only policy, whatever the loudest voices on either side claim. It keeps score, as former President Barack Obama’s White House did in 2016, crediting work to improve the lives of “all Americans, including African Americans.”

In Trump’s first term, the message had authors. Ja’Ron Smith, a domestic policy aide who worked closely with Jared Kushner, got credit for opportunity zones, criminal justice reform and funding for historically black colleges and universities. Turner ran the opportunity zone council, which ended in 2020 and was never restored. Last year, the president ordered Nixon’s minority business agency cut to the legal minimum.

Candidates cannot deliver a message the administration has not articulated.

What it has conveyed is opposition. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, the Justice Department’s civil rights chief, has described past enforcement as a form of “benevolent racism.” She has a point. Government should not sort citizens by race. But opposition alone tells black voters what Republicans are against. It does not tell them what Republicans offer.

Turner turned that opposition into an investigation. Equal treatment under the law is the right standard. So look at the law. Congress wrote special-purpose credit programs into the Equal Credit Opportunity Act in 1976, and President Gerald Ford signed it. Federal regulators encouraged lenders to create them in February 2022. That April, Wells Fargo announced one: $150 million to help minority homeowners refinance at lower rates, paid from its own lending division. This August, seven agencies led by HUD withdrew the guidance. HUD opened its inquiry six weeks later.

Washington wrote the law, encouraged the program and then investigated the bank that took it at its word.

Conservatives were right to fight quotas, but a private company spending its own capital is the market at work. If those programs offend equal treatment, change the rule or change the statute. No candidate can brag about black homeownership while Washington investigates a pledge to raise it.

Candidates are writing their own message instead. Rep. Byron Donalds (R-FL), one of three nominees who would be the first black Republican elected governor in their respective states, held a town hall at Florida A&M University, a historically black university in Tallahassee. Students pressed him on his loyalty to the GOP, and he turned the question back on the party they support. “You’ve been faithful to that party,” Donalds said. “Have they been faithful to you?”

It is the right question. He has also bought BET airtime for an ad touting his support for the school. Nobody calls that un-American. It’s called competing. But a candidate who asks whether Democrats delivered has to say what Republicans will deliver, and Washington is not helping him.

So why do so few black Republicans say this out loud? There are not many of us, and for us, access is the currency. Black Democrats make the same trade. Three weeks after then-President Joe Biden’s debate, just one of roughly 60 Congressional Black Caucus members had called for him to go. The caucus stood by him, and it did not save him. Then-Vice President Kamala Harris later won 83% of black voters, down from Biden’s 91%.

SPIKE IN MORTGAGE RATES COMPOUNDS INFLATION AND DEBT WOES

The path forward is short. Charge a violation or close the investigation. Restore the council. Adopt a number, such as the federation’s five-point homeownership goal, and reach it through sound credit, not loosened standards. Give every Republican candidate the same sentence to say in November and 2028.

Black Democrats’ loyalty did not save Biden. Our silence will not save this coalition.

Melik Abdul is a Washington-based public affairs professional, writer, and Republican strategist.
rival-royal-courts-media-feud:
By REBECCA ENGLISH, ROYAL EDITOR

Published:  10:08 AEDT, 16 October 2026   |  Updated:  11:25 AEDT, 16 October 2026

It was the day two rival royal courts went head-to-head.

And make no mistake, regardless of the spin put on the day and the oh-so casual insistence by Team Sussex that their trip to Nottingham wasn't a classic Palace away-day, there was no missing the message: Harry and Meghan are 'public figures' who can, frankly, do what they like.

And what they like doing, clearly, is cosplaying at being royal.

For Harry, well, it's all he's ever known. And for Meghan, who knows? But she's a clever cookie and will have cottoned on pretty quickly that these types of events work well in terms of meeting and greeting the public in the most effective way possible.

There's a reason the 'real royals' have been doing it this way for decades.

One could only feel for the King and Queen yesterday, who were the epitome of class and classic royal duty, ignoring with enormous dignity a small but vocal band of anti-monarchist protesters as they arrived to formally open the Welsh parliament in Cardiff.

With Camilla on his arm, unmissable in vermillion (take that, Meghan, in your low-key burgundy stealth wealth!) Charles ignored shouts of 'not my king', as he stuck to the script with an official meet and greet on the red carpet – and a deeply emotional moment with a survivor of the 1966 Aberfan disaster, Gareth Jones, who was so overcome he clutched the monarch's hand.

In another highly sobering encounter, they also met Len Moss, an off-duty nurse who rushed to the Welsh mining village after a colliery waste tip collapsed on to its school and spent two days washing the hands and faces of children taken from the rubble so they could be identified by their loved ones.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex and Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex greet well-wishers as they arrive at the Community Recording Studio (CRS), a youth and community charity, on Thursday

King Charles III and Queen Camilla arrive to attend the ceremonial opening of the Senedd in Cardiff

Inside the Senedd, the King gave a speech in which he praised the 'spirit of public service' imbued in the building – all pre-scripted, of course, but a phrase heavy with meaning given Harry's very public spat with the institution about what public service means.

Harry's late grandmother, Queen Elizabeth, backed by the then Prince Charles and Prince William, was firmly of the opinion, as we know, that you simply can't be a 'half in, half out' royal, particularly if you also want to pursue lucrative commercial activities.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex memorably snapped back that 'service is universal' and have spent the past six years trying to push back the boundaries of the so-called Sandringham Agreement to what they wanted in the first place.

William, meanwhile, was wisely missing in action publicly, but, I understand, on a long-planned 'duchy day' (privately working on initiatives with his Duchy of Cornwall).

What was so fascinating about yesterday's events is how little the Sussexes have strayed from their original brief as working members of the Royal Family.

Details of their string of 'official engagements' in Nottingham were revealed in an operational note sent to journalists, including royal correspondents (except the Daily Mail's, it should be noted!), the very individuals Harry once described as 'pirates with Press cards'.

Some were even invited to cover the day's events and share their reports and videos as part of an official Sussex media pool.

This is no criticism whatsoever of fellow journalists. All of us must cover big news stories and report on what we see in a fair and accurate manner.

Prince Harry and Meghan were 'clinging together as survivors' on their first official engagement since returning to the UK after Megxit, a body language expert claimed

Meghan and Harry arrive at Himmah Hub, a food poverty community action group, in Nottingham

What's so remarkable, though, is that this is the way the Sussexes have chosen to fashion their approach to the British media, when they vowed to do the very opposite at the time of their acrimonious departure.

Once again, it seems, they cleave back to the mothership.

Even their staffing yesterday was eerily familiar.

Behind Harry in Nottingham, those with an eagle eye might have spotted the delightful Beth Herlihy, who was employed as a programme coordinator by the prince when he was a working royal (and who also previously worked for William and Catherine at their Royal Foundation).

She and another equally lovely former royal aide Clara Loughran (Harry's former programme manager, who was appointed a member of the Royal Victorian Order in the 2019 New Year's Honours List) have since founded a private advisory firm working with high-profile individuals in the philanthropic sector, whose number one client in the UK is …the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

Both, in other words, have been trained in 'the royal way'. Even the walkabout undertaken by the couple – just hours after their own team pointedly insisted they wouldn't do one because they didn't have the security to manage it, despite the exact timings of their visit being publicly released, presumably in an effort to drum up interest – was royal in all but name.

While courtiers have done their best to make clear the Sussexes have nothing to do with them and should be treated as private citizens (as Harry and Meghan themselves have so frequently requested) events like their trip to Nottingham yesterday come as close to 'official' royal duties as you could get.

Meghan and Harry's walkabout on Thursday mirrored their last visit to Nottingham in 2017, which was their first official royal event together after announcing their engagement

The obvious question is: what can the Palace do about it?

Very little, it seems. They've made their point, Harry and Meghan have chosen to ignore it.

There's no doubt that the Royal Household is irritated and is likely to be even more so when it reads an inflammatory briefing by a friend of the couple to Hello! yesterday that the Sandringham Agreement was 'foisted' upon them – and that they never actually agreed to anything. Which many feel tells you a great deal about their current thinking.

But the Palace is absolutely determined not to be stung into reacting. Indeed, if the King's approach yesterday was anything to go by, he will simply ignore the haters – whether they be random protesters or members of his own family – and stoically get on with his public duties.

And the same goes for the rest of the real royals too.

Don’t go writing the obituary for the U.S. electric vehicle just yet. After sales tanked following the cancellation of tax credits last year, they’ve been growing for the last three consecutive quarters, according to a new report from Cox Automotive.

EVs captured 6.1% of the U.S. market, their best showing since the third quarter of 2025. The recovery in the U.S. mimics what occurred in Germany after the government stopped incentives for EV purchases in November 2023, a year earlier than expected. The following month, sales fell by more than half. But after hitting that low, the market steadily recovered. German EV sales in August, the most recent month for which data is available, were the second highest on record.
