(Graphic by Avery Long)

The U.S. has poured billions of taxpayer dollars into humanitarian aid for Yemen, including hundreds of thousands of tonnes of wheat, but the assistance has been counterproductive — actually undermining local food production while farmers devote the country’s scarce water to growing an addictive drug.

Foreign grain can make it harder for Yemeni farmers to compete, pushing them toward khat (Catha edulis), a highly profitable leaf drug that consumes enormous amounts of water while millions of Yemenis face acute food insecurity. (RELATED: One American, At Least 11 Others Killed After Houthis Launch Missile Attack On Major International Airport)

Khat is classified as an illegal controlled substance in the U.S. and contains cathinone, a central nervous system stimulant with effects similar to cocaine and methamphetamine. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration considers it a Schedule I substance, along with heroin and LSD.

A 2014 policy report by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization described khat as the “mild addictive leaf that dominates life in Yemen,” as the drug accounts for about 10 percent of household budgets, with men spending nearly five hours a day chewing it as women and children increasingly began to partake as well.

Khat also accounts for 37 percent of the country’s water use, according to the UN report. Growing the plant is far more profitable than growing food, despite requiring much more water and offering no real nutritional benefit.

A Yemeni man harvests Khat (Qat), a mild drug used daily by many Yemenis, on a farm on the outskirts of Sanaa on April 15, 2016. (Photo by MOHAMMED HUWAIS/AFP via Getty Images)

An estimated 500 liters — just over 132 gallons — of water are used to produce a single bag of khat needed to achieve one high. Unsophisticated farming techniques exacerbate this water demand, with methods like drip irrigation unheard of among most khat farmers.

Since the 2014 UN report, khat cultivation has expanded by over 40 percent in many parts of the country. Civil war-driven instability has contributed to the trend, as khat remains far more profitable than growing food despite rising diesel prices needed to pump groundwater, according to Musaed Aklan, a senior water researcher at the Yemeni think tank Sana’a Center.

The growth in khat production can be traced to international firms and development agencies that urged the Yemeni government to subsidize cash crops over agricultural production in the 1970s and 1980s. This left the nation dependent on food imports, necessitating further subsidies for grain imports and further disincentivizing local grain production, Aklan reported.

A Yemeni woman walks through a heavily damaged neighbourhood in the war-battered city of Saada, 240 kms (150 miles) north of the Yemeni capital Sanaa, on March 8, 2010, one month after a truce was declared between the Shiite rebels and government forces. (Photo by -/AFP via Getty Images)

These changes artificially skewed grain supply and demand. Along with more disposable income and expanded road networks, they created conditions for farmers to produce khat, which kept prices high and demand strong. The result was a nearly 80 percent profit margin, making khat about 10 to 20 times more profitable than most competing crops, the center said.

For decades, Western countries and international organizations have stepped in after one conflict or another to offer Yemen aid in ways and under conditions that did little to help the average Yemeni and often proved counterproductive to the country’s efforts to gain economic footing.

Yemeni man sells kat, the narcotic plant traditionally chewed by most of the male population, at the market on March 7, 2011 in Kawkaban, Yemen. Yemeni man sells kat, the narcotic plant traditionally chewed by most of the male population, at the market on March 7, 2011 in Kawkaban, Yemen. (Photo by Marco Di Lauro/Getty Images)

Now, 18.3 million people in the country face “acute food insecurity,” creating “one of the world’s most urgent humanitarian crises,” according to the World Food Programme (WFP).

Between fiscal years 2016 and 2024, U.S. humanitarian assistance commitments to Yemen routinely ranged from $800 million to over $1.5 billion annually, according to USAFacts.

In 2018 alone, the U.S. donated 385,000 metric tons of soft white wheat to Yemen, enough to fill approximately 17,000 semi-trucks and more than the entire export of China that year. Wheat donations to Yemen represent approximately 30 percent of all U.S. wheat food aid donations. (RELATED: Trump Invokes Rare Authority To Cancel Nearly $1,000,000,000 In Congressionally Approved Spending)

Yemen’s Huthi rebels dispose of expired aid packages from the World Food Programme (WFP) in the capital Sanaa on August 27, 2019. (Photo by MOHAMMED HUWAIS/AFP via Getty Images)

Since taking office, President Donald Trump has sharply slashed foreign aid, effectively dismantling the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), a major channel for U.S. foreign assistance. The U.S. has historically provided up to 40 percent of all tracked food and emergency relief entering Yemen.

The cuts come as Yemen faces a widening humanitarian funding gap. The international community requested $2.16 billion in emergency humanitarian relief for Yemen in 2026, but as of the latest available UN OCHA data, only 22 percent of the requested amount had been funded.

Some U.S. assistance continued in fiscal year 2025, when the U.S. obligated $54 million for Yemen, including $21.7 million allocated to nutrition and humanitarian assistance.

A Yemeni woman takes part with farmers in harvesting wheat crops from a field on World Food Day, on the outskirts of Sana’a, on October 15, 2022 in Yemen. (Photo by Mohammed Hamoud/Getty Images)

“The WFP strategy of grain dumping harms the future well-being of Yemeni farmers who cannot compete with free food,” Harvard instructor and Yemen historian Asher Orkaby said, adding that much of the aid given to Yemen empowered the local terrorists while incentivizing war instead of “contributing to a resolution of the conflict and developing Yemen’s long-term stability”

Orkaby said this overcorrection stems from media and aid programs exaggerating yet simplifying Yemen’s problem by saying that millions are on the brink of starvation so that they can sell more papers or rake in more donations.

“The unchecked dumping of large quantities of imported food by humanitarian organizations can cripple local farmers, leading to a vicious cycle of impoverishment,” Orkaby said before offering his own solution. “Sustainable aid models draw instead upon locally sourced emergency food supplies to the furthest extent possible, knowing that such an investment-centric approach will reduce dependence in future years.”

A Yemeni boy sits next to bags of Qat, a mild natural narcotic widely used in Yemen, as anti-government demonstrators protest against President Ali Abdullah Saleh nearby in Sanaa on May 29, 2011. (Photo credit MOHAMMED HUWAIS/AFP via Getty Images)

Aklan said funding studies and risk assessments should be a priority for policymakers. He added that aid agencies should account for the specific economic, political and environmental needs of different regions rather than continue pushing a one-size-fits-all program of dumping money and food into the country.

The Yemeni water expert said organizations and governments managing food production, aid and agricultural resources should be answerable to local communities rather than international donors or distant bureaucratic authorities.

Aklan told the Daily Caller that while these recommendations should be followed, “Achieving full food self-sufficiency in Yemen is simply not feasible,” as food imports will remain essential to counter food insecurity and safeguard Yemen’s scarce water resources.

In the meantime, Aklan said, “It is crucial to curb the continued expansion of khat cultivation.”

A State Department spokesman told the Daily Caller that while the department does not fund emergency food aid or food security assistance in Yemen, it has “zero tolerance for waste, theft, fraud, or diversion of U.S. resources” away from the civilian populations who need them most. (EXCLUSIVE: Somali Lawmaker Shares How US Pays The Price Of Somali Terror And Trafficking)

The spokesman added that the department is aware that the heavily taxpayer-funded WFP is active in Yemen but stated that it does not provide food assistance in Houthi-controlled territory.

teen-triathlete-bikes-georgia:
Continuing GNN’s coverage of youth nonprofit leaders, the Pedal Forward Foundation in Georgia has distributed hundreds of bicycles to low income families, and taught hundreds of children how to ride them.

It’s founder, Jonathan Thai, was inspired to step up and serve his community after the local REI closed down a community bike-riding workshop.

At just 17 years old, the Alpharetta resident has already raised $30,000, securing 400 donated bicycles, and distributed 500 helmets, while hosting over a dozen free community bike clinics for children of all ages.

Thai says that in part, inspiration for the Pedal Forward Foundation came from his parents’ upbringing in rural, post-war Vietnam.

“Something like biking might just look recreational at first glance,” Thai told Points of Light, an international nonprofit which honored him with an award. “But it can have such a big impact for a family that doesn’t have access to transportation – getting to school, getting groceries, getting to a job.”

Thai is a high school triathlete, a body of experience he leaned on, together with his family heritage, to organize and drive the initiative forward to what it is today.

Along the way, the Pedal Forward Foundation received assistance from the National Charity League, the Young Men’s Service League, the YMCA, Boys and Girls Clubs of America, the Georgia DoT, the City of Roswell, Thai’s triathlon team, and various Georgia cycling charities.

The free bike clinics teach between 30 and 45 children, starting with balance biking and training wheels, before moving on to more advanced courses on braking, maneuvering, and dealing with traffic.

What Thai started in Georgia has now spread to chapters in New York and Tennessee, while next year, the Foundation will go international—to where it all started—on a humanitarian charity and cycling trip to Vietnam.

Youth nonprofit leaders are more common than you might imagine. In Arizona, a 12-year-old named Sloan recently wrapped up her 5th annual Diaper Drive, which channeled donations in excess of 30,000 diapers to a Phoenix food bank.

From the Upper West Side of Manhattan, GNN spoke with Max Owobu, who founded the Yenko Foundation at just 15 years of age. It sponsors children through private school in Ghana’s chaotic capital city of Accra. Owobu has already secured funding to send 10 children through the current school year, paying for their tuition, meals, transportation, uniforms, and supplies.

On Monday, GNN featured the work of 14-year-old Payton Obert and her lemonade stand, that has to date channeled $5 million worth of gifts and necessities to children facing economic hardship, or prolonged stays in the hospital battling illness.

The quartet of compassionate youth leaders is proof positive that one is never too young to make a difference.

Moderate New York House Republican Rep. Mike Lawler spoke with Fox News Digital about how the tragedy of Sheridan Gorman's killing has affected and motivated his re-election campaign.

Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., faced off against Democrat opponent Cait Conley Wednesday night in a one-hour debate filled with interruptions and fiery accusations less than three weeks before Election Day.

Lawler is vying for a third term representing New York's 17th Congressional District, a politically moderate area in the New York City suburbs that could decide the fate of who controls the House of Representatives for the final years of President Donald Trump's term.

Lawler called out Conley for misrepresenting his voting record, Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act and her own stance on immigration enforcement. Conley, meanwhile, tried to paint Lawler as a Trump acolyte who put the needs of Washington Republicans ahead of the people of his district.

Their most heated clashes came on the immigration front, when the moderator referenced the recent shooting of an illegal immigrant by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents last week in New York City while the man's 5-year-old child was in the car.

The race between GOP Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat veteran Cait Conley could decide the fate of the House of Representatives for the next two years. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"But what we are seeing right now with the conduct of ICE is posing a public safety hazard. To your point, last week, they shot into a car where there was a 5-year-old child. I'll tell you, as a law enforcement officer, you're not permitted to do that kind of stuff."

roman-temple-germany:
Along a series of Roman fortifications cutting across Germany just north of Frankfurt, archeological excavations have revealed extensive floorplans belonging to a temple, a military camp, and craft center.

The discovery, lying in wait just a few inches beneath the soil of the forest, provides extensive insight into what life was like along this frontier, as well as the area’s use following their abandonment.

Since 2024, Hessian state archeologists and colleagues from the University of Frankfurt have been excavating Kapersburg—a Roman fort located in the foothills of the eastern Taunus Mountains.

Kapersburg is located along the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes, a 342-mile fortified border stretching from the Rhine to the Danube that marked the end of Rome’s military and cultural influence. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005, the limes have produced dozens of important archeological discoveries.

“We have conservation layers here that are otherwise unparalleled in Hesse, because no agriculture has passed over them,” Dr. Kai Mückenberger, a state archeologist with the title “Limes Coordinator” said in a translated statement.

“The forest has preserved everything over the last few centuries and largely preserved it for us in such a way that we find layers that are otherwise always gone.”

Most recently, the Hessian archeologists turned up the military camp, called a vicus, where a troop that held Kapersburg would have lived. Inside the vicus, archeologists found the floorplans of living areas, craft centers, and a temple that’s now believed to have been dedicated to Mars, the god of war.

The rectangular temple was about 16 feet long, and contained a smaller, three-walled room at its center where worship would have taken place. Inside, inscriptions make reference to Mars, while fragments of a statue of Victoria, the Roman goddess of victory with her wings and laurel wreath, were found on the site.

ROMAN NEWS, CLOSER TO HOME: Hall of Peacock Frescoes Restored at Pompeii Villa Belonging to Emperor Nero’s Wife

Victoria and Mars were often worshiped together, both by Romans in general, and particularly among the military for obvious reasons.

The temple captures how long-lived Kapersburg was. Built during the reign of either emperor Trajan or Hadrian, it held the frontier for 150 years, much of the time via the strength of a military unit called “Numerus Nidensium.”

The “Nide” in “Nidensium” referred to a nearby Roman settlement called Nida, which would become a quarter of Frankfurt now called Heddernheim. Numerus Nidensium is believed to have numbered around 160 soldiers, with the vicus hosting perhaps as many as 700 support staff and hangers-on.

ROMAN NEWS, FAR FROM ROME: Luxurious Bath Complex Used by Roman Emperor Found in Serbia

Further exciting new insights were made into the history of the vicus before its abandonment in the 3rd century. Extensive remains of craft activities were discovered, including the area of a blacksmith’s shop. Evidence was also found that the Romans leveled part of the camp village and later replaced it with residential development.

civil-rights-advocates-midterm-observers:
Ashley Lopez

A voting center is seen in Scottsdale, Ariz., on Oct. 7, the first day of early voting.
                
                    
                    Olivier Touron/AFP via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

It was loteria night at the offices of Living United for Change in Arizona, or LUCHA, in Phoenix.

A small group of young people were playing this bingo-like card game in the hopes of taking home an array of prizes: a camping chair, reusable water bottles and coolers.

Conveniently, the prizes would be useful if you plan to camp out somewhere for a while. Which happens to be what these players were getting trained to do last week.

LUCHA, a left-of-center community organizing group, has been training volunteers to be what they call "constitutional observers" ahead of this year's midterms. This was the first of many in-person sessions the organization plans to hold as Election Day nears.

Carime Rodriguez, who led the training, told volunteers that their main job will be to just observe.

"Monitor the polling environment," she said. "Stay aware of what's happening on the ground … just make sure you are kind of keeping your eyes open."

For many election cycles, groups have fanned out to monitor polling places, but the charged midterm environment has many organizations stepping up efforts. They plan to have thousands of individuals with eyes on this election.

For LUCHA's Rodriguez, immigration is a concern. She told her training volunteers that during Arizona's primaries earlier this year, there was an uptick in immigration enforcement — including around polling sites in Maricopa County, where Phoenix is located.

And in case this happens again, LUCHA and other similar groups want to have people on the ground, to keep an eye out for anything they think could intimidate voters. Chiefly, groups say they are worried about Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, agents at election sites.

"I feel like these last two years, everyone has been holding on by the edge of their seats," said Alejandra Gomez, LUCHA's executive director. "And so that has made us incredibly forward thinking and making sure that we are preparing. We're hoping for the best, preparing for the worst."

It would be illegal for the Trump administration to send armed agents to polling sites. And administration officials have said ICE has no plans to target polling locations. But right-wing political figures close to Trump like Steven Bannon have been calling for the president to send them anyway, and Trump officials have said ICE could serve warrants at polling places.

Mary Corcoran, co-founder and executive director of the left-leaning Save America Movement, said that's enough for her to take this potential threat seriously.

"The point is to scare people and use fear as an intimidation factor to keep people home," she told NPR. "So, our perspective was that the way that we could make a difference in this election was working in communities that would be most likely impacted by the threat of ICE coming to the polls this fall."

Corcoran's group is partnering with the Rev. Al Sharpton's National Action Network, as well as various unions, like the American Federation of Teachers, in an effort they are calling Vote Safe.

She said members of the effort plan to be in major population centers with large and growing Black, Latino, Asian and immigrant populations — particularly in states with key Senate races, like Ohio, North Carolina, Georgia and Michigan.

"The volunteers are not there to engage with any ICE folks that could show up," she said. "It's really about having a de-escalatory impact by way of really bearing witness."

She said the presence of clergy, veterans, teachers and nurses from the community will hopefully have a "de-escalatory impact and a deterrent impact."

Left-leaning groups won't be the only folks at the polls. The Republican National Committee, for one, recruits observers to keep elections secure and transparent. And leaders of the Justice Department, which regularly monitors polling places, say they plan to step up their usual presence.

Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon speaks to reporters on Capitol Hill on May 29.
                
                    
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

Harmeet Dhillon, the head of DOJ's Civil Rights Division, said on Real America's Voice that she plans to send a thousand people from the agency to monitor polling sites.

"This is going to be the biggest DOJ election observer effort in history," she said. "And I'm so excited to be leading that effort."

She said that DOJ staff will play a similar role to other observers that will be at the polls, which is just to watch.

"They're not going to be interfering in any way or running the election, they're going to be observing, making notes," she said.

Wyoming's Republican governor criticized the actions of DOJ observers in the state in August.

Tammy Patrick with the National Association of Election Officials says election administrators have been hearing of big plans of large groups of observers for a while now. But Patrick said it's important to note that this is something they hear most election cycles.

"Every two years it seems, for at least the 20 or so years I've been doing this, we hear that there's going to be massive observation, and thousands of people are going to show up to observe at the polling place," she said.

"It hasn't manifested in that way in the past, but these are not normal times."

Which is why she says election administrators are educating the public. Rules about who can observe what, or how close you can be to a polling site, for example, vary from state to state.

Also, there is only so much observers can actually do at the polls. If something goes wrong, it's up to election workers and local law enforcement to sort it out.

Patrick said most years many observers get bored and leave.

"The actual process tends to be ... pretty dry," she said. "And one might even say boring to watch people walk in, give their name, sign their name, get their ballot."

But if things are not boring, Jane Kleeb with the Association of State Democratic Committees — which is part of the Democratic National Committee — said she wants people on the ground recording.

For political parties, the stakes of problems at the polls are high — particularly in close elections, where lawsuits are common.

"We're going to record any bad behavior," she said. "So that might be on audio. It may be still pictures, and it will be video that will then be sent to each state party. So, then they can get that information up to the DNC. So, we have a very clear process to make sure that we're documenting all of this in case lawsuits have to be filed."

snap-fraud-ebt-card-skimming-chip-cards:
Juliana Kim

Jayeleauna Lewis and her 3-year-old daughter are from Indiana. When Lewis learned that her state does not replace stolen benefits, she recalled a SNAP worker recommending she go to food pantries for the rest of the month.
                
                    
                    Octavio Jones for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

As Jayeleauna Lewis listened to an automated voice system describe the unauthorized charges on her food assistance card, a pit formed in her stomach. She pictured her 3-year-old daughter and their empty fridge back home.

On the 13th of each month, Lewis, a 20-year-old single mom from Indiana, receives $486 from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP. But in September, just minutes after funds were loaded onto her account, they disappeared.

" I was heartbroken because that's how I feed my daughter," she says.

Lewis is unsure how her benefits were stolen, but cybersecurity experts say she might have been a victim of skimming — when thieves extract card information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts.

In recent years, SNAP has become a fraud magnet for criminals who view both the nation's poorest Americans and the government program's outdated technology as easy to exploit. The U.S. Department of Agriculture Office of Inspector General projected that, over the past two years alone, $233 million may have been lost due to food assistance theft — largely driven by skimming. And in most states, stolen benefits are not replaced.

The Trump administration has vowed to eliminate SNAP fraud, adding that it's preventing the program from serving those who truly need it. But states' efforts to curb skimming are likely to get harder due to federal funding cuts that began earlier this month, according to Kathryn Larin, a director at the Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog agency that has been examining SNAP fraud prevention efforts for years.

"It will increase the budgetary pressure and will make it more difficult for states to allocate funds to benefit card theft prevention," she says.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture, which administers SNAP, told NPR there had been "continued inaction" against skimming long before new funding changes were proposed.

"Skimming has been plaguing recipients for years, and States sat idly, allowing benefits to be stolen from those who need them. SNAP administrative funding changes should not make it harder to fight skimming, as it simply holds these complaining lawmakers accountable," according to a statement from the USDA.

Lewis says she has never been to the Northeast. But on Sept. 13, between 12:11 a.m. and 12:13 a.m., her benefits were spent across eight stores in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Meanwhile, her physical food assistance card, also known as an EBT card, remained tucked in her wallet.

Two weeks earlier, Lewis says she had swiped her card at a gas station to buy a Powerade. Swipe-pay is vulnerable to theft because the magnetic stripe behind cards does a poor job of securing personal information, according to Scott Schober, the CEO of Berkeley Varitronics Systems who has invented several skimming detectors.

A variety of tools used to skim information from credit cards are displayed at the office of the New York Police Department's Financial Crimes Task Force. Over the years, the Justice Department has prosecuted individuals in SNAP skimming schemes, especially from Romanian crime rings.
                
                    
                    Mark Lennihan/AP/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

It typically goes like this: When a cashier is distracted, fraudsters secretly place a skimming device onto a payment terminal. The device captures troves of card information, which thieves later collect in order to clone cards. With stolen food benefits, criminals typically mass-purchase items that are easy to resell, such as baby formula.

"So it's a very quick ecosystem from the point of stealing the card to drain," Schober says. "Sometimes it's within hours. It's that well-orchestrated."

Skimming first emerged over two decades ago. Most banks in the U.S. have since upgraded their debit and credit cards with microchips that make it harder to copy personal information. SNAP, on the other hand, has lagged in making the switch. Organized criminal rings caught on and zeroed in on food stamp recipients — often timing their theft to the start of each month when benefits arrive, according to Michael Peck, an assistant special agent in charge of the Secret Service's Criminal Investigative Division. Peck oversees the agency's skimming investigations.

"These transnational organized crime groups are coming into the U.S. specifically to target our benefits system," he says. "They know they're stealing from the poor."

Anti-hunger advocates say part of what makes food assistance theft striking is the double standard compared to other victims of fraud.

Christopher Branch, a part-time Walmart employee from Illinois, says he has experienced both credit card and food stamp theft before. While his bank refunded him for the money he lost, the food benefits he used to feed himself and his two children were never recovered. During the month without his food assistance, Branch says he had to take on side jobs such as fixing cars to afford groceries.

" I was very upset and disappointed," he says. "I couldn't get no type of help."

Debit and credit holders are reimbursed for unauthorized transactions under the Electronic Funds Transfer Act. In 1996, Congress voted to exclude SNAP recipients from receiving those same protections due to concerns that it would be too costly, according to a 2025 report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO).

The federal government temporarily replaced more than $320 million in stolen benefits for nearly 670,000 households between October 2022 and December 2024 — giving some insight into the scale of this type of fraud.

Skimming incidents can take place at small convenience stores to big box retailers.
                
                    
                    Damian Dovarganes/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

But now, there's no federal recourse — so when food assistance disappears, SNAP recipients are forced to make difficult choices. Earlier this year, Propel, an app that helps users check their SNAP balance, surveyed individuals who said they were victims of SNAP theft. A majority of respondents said they skipped or ate fewer meals as a result. Nearly half said they borrowed money or went into debt, while more than a third said they struggled to pay their bills or rent.

"That's the real kind of human cost of SNAP benefits being stolen," says Jimmy Chen, the CEO of Propel.

Then, there's shame. After Mary Barclay from Massachusetts saw her food assistance vanish, she recalled her SNAP caseworker faulting her for not taking more security precautions, like locking her EBT card. When Barclay went to the police, she says her story was met with skepticism.

"They made me feel as if I had something to do with it," she says.

In early 2025, California became the first state to start issuing chip-enabled EBT cards. It wasn't a silver bullet, but over the next several months, the state reported a consistent and rapid decline in SNAP theft.

So far, fewer than a third of states have upgraded or plan to upgrade their EBT cards, according to the USDA. States are addressing skimming in other ways, but most of them put the burden on SNAP recipients to be hypervigilant — like changing their card's PIN number on a monthly basis or keeping their cards locked until they're ready to make a purchase.

"It can be difficult for some people to do that if you don't have a cellphone, for example, that has the app that allows you to do the locking," says Larin from the GAO.

Kathryn Larin is a director at the Government Accountability Office. The agency has been reviewing SNAP fraud prevention efforts for years.
                
                    
                    Nathan Howard/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

On the law enforcement side, federal and state authorities are working to find and remove skimming devices. But Secret Service agent Peck says operations alone can't solve this problem.

"The issue we run into is the fact that the groups that conduct this fraud aren't afraid to go right back to a store and install again," he says.

The biggest barrier to chip-enabled cards is cost.

In a report published last year, the GAO found that chip-enabled cards are about 10 times more expensive to produce than magnetic strip ones. The initial transition alone can cost states millions of dollars upfront.

The USDA supports chip adoption, but it provides limited funds to help states do so. For instance, last year, the department awarded seven states a combined total of $5 million to address fraud.

Starting this month, states have fewer federal dollars to operate the food assistance program altogether. That's because of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut federal funding for states' operational costs by half. At the same time, the law requires state SNAP agencies to focus on reducing their payment error rate — which is a measure of overpayments and underpayments to SNAP recipients — or they'll face harsh financial penalties.

Gina Plata-Nino, the SNAP director for the Food Research & Action Center, says these changes will make it harder for states to combat skimming.

" The likelihood of states being able to switch to chip-tap technology without federal support is going to be even more less likely," she says.

At least five states have said they plan to delay issuing chip cards or related investments as a result of the federal funding changes, according to a survey conducted by the American Public Human Services Association and the Urban Institute earlier this year.

While modernizing SNAP may be costly and slow, the country has done it before. When states switched from paper food stamps to electronic benefits in the early 2000s, it was largely driven by a desire to prevent food stamps from getting lost, stolen or sold. They did so through federal legislation.

In recent years, Congress has introduced legislation to upgrade EBT cards nationwide or replace stolen food benefits. Right now, the Senate version of the Farm Bill, which provides funding for an array of programs, includes a provision to move toward chips. But the House version does not, meaning it's unclear if the measure will make the final cut. Although the program has bipartisan support, Congress is at a major impasse over SNAP — in particular, the hundreds of millions of dollars possibly imposed on states with high payment error rates.

" The conversation about boosting cybersecurity standards is hard to make as long as Republicans refuse to restore the food assistance," says Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR), who has been pushing for more secure EBT cards since the Biden administration. " What I'm committed to doing is getting both of these over the finish line."

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) says he has been pushing to modernize food assistance cards since the Biden administration.
                
                    
                    Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

Back in Indiana, Lewis' stolen food assistance has had a ripple effect. Her mother, Johna Hammontree, says she typically lives paycheck to paycheck, but has been stretching every dollar to ensure her daughter and granddaughter do not go hungry.

"It's really, really rough for me already," Hammontree says. "But I will take from my rent money, my bill money, my grocery money … Whatever I need to pull from financially to make sure that she's okay."

During the month without food assistance, Lewis says she has been able to get by with help from her mother.
                
                    
                    Octavio Jones for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Celebrating the complexity of the natural world and the importance of protecting it, this year’s competition has attracted a record-breaking number of entries

A poignant image (see below) of a female elephant carrying her dead calf in the Huab River Valley, Namibia, has won the top prize in this year’s wildlife photography competition.

Italian photographer Federico Veronesi claimed the overall title of wildlife photographer of the year with his shot, The Aftermath, which offers a glimpse into elephant behaviour and the possible expression of grief in animals.

Run by London’s Natural History Museum, the annual competition received a record-breaking 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories this year.

“This photograph works on so many levels,” said Kathy Moran, chair of the judging panel. “Emotionally it’s a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant. Intellectually it’s proof that animals have cognition. This photograph says it all!”

The winner of the competition’s youth category was British photographer Oscar Whitfield, who lives in Zimbabwe. His image, Labour of Love, captures a dung beetle pushing a ball of dung across dusty ground, highlighting the remarkable effort behind the insect’s everyday work.

Now in its 62nd year, the competition continues to use photography to deepen our understanding of the natural world, capturing its beauty and complexity and the importance of protecting it.

'The Aftermath'. Winner, Behaviour: mammals and overall, Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026. Federico Veronesi (Italy) witnesses a powerful moment of an elephant carrying a dead calf, a rare glimpse into complex animal behaviours. Credit: Federico Veronesi, courtesy Wildlife Photographer of the Year

For the first time in its history, both the adult and young overall winners were recognised for black and white images.

“This year’s winning photographs demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently,” said Dr Doug Gurr, director of the Natural History Museum. “Together they remind us that every species plays a role in the complex web of life, and why understanding and protecting the natural world has never been more important.”

An exhibition of the winning images launches on Friday 16 October at the Natural History Museum. More information can be found here.

An influencer has been furiously slammed online after she posed amid the rubble and destruction in Panama following the devastating earthquake last week.

Popular social media star Gracie Bon, who has nearly 12 million followers on Instagram, came under fierce fire after she shared a series of photos of herself standing among destroyed buildings on Sunday.

One image showed her standing on top of wreckage with her hands up in the air, while another saw her kneeling in front of a broken house as she looked away from the camera.

The social media star donned a pair of blue jeans and a white, button-down crop top that accentuated her curves.

'The reality of my country after the earthquake,' she captioned the post.

'We have to remember that the material is recovered, but life is priceless. Live the present, be grateful for what we have and extend help to those who need it today.'

Bon's post sparked immense backlash, as many rushed to the comment section to bash her for doing a 'photo shoot' amongst the debris and accused her of using the tragedy for content.

'I would never take a picture in the middle of a tragedy, people and their stuff,' wrote one user. 'Strength to those going through a difficult time right now.'

Bon's post sparked immense backlash, as many rushed to the comment section to bash her for doing a 'photo shoot' amongst the debris and accused her of using the tragedy for content, however, she claimed it was posted to try to help get donations for victims

'Unbelievable... Just for looking for likes,' slammed another.

'Posing with someone else's misfortune must be a joke,' someone else added.

'"How do I make this about me?" What a need to go out posing in the middle of a disaster,' read a fourth comment.

A fifth said: 'I can't believe she actually asked someone to take pictures of her in front of someone's destroyed house.'

'Did you seriously hire a photographer to go to the affected area to take some photos?' asked a different user.

'There is a huge difference between documenting a tragedy to raise awareness and using the location where it occurred as a backdrop for a photograph,' pointed out another outraged fan.

The massive magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit Panama southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a village of just over 100 residents in Herrera province, on Friday.

Reports of collapsed buildings, split roads and caved-in roofs emerged after the quake, with authorities saying damage was concentrated in central Panama.

No deaths have been reported, but at least 27 people were injured and nearly 900 homes have been damaged, according to Reuters.

Amid the backlash, Bon defended herself in a comment, explaining that she posted the photos to try to show the 'reality of her country' after the earthquake because 'many news [sites] don't show it.'

'CONTEXT: These photos are the reality of the country. Many news [sites] don't show it, many media says "Panama is fine" and they don't show the reality of the affected areas, the people who lost their homes,' she wrote.

She said she wanted to encourage her followers to 'make donations' and knew that if she 'appeared in the photos' they would have a 'better reach.'

'I decided to appear in my photos because I want people to make donations and if I appear in my photos they have a better reach on MY NETWORKS than if I put the images alone,' she continued.

'I'm not in a photoshoot or posing, I'm telling y'all "Look, this is how Panama really is."'

'But you have a damaged heart that prefers to insult and not help the cause,' she added to her haters.

The massive magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit Panama southwest of Pitaloza Arriba, a village of just over 100 residents in Herrera province, on Friday

'If I hadn't been in the picture, would it be okay? The [more important] question is: What is everyone doing to contribute?'

Earlier that day, Bon shared a video of herself stocking up on supplies like cases of bottled water and bags of rice to donate to victims.

She was then seen traveling to the area and handing them out to families.

'Panama needs us. While some today are fortunate enough to be safe in our homes, there are families who have lost almost everything and do not know where they will sleep tonight,' she captioned it.

'Today I bring a grain of [rice], what to us is little, to someone else it may mean so much.'

She also included addresses of places where people can drop off 'water, non-perishable food, hygiene products, diapers and basic necessities' to donate.

'If you can't donate, sharing is also a way to help,' she added.

Bon posted a video addressing the backlash on Monday, insisting that she hadn't made any money from the post.

'Instead of talking about [the families who lost their homes], they are talking about a picture of me,' she said.

'Many are only behind the keyboard criticizing and they do not [answer] the question, "What have you done so far to help Panama?"

'Tomorrow you will forget about my photo, but that family will remain without a home.'

'There are people who get more outraged by a photo than by seeing families lose everything. Sometimes the problem is not what we do, but the eyes with which you decide to see it,' she added in the caption. 'Let's help Panama.'

By Yunior Rivas

October 12, 2026

Federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington-area home Monday, just 22 days before the Minnesota Democrat faces reelection. The extraordinary move against a sitting member of Congress drew scrutiny over the Trump administration’s departure from longstanding Department of Justice (DOJ) guidance meant to prevent federal law enforcement from influencing elections.

Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative arm of ICE, carried out the search pursuant to a warrant obtained by the DOJ.

The investigation reportedly concerns Omar’s immigration history, including allegations of fraud that she has repeatedly denied. DOJ has not publicly detailed the evidence underlying the investigation or disclosed why agents executed the search so close to the election.

DOJ said only that the action was part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation.”

Join 350,000 readers who rely on our daily and weekly newsletters for the latest in voting, elections and democracy.

The timing is especially notable because DOJ’s own rules caution prosecutors and agents against taking actions that could affect an election — or even create the perception that they are doing so.

The Justice Manual states that federal prosecutors and agents “may never select the timing” of investigative steps, charges or public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or giving an advantage or disadvantage to a candidate or political party. Any action likely to raise even the perception of such interference requires consultation with DOJ’s Public Integrity Section.

Separate DOJ rules require Public Integrity Section consultation in all investigations involving members of Congress, including before obtaining a search warrant for property belonging to a lawmaker. DOJ also requires urgent reports to department leadership for investigations involving declared candidates for federal office.

It is not yet clear whether those procedures were followed before agents searched Omar’s home.

“The Trump DOJ tears up yet another long-standing policy/norm, this one of refusing to take actions like this before an election,” immigration policy expert Aaron Reichlin-Melnick wrote following reports of the raid. “The DOJ today, after not even two years of Trump, is a rotten shell of what it once was; untrusted by sizeable portions of the federal judiciary, hollowed out at the core, and run without principle.”

DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The existence of a judicially authorized warrant means a judge found probable cause sufficient to permit the search. But the warrant itself does not resolve the separate question of why DOJ chose to execute such an overt law-enforcement action against a candidate less than a month before Election Day.

The Justice Department has long treated that distinction as significant. Further election-year guidance dating back to at least 2008 has emphasized that “politics must play no role” in investigative or charging decisions and that prosecutors should exercise particular caution around overt investigative steps close to elections. Similar guidance was subsequently issued across administrations.

Omar, who is seeking reelection to Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District, accused the administration of using federal law enforcement against a political opponent.

“Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar wrote in response. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.”

The search comes after months of public statements by senior Trump administration officials about investigating Omar.

Vice President JD Vance previously accused Omar of immigration fraud without providing evidence and said publicly that he and other administration officials were discussing how to investigate her and “build the case necessary” to pursue her.

President Donald Trump has also repeatedly singled out Omar, a Somali-born Muslim who became a U.S. citizen and was elected to Congress in 2018. As recently as this weekend, Trump attacked Omar at a rally and suggested that Vance and administration officials were investigating her.

Those attacks have unfolded alongside Trump’s broader bursts of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric.

Democratic officials immediately blasted the timing of Monday’s search.

Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin called it “a new low for the Trump administration,” pointing specifically to the decision to search “the home of a U.S. congresswoman weeks out from Election Day.”

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) similarly highlighted the timing, writing: “Twenty-two days away from the midterm election, another politicized ‘investigation.’ Straight out of the authoritarian playbook.”

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Democratic Whip Katherine Clark and Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar also condemned the search, calling it “deeply disturbing” and saying it raised “serious questions” about what they described as the Trump administration’s weaponization of the federal government against political adversaries.

The Democratic leaders pointed to Trump’s years of attacks on Omar and emphasized the timing of the search less than a month before the midterms.

“Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family,” they said.

They also vowed congressional scrutiny, saying the public deserved transparency and promising “full accountability” for what they called an abuse of power by the Department of Homeland Security and DOJ.

The Trump administration continued airing taxpayer-funded ads promoting President Donald Trump after a federal judge ordered the campaign halted, then told the court that an internal email delay was to blame.

Iran’s top national security official on Sunday called Washington’s response to Tehran’s demands over the Strait of Hormuz “inadequate” and threatened to strike American-linked undersea communications cables, data centers, and artificial intelligence facilities across the region if war resumes.

Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, the powerful body overseeing the Islamic Republic’s national security and defense policies, delivered the warning as Tehran sought concessions from President Donald Trump’s administration despite an ongoing U.S. naval blockade and mounting economic pressure.

Speaking to Iranian state broadcaster Press TV, Rezaei put the value of American-linked technology infrastructure in the region at more than $2 trillion and warned that those assets could become targets in another war.

“The pulse of the American economy in this region runs through our part of the world,” he said, warning that previously excluded infrastructure, including undersea cables and artificial intelligence facilities, would be targeted if fighting resumed.

The threat goes beyond earlier Iranian demands to impose fees on undersea communications cables passing through the Strait of Hormuz, raising the prospect of attacks on infrastructure supporting international communications, financial transactions, and technology services throughout the region.

Rezaei’s remarks came as Tehran pressed Washington to accept seven conditions for reopening the strategic waterway and resuming negotiations, including lifting the American naval blockade and restrictions on Iranian oil sales.

The Iranian official asserted that Washington had accepted some of Tehran’s demands but did not identify which ones, and the Trump administration has not publicly acknowledged agreeing to any of the conditions.

“We are not in the process of responding to the Americans. They have responded to us, and we consider their response inadequate,” Rezaei said.

He also insisted that Iran would not return to its previous negotiating framework, while maintaining that Tehran had not abandoned diplomacy.

Trump had already rejected Tehran’s earlier proposal, which sought American concessions in exchange for reopening Hormuz, telling reporters, “I reject their proposal.”

The president has nevertheless kept diplomatic channels open, describing recent exchanges with Tehran as “productive discussions” while maintaining the blockade and refusing to retreat from his demand that Iran be prevented from obtaining a nuclear weapon.

Trump also said last week that he did not intend to launch new attacks against Iran before the November midterm elections, although he has repeatedly left open the possibility of renewed military action if negotiations fail.

“We’re going to win,” Trump said during earlier remarks on the negotiations. “As far as I’m concerned, it’s going to be one way or the other. And it’s going to go pretty quickly.”

The administration’s objections extend beyond Tehran’s demands over Hormuz to its refusal to make the nuclear concessions Washington considers essential to any broader agreement.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz dismissed Iran’s earlier proposal as a “garbage deal,” emphasizing that Trump would not accept an agreement allowing the regime to continue pursuing nuclear weapons.

Vice President JD Vance similarly said last week that Tehran must meaningfully reduce its uranium-enrichment capabilities to secure an agreement.

Iranian officials, however, have continued rejecting those demands.

Mohammad Eslami, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, said Thursday that Tehran would neither relinquish its asserted right to enrich uranium nor surrender its existing enriched uranium stockpile.

Asked whether Iran would abandon enrichment, Eslami responded, “Under no circumstances.”

Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the administration’s campaign to cripple Iran’s economy had moved beyond maximum pressure to “absolute isolation,” as Washington seeks to cut off the regime’s remaining sources of revenue and access to international financial markets.

Through Operation Economic Outcast, the Treasury Department has targeted Iran’s oil exports, shadow-fleet shipping network, and sanctions-evasion operations while tightening restrictions on the regime’s access to overseas assets.

Bessent pointed to the halt in new Iranian crude shipments, the collapse of the rial, and dwindling foreign currency reserves as evidence of the mounting pressure on Tehran, describing an economy increasingly unable to sustain normal activity.

The Treasury secretary suggested that continued economic isolation could ultimately force a breakthrough, comparing the uncertainty surrounding Iran’s future to the sudden collapse of the Berlin Wall.

“I don’t know how this ends. You never know how this ends. The Berlin Wall just came down one day,” he said.

Washington’s economic offensive is backed by a U.S. naval blockade that has sharply curtailed Iranian oil exports while allowing shipments from neighboring Gulf producers to continue.

On Saturday, U.S. Central Command announced that an American fighter jet disabled the Panama-flagged cargo vessel M/V Ocean Molica, also known as Arika Sun, after it ignored repeated warnings and attempted to breach the blockade following its departure from an Iranian port.

The precision strike disabled the vessel’s propulsion system without injuring its crew.

Since the blockade resumed in July, CENTCOM has turned back 135 vessels, disabled four commercial ships, and destroyed ten tankers linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ shadow fleet.

Despite the blockade, Rezaei insisted Tehran would retain authority over the Strait of Hormuz, including the ability to impose charges related to shipping security, insurance, and environmental protection — conditions Washington has repeatedly rejected.

Iranian forces have also threatened vessels using routes they consider unauthorized, amid additional attacks on commercial shipping through the waterway.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attributed several recent tanker incidents to vessels encountering naval mines, although those accounts have not been independently confirmed.

Iran’s threats have also extended to American military forces as additional U.S. assets move toward the region.

On Sunday, an IRGC spokesman posted an image depicting a missile system targeting an American aircraft carrier, accompanied by the message: “We are waiting.”

The warning came amid reports of further American military deployments and continued preparations for possible operations against Iran, despite Trump’s decision to hold off on new strikes before the midterm elections.

For now, Washington is maintaining its blockade and tightening economic pressure while leaving open the possibility of a negotiated settlement, with Trump making clear that the confrontation will ultimately be resolved “one way or the other.”

And as a stand-up comic, she must do that every time she steps on stage.

Now, she is combining her two careers, taking the skills she’s learned on stage and bringing them to her fellow researchers. Together with two colleagues — researcher Myeshia Shelby and comic Kelsie Huff — Copeland-Hardin created “Reading and Working the Room,” a free-to-use workshop and curriculum that teaches scientists in similar situations to use on-stage techniques to better engage with the communities they’re researching. 
Copeland-Hardin has been drawn to the world of comedy since she was a child — she even listed “stand-up comedian” as her future career of choice in her school yearbook as a 9-year-old. However, it was not until 2019, after nearly 10 years as a researcher, that she indulged that dream.

“I started comedy to cope with a lot of the stress and isolation that I felt in graduate school,” she said.

Though her two careers may seem unrelated, “Reading and Working the Room” shows how they intersect. Much of Copeland-Hardin’s work involves community-engaged research, which brings together researchers and community members and places them on equal footing.

“You work with community instead of on communities,” Copeland-Hardin said. And given that she and her colleagues often work with Chicago communities that have been “historically harmed” by scientists, she said, “the trust-building process is important and required.”

On stage, Copeland-Hardin (who performs under the name LT) is an expert at winning over an audience. In September, she appeared as part of The Lincoln Lodge’s Future of Comedy Festival.  Early in her set, she asked the crowd, “Y’all are familiar with Froot Loops, right?” This simple question turned her monologue into a conversation, inviting the  audience to be a part of the show.

There was an ease to her performance that belied how intricately the jokes were woven together. She introduced complicated scientific topics, but her audience, once invited into her world, was more than willing to listen to a story about dissecting the brain of a fruit fly. And once she delivered the punchline (which is worth hearing, unspoiled, in person), the crowd was ready to follow her anywhere.

She hopes the curriculum can help her fellow researchers borrow techniques like building audience trust in order to address what she feels is a meaningful gap in scientific training: Researchers know how to communicate with academic audiences, but not necessarily with the general public. The curriculum makes it plain that not every research conversation needs to be funny in and of itself; but by using the stage savoir-faire explained throughout the workshop to personally engage those they address, researchers can repair the trust lost in some of these communities and walk away with better, clearer data.
“Reading and Working the Room” is designed as a workshop curriculum anyone can teach or read on their own.

“Anyone who is interested can go to the link (at zenodo.org) … and they can download the slides,” she said. “They can download the facilitator’s guide.”

She credits Research!America for providing the  initial funding, as they were specifically looking for curricula that addressed a gap in scientific training as it relates to public engagement.

“As scientists, it is our responsibility to share our information with the public,” Copeland-Hardin said.

Which, at her core, is why Copeland-Hardin entered both of her fields.

“I have a strong desire to connect,” she said.

And be it with an audience, her community, or even a fruit fly, Copeland-Hardin always finds ways to do just that.

Category 4 Hurricane Simon threatened coastal communities and popular tourist destinations along Mexico’s Pacific Coast on Sunday, as authorities urged residents to take shelter.

The international airport in Puerto Vallarta, a resort city on the shore of Bahía de Banderas, suspended operations as the powerful storm moved north-northwest offshore, along the coast of Mexico.

After initial models projected that Simon would make landfall on Sunday, the storm changed course and its path is getting harder to predict. It’s now expected to remain offshore through Monday, and the models are split on whether it will actually move inland or stay entirely offshore.

The hurricane is moving at a speed of 7 mph with maximum winds of 140 mph, according to the 1 p.m. ET report issued Sunday by the US National Hurricane Center (NHC).

The “extremely dangerous” storm is about 85 miles west-northwest of Manzanillo, a coastal city in the Mexican state of Colima, and 65 miles south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes, in the state of Jalisco, according to the NHC report.

The national coordinator of Mexico’s Civil Protection Agency (CNPC), Laura Velázquez Alzúa, told reporters that despite the hurricane not yet making landfall, it is still “very close to the Mexican coast.”

But authorities are urging residents to take shelter, as the storm’s path is still somewhat uncertain.

“We ask that you remain vigilant,” Velázquez said.

The coordinator said that the effects of Simon — which include “strong winds, high waves, and storm surge,” particularly along the northern coast of Jalisco state — will continue through Monday.

The storm’s current projected path indicates that it has several “probable impacts” on certain states, which is why “Simon concerns us greatly,” Dr. Jorge Zavala, a climate scientist at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, told CNN.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged residents of Jalisco, Colima, Michoacán, and Nayarit to remain in shelter “until an official announcement that the danger has passed” after the CNPC warned of “exceptional rainfall” and “intense winds” in those states.

“The wind and rain will suddenly and deceptively subside, creating an apparent calm that does not mean the danger has passed,” the agency warned in a statement.

Nonessential activities have been suspended, and precautionary evacuations are continuing, Sheinbaum said on Sunday.

Along the boardwalk in Puerto Vallarta, police reminded tourists that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter as the storm approaches, the Associated Press reported.

“We don’t know the extent of the danger yet,” visitor Brenda Villareal told the AP. “We’re just starting to see what’s going on.”

Mexico’s Navy deployed more than 4,600 personnel to help with the response to the incoming storm, along with excavation equipment, heavy machinery, and other emergency resources.

As Simon moves closer to the coast, its heavy rain has already caused damage.

Federal authorities are working to restore power in some areas, including Acapulco, a coastal city in Mexico’s Guerrero state that was devastated three years ago by Hurricane Otis.

In Manzanillo, the Navy helped remove water from some houses that were flooded by the storm.

Manzanillo resident Cecilia Palomar told Reuters that the water started rising in her home at dawn.

“It had risen before, but not like this,” Palomar said. “Beds, refrigerators, heaters, all the furniture got wet, the whole house is flooded.”

The Pacific Airport Group (GAP) reported that the Puerto Vallarta airport will remain closed until 10 a.m. ET on Monday. Flights at the airport in Manzanillo were also suspended for the day.

Uriel Blanco contributed to this report.

Friday's weaker-than-expected jobs report may feel especially lousy for men.

Women outnumbered men in the workforce for eight straight months as of September, according to an analysis of government data by Indeed. That's the longest stretch since 2010, the job search platform found.

"Back then, the gap emerged because men were losing jobs," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed. "This time, it's because women are gaining them."

Across the board, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Friday that U.S. payrolls grew by 29,000 jobs on net in September, lower than economists consensus forecast for an increase of 84,000.

Men represented slightly over half of net job growth in September, according to a CNBC analysis of Friday's BLS data. A month prior, men represented just 2% of payroll growth.

Despite the monthly increase, the seasonally adjusted number of employed men in the U.S. was lower by about 1.2 million in September compared with a year ago. Women's employment rose by more than 650,000 in the same period.

This divergence in labor market performance by gender can be partially explained by which industries are growing, according to Stahle.

Healthcare, a key driver of the U.S. job market for the last several years, accounted for more than half of overall payroll expansion in September. Women make up nearly four out of every five workers in the sector.

But the BLS said in its Friday release that healthcare hired at a slower pace in September than on average over the past year. Because of that, women may not have gotten as big of a boost from the sector as they did in prior months.

Monthly payroll contraction in industries with a higher share of women workers like government also diluted overall gains for women in the month, Stahle said.

Mary Butler

For many years the pace of investment in mental health has been slow, but Minister of State for Mental Health Mary Butler said this week that this year’s allocation to mental health is the largest the state has ever seen.

The group, Mental Health Reform, has welcomed the allocation of an additional €108 million for mental health services in Budget 2027, which brings the overall mental health budget to more than €1.65 billion, representing a 7% increase on 2026.

The funding will allow for additional out-of-hours ‘Solace’ peer-support cafés in Carlow, Louth, Wexford, North Tipperary and Dublin, with the minister stating that where these cafés are located, a reduction in the number of presentations to emergency departments is being seen.

However, there is a point of criticism of the minister.

At the post-budget health press conference this week, Butler confirmed that a new mother and baby psychiatric unit will be located at St Vincent’s Hospital, however, it will not be delivered next year.

The minister said it could take three to four years before it is opened, which will be 13 years after it was first recommended. Not really good enough.

Minister for Culture, Communications and Sport Patrick O'Donovan.                    Alamy Stock Photo

Patrick O’Donovan and RTÉ (oh, and the culture card)

Dear oh dear. Where do we start? What a week it has been for Arts Minister Patrick O’Donovan.

Budget week began with news that his culture card idea was dead in the water (though Tánaiste Simon Harris denied this, probably just to be kind to his party colleague).

It had been floated weeks ago as a definite for the budget. However, when O’Donovan got in the room with Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers, he was told his numbers didn’t add up and there was no money to give every 16-year-old in the country €100 to go see arts events.

There were reports O’Donovan stormed out of the meeting, though he denied this later in the week. Chambers said it is not happening in 2027; O’Donovan said he will bring a memo to cabinet on how he plans to develop it. Either way, it’s not happening anytime soon.

So, all in all, not a great week for the minister.

Rep. Nancy Mace (R-SC) started a social media firestorm late Thursday after implying that the so-called “Cornell 7” assault case was not rape but consensual.

“IDK who needs to hear this, but a consensual gangbang is not a rape,” Mace wrote on X in a message viewed more than 2.6 million times since she posted it late Thursday:

The alleged victim, a female Cornell student identified anonymously as “Jane Doe,” has accused seven fraternity brothers of raping her in a lawsuit, prompting local authorities to reopen a criminal investigation for a grand jury review.

Mace’s viral post came after a trove of texts surfaced this week showing the accuser engaged in friendly chats with some of the men after the October 2024 sexual encounter, telling them that they shouldn’t “feel any shame.”

“Our body our choice,” the accuser wrote in one.

However, the woman’s attorney in her civil case, Thomas Giuffra, told the New York Post Thursday that the seemingly exonerating texts for the men were part of the early stage of her mentally and emotionally processing that night as she “was going through denial, shame, and ultimately acceptance.”

The accuser’s recollections changed in part when she saw group chats between the frat brothers advertising “free p—y,” including one later bragging that she’d been part of an “eightsome,” the Post reported.

Reaction to Mace’s post was no doubt fueled by dramatic claims she had made on the floor of Congress in February 2025 claiming that, based on videos and photographic evidence she allegedly found, her ex fiancée Patrick Bryant had participated in the apparent rape of an incapacitated woman.

Mace told Congress, “The two of them, the three of them business partners, the two of them had their phones out just like this. Filming her as she was being raped.”

She continued, “And she was completely laid out. There was no movement. There was no life. I couldn’t even tell if this young woman was alive.”

Bryant emphatically denied the claims and filed a lawsuit accusing her of “blackmail,” which was ultimately thrown out by a Charleston judge.

An investigation by state authorities into the allegations made on the House floor against Mace’s former fiancée still reportedly remains open nearly two years later.

Her advocacy in the speech on the house floor triggered charges of hypocrisy among the thousands of reactions she received for her comment on the Cornell 7.

“Welp, so much for your ‘crusade’ for women’s rights!” one person wrote.

But not all condemned her.

“And making false rape accusations to police or in court should carry the same penalty as rape,” wrote one responder.

The case has created some sharp divides, much like the high-profile 2006 alleged gang rape case where Duke University lacrosse players were falsely accused of sexually assaulting an exotic dancer at a team party in Durham, North Carolina. Authorities and news outlets were quick to believe the accuser, who was later completely discredited and the local district attorney ended up resigning in disgrace.

The recent lawsuit triggered an explosion of national interest several years after the incident occurred, with the local prosecutor on the case, as Breitbart News reported, explaining why no charges were filed in 2024.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said the accuser’s story today is different than the one his office considered after the incident.

He explained to ABC News, “She never says that she was drugged without her knowledge. She admits to taking drugs and alcohol voluntarily and with knowledge. She does not allege that she was forced to engage in any acts. She does not say that she was physically helpless or unconscious or incapacitated at any point during the time at the fraternity house.”

As for Mace’s future, that remains unclear.

The three-term Congresswoman finished a distant fifth in her state’s Republican primary for governor earlier this year.

Mace has said she will transition into the private sector after she leaves office but promises to remain active commenting on politics.
