The House of Representatives voted 220-205 on Tuesday to extend funding for the government at existing levels through Dec. 4.

Six Democrats joined with Republicans to advance the bill. The government is currently set to run out of money at the end of September, just before the midterm elections.

House Republican hard-liners have lately been holding up legislation in a so far fruitless effort to pressure their Senate colleagues into passing President Trump's election overhaul bill, the SAVE America Act. The legislation would require voters to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote and photo ID when casting a ballot. After some speculation the government funding bill could be caught up in that fight, the lawmakers let it proceed without incident.

Democratic leaders opposed the funding extension, writing in a statement that the bill "fails to block funding for Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine."

"Their my-way-or-the-highway approach has consistently failed to address the high cost of living or meet the needs of the American people," said Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif.

Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., criticized Democrats ahead of the vote for their opposition to the funding plan.

"They do this to try to score political points. I think they're making the wrong calculation here," Johnson said.

The bill now heads to the Senate, where it will require Democratic support to clear the 60-vote threshold required to pass most legislation through the chamber.

The funding effort comes after two record-setting government shutdowns during this Congress. Democrats forced a 45-day total government shutdown last year in a failed attempt to force congressional Republicans to extend federal healthcare subsidies. That shutdown was, at the time, the longest in U.S. history.

A 76-day Department of Homeland Security shutdown followed at the beginning of this year after federal immigration enforcement personnel killed two American citizens in Minnesota. Democrats refused to support funding for the agency unless Republicans backed reforms, including restrictions on face coverings and the deployment of body cameras for immigration enforcement officers. Ultimately, Republicans used a parliamentary procedure known as reconciliation to fund the agency on a party-line vote for the rest of President Trump's time in office.

The bill's path through the Senate is uncertain. Speaking with reporters at the Capitol on Tuesday, Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he would put a government funding plan to a vote before senators leave Washington for the August recess.

If Republicans are unable to reach a deal with Democrats to extend government funding, Thune said he would consider turning back to the reconciliation process to pass the bill on a strictly party-line basis.

"I hope that's not necessary," he said.

Victor Davis Hanson’s latest book, ‘The Counter Revolution,’ provides a definitive account of Donald Trump’s unprecedented political comeback.

Americans love a comeback kid. It’s why we celebrate Muhammad Ali, who, after being stripped of his title and barred from professional boxing in 1967 for refusing the military draft, returned to reclaim the heavyweight championship in 1974 against George Foreman in the “Rumble in the Jungle.” It’s why we honor people such as Robert Downey Jr., who recovered from drug addictions and arrests to become one of the highest-grossing actors of all time. And, as prolific author and historian Victor Davis Hanson shows in his new book The Counter Revolution: The Fall and Rise of Donald Trump and the MAGA Movement, it’s also why so many Americans find President Donald Trump so compelling.

Though American politics has had its fair share of comebacks — Nixon losing the 1960 presidential election only to win it in 1968; Grover Cleveland losing the presidency in 1888 and then regaining in 1892 — none can compare with that of Trump. Abandoned by many of his allies after the January 6 riot and hounded by a long list of investigations that seemed destined to end his career if not bankrupt him, Trump somehow overcame every doubter and waged a political campaign for the ages that ultimately returned him to the White House. Regardless of how it ends, it’s an incredible story, and Hanson deserves credit for giving us the definitive account.

Hanson reminds us that after the results of the November 2020 presidential elections, things looked bleak for Trump. Appointees, both current and former, were competing with each other to prove their disdain for their seemingly ruined president. After the January 6 riots, which were exclusively blamed on Trump even though Nancy Pelosi was on record admitting, “I take responsibility for the security failures of the Capitol that day,” administration officials ran for the doors.

Two days after January 6, Twitter banned Trump “for life” and Facebook followed suit six months later. When Trump tried to switch to the social media app Parler, Amazon, Apple, and Google all removed the app from their app stores. Even the banking industry largely closed its doors — Deutsche Bank announced it would no longer do business with Trump or the Trump Organization; Signature Bank closed two personal accounts held by Trump; and JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America said they would no longer finance future Trump Organization projects. “Popular wisdom held that his political career was over,” writes Hanson.

Between 2021 and 2025, Trump was “targeted in five different courtrooms, facing ninety-one felony charges and some $500 million in combined fines.” In August 2022, the FBI raided his home, making him the only ex-president to enjoy that honor. When he ran for office again, almost half the states made attempts to ban him from the ballot.

The sheer force of anti-Trump activity after 2020 — which included efforts by current and former members of the federal workforce, academia, mainstream media, and senior retired and active-duty members of the U.S. military — is incredible to consider, given, whatever one thinks of the man, his administration left behind a 1.2 percent inflation rate, near record-low peacetime unemployment, a secure border, and the Operation Warp Speed COVID-19 vaccine. Or consider how much energy was invested in vilifying Trump for the January 6 fiasco when compared to the several-month post-George Floyd riots, which in addition to prompting a mob attack on the White House, caused 35 deaths, $2 billion in damage, about 1,500 injured officers. Trump Derangement Syndrome is real.

Given the forces arrayed against him, how could a seemingly politically impotent Trump have any chance of a resurgent campaign? Hanson lists several critical sources for this political resurrection. how_chinas_attempt_to_ban_a_book_backfir:
Emily Feng’s ‘Let Only Red Flowers Bloom: Identity and Belonging in Xi Jinping’s China,’ has become an important book for understanding China’s authoritarian abuses.

On July 15, 2026, Hong Kong national security police raided two independent bookstores and arrested five people on suspicion of displaying and selling publications with “seditious intention” under the city’s national security laws. One of the books reportedly seized was Emily Feng’s Let Only Red Flowers Bloom: Identity and Belonging in Xi Jinping’s China.

Feng is an American journalist born to Chinese parents in Connecticut. From 2019 to 2022, she served as an international correspondent for National Public Radio in Beijing, where her reporting highlighted critical issues such as the mass incarceration of Uyghur Muslims. In 2022, after a reporting trip, Chinese authorities barred her from returning.

Her case reflects a broader pattern of the regime’s tightening grip on press freedom. Spring 2020 saw China expel about nineteen reporters from major outlets like The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Washington Post, in retaliation for U.S. restrictions on Chinese state media. In the years that followed, foreign correspondents continued to face visa delays and denials, shortened press credentials, constant surveillance, online smear campaigns, physical obstruction, and threats of legal action.

Ethnic Chinese journalists with foreign passports often endure harsher treatment, because the Communist Party regards all ethnic Chinese, regardless of citizenship, as owing loyalty to the motherland. Therefore, state media labeled Feng a “race traitor” and a “banana” (yellow on the outside, white on the inside), for her reporting that shed light on the regime’s oppressive practices.

After being denied re-entry to China, Feng relocated to Taiwan. While her personal journey inspired her to write the book, she deliberately keeps herself in the background, allowing the experiences of others to take center stage. The narrative is a collection of intimate portraits of nearly two dozen individuals whose lives intersect with the state’s strict definition of being “good” Chinese, including a human rights lawyer who lost his license for representing a Hong Kong activist, an Inner Mongolian teacher punished for supporting his mother tongue, and a Uyghur family torn apart by internment camps.

This book stands out for two main reasons. First, while it references important historical events like the incarceration of Uyghurs starting in 2017, the Hong Kong protests of 2019, and Covid pandemic starting in 2020, Feng treats these as backdrops rather than the main focus. As she notes in the preface, “This is not a history book … it focuses on people living in the present day.” Second, she weaves individual stories around a central theme of identity, suggesting that understanding the Chinese state’s self-perception and its desired citizenry is crucial to grasping its policies.

Feng argues that Xi Jinping’s greatest fear is that the Chinese Communist Party could face a downfall similar to the Soviet Union. To prevent this, Xi aims to eliminate any opportunities for what he deems “incorrect” ideas and thinking. He seeks to mold the Chinese population into “good” Chinese: ethnically Han, Mandarin-speaking, without religious beliefs, and loyal to the Party. Anyone outside this narrow definition, whether in ethnicity, language, faith, or political views, must conform.

Feng points out that this restricted identity has driven oppressive policies in China. For instance, children from Mongolian, Tibetan, and Uyghur communities are subjected to Mandarin-only education and political indoctrination, while adults who promote their mother tongues face intimidation or imprisonment. In Xinjiang, millions of Uyghurs have been detained simply for their ethnicity.

This pressure of conformity extends to Han Chinese citizens as well. Dissenters, including lawyers, citizen journalists, feminists, or anyone who speaks out, risk surveillance, job loss, or worse.

One story that resonates particularly strongly is that of the “chained woman.” In late January 2022, as Beijing prepared for the Winter Olympics, a video surfaced on Douyin (Chinese version of TikTok) showing a disheveled woman, chained by the neck inside a doorless shed in rural Feng County, Jiangsu. She had given birth to eight children. Officials claimed she was legally married and restrained due to schizophrenia, but the public rejected this absurd explanation.

Public outrage led to investigations revealing that the “chained woman” was a victim of human trafficking. This case exposed the human costs of the one-child policy, which resulted in mass female infanticide and a severe gender imbalance, driving many Chinese men, especially in rural areas, to resort to trafficking girls and women for marriage.

To quell public anger, a Xuzhou court sentenced the woman’s husband to nine years in prison and five accomplices to terms ranging from eight to thirteen years for trafficking and abuse. Still, rather than addressing the broad issue of human trafficking, the Chinese government focused on covering it up, fearing it undermined the positive image Xi Jinping seeks to portray.

State media were ordered to suppress coverage, and censors quickly removed online references to her plight. Local police even detained two women who tried to visit her, underscoring the authorities’ commitment to silence. One of the citizen journalists who investigated the story on his own felt so threatened by repeated visits from the authorities that he eventually sought political asylum in the U.S. Foreign journalists such as Feng who tried to report the story were followed and harassed by public security personnel. Even today, who the “chained woman” is and what her real story is remain a mystery.

The book’s title comes from a Hui Muslim man named Yusuf. He wryly referenced Mao Zedong’s short-lived 1956 “Let a hundred flowers bloom” campaign, in which the Party briefly invited criticism only to persecute those who spoke out. Mao later called it a ploy to “entice the snakes out of their caves.” Xi, Yusuf observed, no longer bothers with the pretense. His relentless campaigns to enforce cultural and political conformity amount to a simpler decree: let only red flowers bloom.

The English edition of Feng’s book was published in March 2025 and garnered modest attention. Unlike more confrontational works such as Yang Jisheng’s Tombstone, her critique of the party and its policies is nuanced and rooted in personal stories. This year, her book’s Chinese-language edition was released in Taiwan, sparking significant interest from Beijing. The July 2026 raids on Hong Kong bookstores selling the title aimed to limit its reach, but they had the unintended consequence of driving demand, as the book quickly sold out in Taiwan, leading the publisher to order an emergency reprint of ten thousand copies.

By labeling a meticulously reported account of everyday Chinese lives as seditious, the authorities only reinforced Feng’s main argument. Many individuals now see purchasing and reading this book as a subtle yet powerful act of resistance against a regime committed to enforcing conformity and silencing dissent.

By treating a carefully reported account of ordinary Chinese lives as seditious, the authorities only confirmed Feng’s central argument. The people she profiles refuse to fit the state’s narrow definition of identity, and their stories continue to circulate despite efforts to silence them. For many ethnic Chinese everywhere, buying, reading this book, or even writing a book review,  has become more than an act of curiosity. Rather, it is a quiet, deliberate defiance to an authoritarian system determined to enforce conformity.

TOPICS

systems

Suggests Big Green knows its component prices will remain steady

Hewlett Packard Enterprise has changed its pricing policy and will now honour quoted hardware prices from the day of issue until the kit leaves its factories.

The new policy came into effect on Wednesday.

The back story to this change is the AI boom, which has seen demand for servers, memory, and storage skyrocket, and the prices for critical components rise steadily while also fluctuating from day to day. That chaotic situation saw HPE and other enterprise hardware players change policies so that the price in their quotes was only valid for 14 days. Cisco’s terms were sometimes set at seven days.

That’s obviously difficult for buyers, who often seek a quote for hardware while they are building a business case for a new project. Big price changes could make those projects infeasible.

Yet short-lived quotes also make sense for vendors, who could otherwise give buyers prices that they could only deliver at a loss.

In June, HPE extended the life of its quotes from 14 to 30 days.

Yesterday, the company changed the policy so that quotes that customers agree to remain valid until HPE ships products – at least for purchases of up to $1 million for its own Compute, Storage and GreenLake Flex deals. CRN was first to report the change, which The Register has verified.

HPE says it gives “customers and partners greater pricing certainty and will offer greater simplicity and predictability” – and perhaps for months, because lead times for servers sometimes stretch that far into the future.

The company hasn’t said what has changed to allow it to revise its policies.

Recent news suggests one possible factor: Memory-makers Micron and SK Hynix have struck numerous long-term deals that set long-term prices for their customers. If HPE has such deals in place, it now has greater certainty of its own costs, allowing it to extend the validity of its quotes.

While longer-lived quotes are good news for buyers, they still face inflated prices for hardware. Analyst firm TrendForce recently predicted server memory prices will rise between 13 and 18 percent in calendar Q3, and ongoing tight supply. Rival firm Gartner this week found contract DRAM prices “surged” 90 percent to 95 percent quarter over quarter in the first half of 2026, while NAND flash contract prices rose between 55 and 60 percent.

Gartner also predicted DRAM prices will increase 271 percent, year over year, during 2026.

So while HPE will hold its prices, its quotes may still be eye-poppers if you haven't shopped for hardware lately. ®

Over the last few years, Chinese Android manufacturers have followed Vivo’s example of launching add-on “teleconverter” lenses for their flagship phones, enabling long-distance photography that the phones on their own could never match. Today, Huawei one-upped everybody with the add-on lens for its Mate 90 Pro Max flagship, which is not only a comically huge zoom lens, but also includes its own image sensor.

The 1-inch-type, 50-megapixel RYYB sensor inside the Ruiying Z10 is bigger than any inside the phone itself, so attaching this lens doesn’t just give you better glass, it’s actually a complete overhaul of the camera capabilities. And while other teleconverters have so far had fixed focal lengths, this is a true zoom lens that covers 24–240mm, with a variable aperture of f/2.0-f/4.5. This is almost a camera in its own right, only using the phone for power, processing, and software.

Impressively, Huawei also appears to have designed the lens to attach directly to compatible phones, instead of needing an intermediary case for a mounting point. The obvious downside to the Z10 is that it’s absolutely enormous, even by teleconverter standards — you’re not going to fit this thing in your pocket. But at 346g, it’s still smaller and more portable than even most mirrorless cameras, and you’ll probably be able to take it into venues where cameras aren’t permitted, like concerts and sports matches. Then there’s the price: at ¥5,999 (around $895), this is more expensive than some flagship phones.

Huawei says the Z10 is compatible with the collector’s edition of the Mate 90 Pro Max and its Mate 90 RS variant, the only two models in the new Mate 90 series with the screw-mount around the camera island. They have impressive cameras in their own right, with an f/1.4-f/4.0, 50-megapixel, variable aperture main camera using a 1.1.28-inch-type sensor; a 200-megapixel 4x periscope telephoto with the same size sensor; and a 40-megapixel ultrawide. The 6.9-inch OLED display can hit 12,000 nits of peak brightness, and it’s powered by a 6,800mAh battery and Huawei’s own Kirin 9050 Pro chip. The Mate 90 and Mate 90 Pro are both slightly smaller, with streamlined specs across the board.

Get the FREE App

Get the FREE App

For years, Tui Davidson has been thinking about what happens after death.

The Canberra-based founder of advocacy group Earthly Remains began researching alternatives to traditional burials after the death of a friend's father in 2019.

An urban planner committed to sustainability, he left Ms Davidson questioning why a life lived in service of the environment could not be fittingly farewelled.

Burials require land, materials and maintenance while cremation relies on high-temperature furnaces that release greenhouse gases.

That search eventually led her to a little-known process called natural organic reduction, better known as human composting.

Now, after years of advocacy, Ms Davidson is celebrating a milestone.

Independent Sydney MP Alex Greenwich plans to introduce a bill on Thursday that would pave the way for human composting in NSW.

The process places a body in a vessel with organic materials such as wood chips and straw.

Over several weeks, microbes break down the remains into organic material that can be used in reforestation, soil regeneration or memorial plantings.

The proposal has already attracted a cautious response from NSW Premier Chris Minns.

"I feel a bit weird about it," he told reporters on Sunday.

"I never even heard of that until Alex (Greenwich) mentioned it, so really, going to have to kick the tyres on this one before we automatically agree."

For Ms Davidson, that reaction is understandable.

"People don't like talking about death," she said.

She believes public attitudes are changing, even if the concept sounds confronting.

"Once people get over the idea of composting ... and actually start to think about beautiful nutritious soil and growing things in it ... people really embrace the idea," she said.

Mr Greenwich's bill would allow the state government to establish rules governing human composting facilities, processes and oversight.

The proposal would not replace burial or cremation, he said, but add to the available options.

"This is not about taking away the current options," Mr Greenwich said.

"It's simply providing an alternative for people to choose if they wish to do so.

"We want to be able to give people a choice that is more financially and environmentally sustainable."

Human composting is currently legal in 14 US states, including Washington, California, Colorado and New York, and is also available in Germany.

Advocates say it is gaining momentum internationally as people seek lower-impact end-of-life options.

Seattle-based provider Recompose estimates human composting saves between 0.84 and 1.4 metric tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions compared to traditional methods.

For Ms Davidson, this is key to its appeal.

"Being able to give back at the very end to the planet ... that's a great thing," she said.

She said she would choose the option herself if it became available.

"No doubt about it," she said.

humanity_crossroads_audit:
Both public figures have urged us to be active makers of the world we want our children to inherit

James Valentine meets the pope at the Pearly Gates. This is not the lead-in to a punchline delivered too soon, but a match made in heaven that could help those of us left behind preserve our humanity.

While the wave of grief that followed the Sydney presenter’s passing in April may be slowly subsiding, the brio of his departure has settled deeply with those of us who were part of his vast network of goodwill.

I was lucky to be a small part of this world. For a few years I would run the “people’s poll” for afternoon listeners where we explored everything from our showering habits (58% mornings to 42% evenings) to the opening move in rock-paper-scissors (55% rock).

Like so much of his work, this was not just a frivolous way to pass the time with his audience; what James created with skill and intentionality was a living organism that offered to sustain anyone who chose to join in. This was his gift.

While James was effusively equivocal about religion, I couldn’t help thinking about his earthly contribution as I read the papal encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, released a few weeks ago.

Pope Leo XIV’s letter to the Catholic flock and all people of goodwill is a much-anticipated intervention in the hyper-scaling of so-called artificial intelligence.

It builds on the work of his predecessor, Leo XIII, who he named himself after, whose Rerum Novarum  on the Industrial Revolution asserted the dignity of labour, a clarion call for believers to join unions and work collectively to civilise capital.

The first US-born pontiff, who grew up on the South Side of Chicago, has been dubbed the “woke pope” for his willingness to push back on the Trump administration’s ICE raids and reckless warmongering. To be clear, he is no progressive saint; he was politicised opposing female reproductive rights, while the church’s dark history of abuse remains his cross to bear.

These caveats aside, read on its merits, Magnifica Humanitas offers a moral clarity that has been absent from a public AI discourse that vacillates between existential doom and naive faith.

In forensic detail the pope audits the risks of this technology, from the concentration of wealth and power in the hands of the few, to the automation of state-sponsored killing, to the erasure of cultural diversity and, most pointedly, to the manifest exploitation of those trapped in its production line, particularly those in the global south.

Leo frames the choices we currently face in biblical terms. On one hand a Tower of Babel where humanity is reduced to a brittle uniformity that neutralises difference under the pretence of a single language model. In contrast, he casts the rebuilding of Jerusalem undertaken by Nehemiah as a shared enterprise driven by returning exiles working in communion.

This is the principle of “subsidiarity” where authority is vested in those participating in their community in service of the common good rather than designated up to governments or, more pointedly, corporations.

The idea of distributed power seems counterintuitive coming from the titular head of a unitary religion, but as Dr Michael Walker explains, “subsidiarity” lies at the heart of Catholic social teaching.

Without conscious rebalancing of power, we are left with technology that dehumanises us all by putting the relentless pursuit of the material at the centre of everything.

The alternative? The pope argues we need to get our hands dirty and build together, not as consumers of product but as active makers of the world we want our children to inherit.

In his wonderful tribute in the Sydney Town Hall, Roy Valentine made the point that his father never asked his kids, “What do you want to be?” but rather “How do you want to live?”

This strikes me as more than just an enlightened model of parenting. It is a challenge to all of us to mindfully choose our path at a time when we are told that both anything is possible and resistance is futile.

How do we want to live? In a world where AI agents and companion bots cater to our every whim until we lose the ability to even discern what we actually want? In workplaces where co-pilots erase friction until they can simply fly themselves? In a culture that synthesises the past until there is nothing left to steal? Where we outsource ideation and connection until we are dragged into lonely universes of one, insulated from the friction of other people by an automated layer of a simulated self.

The sense of inevitability around this digital Babel has already taken hold and will take more than a single government or a law or a consumer boycott to change its course. It will take all of us acting in communion to resist these false idols by seeking joy in each other. As the pope writes: “True progress always stems from a heart open to others, an intelligence willing to listen and a will that seeks what unites rather than what separates.” Sounds like someone we know?

How do we want to live? Leo’s encyclical is the invocation to human composition. Now it’s over to us to tap James’ enduring spirit, step in and join the ensemble.

Peter Lewis is the executive director of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host of Burning Platforms, a weekly podcast focusing on the politics of technology. His columns are accredited “Proudly Human”

Some coastal regions were flooded even before the storm made landfall

Hurricane Polo has made landfall along the northern Pacific coast of Mexico, lashing the state of Baja California Sur with life-threatening winds and heavy rain that has already flooded some coastal areas.

Mexican officials said Polo moved ashore just south of the surfing and fishing village of Las Barrancas bringing maximum sustained winds of 110 mph (175 km/h).

Polo is moving northeast and on the forecast track, its core is predicted to continue passing over Baja California Sur before moving inland over the southern part of the Mexican state of Sonora later on Tuesday.

Residents in threatened areas have been encouraged to seek shelter.

Shopkeeper MarÃ­a Palomino, 57, spent the night at a high school which has been turned into a temporary shelter. "If something happens, it's better to come to the shelter," she told AFP news agency.

A whale-watching and fishing guide who was boarding up the facade of his home told AFP the storm was "coming with full force".

The US-based National Hurricane Center (NHC) said that while Polo was expected to weaken as it moved over the Baja California peninsula, it was forecast to still be at hurricane strength when it makes its second landfall in mainland Mexico.

Meteorologists said Polo could dump between 6 and 12 inches (150-300mm) of rain across parts of Baja California Sur, which they warned could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain.

The NHC said a storm surge was also expected to produce significant coastal flooding in areas of onshore winds. "Near the coast, the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves," it said in an update.

Even before Polo made landfall, residents said there were power cuts in Baja California Sur.

US media reported some flooding in the fishing town of Puerto San Carlos and the Associated Press said waves crested sea barriers in the area, where many residents had been evacuated due to the threat.

Flooding has already started in parts of Baja California Sur

Meteorologists said dangerous surf and rip currents were likely to continue along portions of the north-western coast of Mexico and Baja California for the next day or so.

The south of the peninsula is popular with tourists and acts as a base for surfers, sport fishers, and whale watchers.

In Cabo San Lucas, famous for its natural rock arch, authorities had restricted access to the beaches on Monday.

Polo has been slowly moving towards Mexico's coast line for days.

Meteorologists said it was being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El NiÃ±o climate phenomenon, which has led to a more active hurricane season in Pacific waters.

As Polo moves north-east, it is expected to also affect the US, sending a surge of tropical moisture northwards for the next few days leading to excessive rainfall and flash flooding.

Rain has already been falling across Arizona and California but the remains of Polo and another hurricane - named Odalys - will become absorbed into that weather system, boosting the amount of rainfall. These fronts will push eastwards across the southern plains.

Some spots could see as much as 6 or 7 inches of rainfall by Thursday.

States affected include Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah into Tuesday.

I have seen quite a bit of Johan Manzambi at this World Cup. Watching a lot of matches and I do always take an extra bit of interest when Switzerland play, a legacy from when Fabian Schar was pretty much the only high profile quality United player at major tournaments.

I am an early riser anyway but I did make sure I was up for 4am to watch Switzerland this Friday morning, Johan Manzambi and Switzerland taking on Algeria in Vancouver for a place in the last 16. Obviously I wanted to take special notice of the 20-year-old Swiss midfielder with Newcastle United now reported to be in advanced talks to sign him.

All I can say is that I just hope Newcastle United have the Johan Manzambi signing tied up after watching this.

Algeria actually started the better team, only then for Manzambi to put Switzerland in command when from nothing he laid on the opening goal in the 10th minute.

Johan Manzambi with brilliant play as he ran with the ball from just inside the Algeria half, skill and pace as he dribbled into the heart of the opposition defence, beat his opponent before delivering a lovely cutback for Embolo who couldn’t miss.

This set in motion a brilliant performance from Johan Manzambi as he helped Switzerland dominate the match, Ndoye scored on 46 minutes and Switzerland cruised into the last 16.

In his last three matches at this World Cup, Johan Manzambi has scored twice against Bosnia and Herzegovina,, he scored and got an assist against co-hosts Canada to see Switzerland top their group. Now he has assisted that opening goal against Algeria.

At the age of 20 years 261 days, Johan Manzambi becoming the youngest player to get five direct goal involvements at a World Cup finals since 1966.

Switzerland have now reached the last 16 of the World Cup for the fourth successive tournament and they will face the winner of Colombia and Ghana on 7 July at 9pm (UK time) in Vancouver.

Newcastle United are targeting a number of young talents at this World Cup, players who have their best years ahead of them and time to develop into even bigger talents.

That has certainly been the case with Bazoumana Toure, like Johan Manzambi he is also only 20 and has also excelled in the Bundesliga this season, in his case with Hoffenheim..

With Ivory Coast exiting the World Cup this midweek, that then saw news breaking that Newcastle United had agreed a transfer fee of around £43m for the exciting young winger. With his World Cup over, Toure flew direct from the USA to Newcastle on Thursday in order to take his medical and then be formally announced as another summer signing for NUFC.

I just hope it is a similar story with Johan Manzambi, that a move to Newcastle United has been agreed behind the scenes with both the player and Freiburg, with hopefully keeping it under wraps until the player and Switzerland exit the tournament. Then allowing the Swiss midfielder to travel to Tyneside and formally complete his move.

He looks a massive talent and it would be gutting now if he signed for another club.

The thing is, the way Johan Manzambi and Switzerland are now playing, it could still be some time before they get knocked out of the World Cup. iaam_furlough_charleston:
The institution cited “a shift in the political and funding environment” and said staggered furloughs would help avoid layoffs.

Along the Charleston waterfront, the International African American Museum (IAAM) has furloughed all its staff — including leadership — due to challenging financial conditions.

In a statement shared with Hyperallergic, the museum, which opened in 2023, said that it was “navigating a shift in the political and funding environment” and added that the furlough was intended to reduce expenses and avoid layoffs while it restructured its fundraising model. Across all departments, the 20-day furlough period will be staggered between July 1 and December 31 to ensure the museum remains open to the public six days a week.

“We know this affects our employees and their families in real ways,” the museum's statement continued. “Keeping this team together and supporting them through difficult times is why we chose this path rather than deeper cuts.”

Museum President and CEO Tonya Matthews told the city's Post and Courier that IAAM was operating on a 10 to 20 percent deficit, and that it had also lost some federal funding.

“We've watched shifts in state-level funding and in the priorities of corporate and institutional donors,” Matthews explained. “It’s important for us to be open with our community about the challenging situation we are going through.”

After over 20 years of planning, the IAAM opened in June 2023 at Gadsden's Wharf — the site where at least 100,000 enslaved Africans first arrived in the United States. On top of sponsored events, the museum features rotating art and historical exhibitions, and maintains permanent displays devoted to different facets of regional, national, and diasporic Black history. These include the stories of the Gullah Geechee and others who were enslaved at Carolina Gold rice plantations, as well as the interlaced identities, traditions, and cultural specificities that traversed from Africa to the US.

Matthews told the Post and Courier that the furloughs will help give the museum time to pursue new financial strategies and revenue efforts, adding that the institution is “reinventing” itself in the philanthropy landscape.

The furloughs in Charleston are a symptom of nationwide funding challenges in the arts and culture institution sphere. A 2025 survey from the American Alliance of Museums found that among more than 500 US museum respondents, over a third reported having their federal grants or contracts cut. Two-thirds of those who lost federal support reported that the funds were not replaced by sponsorships, donations, or foundation grants.

ice_protester_shackling:
Minneapolis

The story of one progressive activist arrested in Minnesota in January shows what critics say is the aggressive nature of the Trump administration’s response to those who have protested its immigration crackdown.

By Alan Feuer

On the night of his arrest, Paul Johnson says he lay for hours in a hospital bed in Minneapolis, woozy from the pain pills and addled from the head blows he claims he received from federal agents. He was alone, he said, unable to communicate with anyone and strapped in place by the shackles on his leg.

Waking on a January morning, he tried to call his wife to tell her he had been taken into custody during an immigration protest, but the agents would not let him, according to court papers filed last week. When a nurse tried to sneak a phone into his room, he said, the agents stopped that too.

Eventually, careful not to dislodge the IV in his arm, Johnson, a longtime progressive activist, reached out with his free leg and managed — with his toes — to hook the cord of a nearby landline. He dragged the receiver toward himself, he said, and quietly placed a call.

By the end of the day, his lawyer finally arrived, finding him in a state of panicked isolation. “Mr. Johnson began sobbing from relief that someone had come to see him,” the lawyer later wrote.

On Thursday evening, after The New York Times repeatedly over four days asked the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security about Johnson’s case, federal prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the charges he faced of assaulting federal officers during the protest. In a one-page filing in U.S. District Court in Minneapolis, the prosecutors also said they would investigate the allegations of misconduct he had raised.

“I’m ecstatic,” Johnson said in a brief interview with the Times. “I hope there’s actual action behind these words.”

Johnson’s story reflects what critics say is the aggressive nature of the Trump administration’s response to those who have protested its immigration crackdown, especially in Minnesota, where hundreds of heavily armed and masked federal agents were sent this past winter. But even among the many troubling tales that have emerged from the state, his claims are particularly startling, including allegations that federal agents assaulted him after he followed them in his van and then, after arresting him, left him shackled to a bed for days — except for bathroom breaks and medical treatment — before he was even charged.

The weekslong action in Minnesota, known as Operation Metro Surge, led to the detention of more than 4,000 immigrants, according to officials. But it also resulted in the violation of scores of court orders, the dismissal of criminal cases against more than a dozen other people accused of assaulting agents during protests and the deaths of two demonstrators — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — at the hands of federal agents.

In their initial charging document filed in January, prosecutors said Johnson approached the immigration agents one evening that month with a baseball bat in hand and later sprayed them with a chemical irritant.

Those charges, first filed as a felony, were quickly reduced, without explanation, to a misdemeanor.

Because Johnson spent much of his time in the Hennepin County Medical Center alone and unable to receive visitors, it was not possible to independently verify each of his claims. Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security officials did not respond to multiple requests for comment about his stay in the hospital, as each agency referred the issue to the other.

On Thursday, after the dismissal motion was filed, the Justice Department denied that it had asked to end the case because of questions from the Times.

Johnson, however, remains daunted by his ordeal, erupting into sobs several times during the interview.

“I had no idea the entire time I was there what was actually going on,” he said. “I was just thinking, ‘I’m in here on my own, and if anyone is going to protect me, it would have to be myself.’”

The court papers filed last week by Johnson’s lawyer, Kevin Riach, laid out the account of his five-day stay in the hospital and accused the federal agents who arrested him of “outrageous government conduct.” Riach claimed that the agents had “manufactured a dangerous situation designed to develop a false basis to arrest Mr. Johnson” and then held him “incommunicado” at the hospital for days.

From the moment President Donald Trump began his expansive effort to round up immigrants across the country, the department has forcefully pursued criminal cases against demonstrators who have protested the moves in Minneapolis and other cities. On Tuesday, for example, prosecutors filed conspiracy charges against 15 members of what they described as antifa groups in Minneapolis, accusing them of injuring or impeding federal officers while opposing immigration enforcement efforts.

In the rush to bring indictments, however, several cases accusing protesters of going after federal agents have, like Johnson’s, failed as judges have questioned the evidence presented. Some have pointed out that accusations made in criminal complaints were later contradicted by video footage.

Riach has said that almost half of the 36 cases filed in Minnesota accusing protesters of assaulting agents during Operation Metro Surge have been dismissed in the past few months. In a recent case in Chicago, prosecutors threw out the charges against four protesters accused of interfering with agents at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility after a judge discovered an extraordinary series of grand jury violations.

Johnson has been involved in the protest scene in Minneapolis since at least 2018, when his best friend was fatally shot during a mental health and wellness check by police. Two years later, he joined the demonstrations against the killing of George Floyd by police, and in 2021, he ran for mayor of the city on the Humanitarian-Community Party line, earning a couple of hundred votes.

So it was hardly surprising that he joined the protests against ICE this past winter when thousands of agents arrived in Minnesota. Like scores of other demonstrators, he started following the agency’s vehicles through immigrant communities on the north side of the city, alerting people to their presence.

On Jan. 22, he recalled, he was trailing two ICE trucks that had been following some young Black men then abruptly veered from their targets and followed him instead.

Johnson said he pulled his van into the parking lot of a nearby convenience store, where agents swiftly boxed him in. They approached him from both sides, he said, demanding that he step out of his van. Videos reviewed by the Times show agents shattering his windows and punching him repeatedly.

Johnson was taken first to the B.H. Whipple Federal Building, which served as ICE’s home base, and then to the Hennepin County Medical Center.

At one point, he woke up, he said, and found federal agents taking photos of him in his hospital gown. When he came to in the morning, he discovered that one of his legs had been shackled to the bed.

He immediately asked to call his lawyer but said that the agents would not let him. After they stopped a nurse from giving him her own phone, he recalled, he toe-tapped the landline from its housing and managed to call his wife, Allison Reinke-Johnson.

She had spent a sleepless night trying to find him after seeing a video clip of his arrest, around 7 p.m., on a group chat of ICE protesters. By the morning, she was in a state of panic when, out of the blue, her husband called at 8 a.m.

“All he said was, ‘I’ve been kidnapped by ICE; I’m at HCMC; call a lawyer,’” Reinke-Johnson recalled. “I breathed a huge sigh of relief at least knowing where he was.”

But while Riach was able to talk with Johnson that same evening, neither he nor Reinke-Johnson were allowed back into his room until he was finally discharged Jan. 27, court papers say. He spent those five days shackled to his hospital bed with armed guards at his door, he said, even though the criminal complaint accusing him of assault was not formally filed until Jan. 26.

Until the motion to dismiss had been filed, Johnson was fighting his case despite having suffered, by his own account, a traumatic brain injury and serious damage to his shoulder.

He says he no longer has the stamina to work his former job as a general contractor and has instead started a hot sauce company, selling a special flavor called “ICE OUT.” The scars on his body are not the only ones left behind from his encounter with the immigration agents.

“Now that it happened to me,” he said, “I realize that anyone could be next.”

Women are far less likely to be attracted to someone who earns less than them than most men are, a new poll found.

Only an average of 11% of women said their “ideal partner” could earn less than them, while an average of 61% of men said their ideal partner could make less, the poll from matchmaking service Keeper found.

That means a vast majority of women — 89% — cared about their partners being the breadwinners, while men were much less concerned about it, with just 39% of men saying they were interested in higher earners.

The poll drew on 9,630 Keeper users — 6,251 men and 3,401 women, most of whom were heterosexual — between July 1 and Sept. 8, whose sign-up forms asked about marriage preferences to help the AI-driven platform better align them with potential matches.

Those preferences buck recent social trends — wives earning more than husbands tripled in the last 50 years, according to a 2023 Pew Research Center study which found 55% of American households have a male breadwinner and 16% have a female.

But Keeper founder Jake Kozloski thinks contemporary culture and historical culture — along with people’s interior inclinations born of those cultures — will inevitably be out of step, leading to the kind of results his study found.

“We’re evolved to have certain preferences as men and women on average, and I think one of the preferences that women pretty clearly have — and that’s been replicated cross-culturally and in a lot of academic research — is a preference for higher socioeconomic status,” Kozloski told The Post.

“Culture can only override so much biology, right?” he added, pointing to a 2020 study of 45 countries which found women tended to prefer older providers and men tended to prefer younger lookers.

However, men and women’s preferences did tend to change as each earned more money in the Keeper study — sometimes drastically.

Only 10% of women making less than $50,000 per year said their ideal partner could earn less than them — while women earning $250,000 and above were twice as likely — 20% — to say ideal partners could make less.

That trend also followed for men, though not as severely — 57% of men making $50,000 or under said their partner could make less than them, while 79% making $250,000 or more said the same.

And while the Keeper survery asked users about their ideal partner’s income profile — speaking to a general image of overall attractiveness — nearly none listed income profiles as “dealbreakers” that would exclude a potential match in their search for love.

Only about 1 in 200 Keeper users — about .5% — listed financial needs as a non-negotiable, while just 1 in 1,000 — .1% — explicitly specified an earning threshold on their profile, Kozloski said.

“In practice, true deal breakers are rare,” he said. “You’d be hard pressed to find any married person who says, ‘Yes, my spouse has zero flaws.’ So it’s just a matter of getting as close as you can, not finding true perfection.”

Another study, meanwhile, found that the husbands who made less money than their wives were more likely to report mental distress than those who are the breadwinners.

Among husbands whose wives earn at least 70% of household income, the risk of “serious psychological distress” is almost two and a half times as high, according to the study from the Economist, which analyzed 17 years of data.

Keeper — which has users fill out an extensive questionnaire and uses AI to identify matches — boasts about 1.6 million sign-ups, and claims an impressive 1 in 10 marriage rate for first dates it set up.

“Instead of a swipe app that gives you a thousand matches, we’ll give you one match,” said Kozloski. “But it’s going to be a damn good match.”

india-cockroach-movement:
By

Diaa Hadid

,

Omkar Khandekar

A protester holds a placard after India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following nationwide protests as part of the Cockroach Janta Party's protest movement in Mumbai, India on Saturday.
                
                    
                    Ashish Vaishnav/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

NEW DELHI — India's education minister tendered his resignation on Saturday, meeting a key demand of students whose anti-government protests swelled this week beyond the capital New Delhi and onto the streets of more than a dozen cities.

Following news of the resignation of the education minister Dharmendra Pradhan, a spokesman for protest leaders Saurav Das, called on demonstrators — mostly students — to go home. He said the protests, which began in early June, would end "in good faith."

The students held Pradhan responsible for a series of leaks in nationwide exams for university seats or government jobs, which millions of students take every year.

The protests posed the most serious challenge to the 12-year rule of India's Hindu nationalist prime minister Narendra Modi. For weeks, the government had ignored the protesters, then vilified them, with the education minister calling protest leaders "the B team of terrorists," according to the Indian daily The Hindu. Presenters of Modi-loyal media outlets suggested the protest leaders were paid by India's enemy and neighbor, Pakistan.

"The government realized that the familiar playbook that it's often deployed to deal with these kinds of agitations was not working," said Milan Vaishnav, senior fellow and director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, and host of a popular podcast, Grand Tamasha.

He added: "They were not easily able to undermine the credibility of the protesters. The pressure was mounting … I think this was their way of trying to cut their losses."

In a two-page letter posted on X, Pradhan said he was resigning because he didn't want the students' anger to be exploited by "anti-national forces." He did not clarify what he meant by "anti-national forces," but it appeared to be a dig at insinuations that the protesters were led, or infiltrated by enemies of India. Pradhan did not apologize for the paper leaks.

Near the main protest site in New Delhi, streets echoed with cheering students, whose celebrations went on well into the evening. Abhijeet Dipke, a 30-year-old whose satirical group 'Cockroach Janta Party' has been leading the protests, fell to his knees on hearing the news. Then he raised his fist and announced: "We have done it."

Even as leaders told protesters to go home, Dipke said in a statement that the students had other demands: compensation for the families of students who died by suicide after questions of a medical entrance exam paper leaked in May, forcing some 2 million students to retake the test – one of the incidents that initially sparked these protests.

Protesters react after India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned following nationwide protests as part of the Cockroach Janta Party's protest movement in Mumbai, India on Saturday.
                
                    
                    Rafiq Maqbool/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

The local newspaper The Indian Express reported at least a dozen students died by suicide following the announcement, with some leaving notes behind saying they could not bear the idea of resitting the exam.

The student leaders also demanded action against the security personnel who attacked protestors as they marched to Parliament in New Delhi earlier this week.

The resignation of Pradhan, seen as a confidant of the prime minister Modi, suggests that the government had to shift tactics after protests, which began in New Delhi on June 7, dramatically swelled in size. Unlike previous protests in India's recent history, these demonstrations cut across the country's traditional demographic lines.

India has the world's largest number of young people, with around 367 million people between the ages of 15 and 29. Education is "a kind of leveler, bringing everybody together," said sociologist Raheel Dhattiwala.

Sushant Singh, a political analyst at Yale University said because the crowd "cuts across caste, class, religion, language," the government struggled to deploy its usual playbook. "It has become very difficult for the state to demonize them," said Singh. "That is the uniqueness of this protest at this point."

Many protesters came from the heartland of the ruling Hindu nationalist party, a belt of territory from central to north India. Brothers Rishabh, 23, and Mohit, 22, traveled 50 miles by rickshaw, train, and metro to reach the central protest site in New Delhi. Like many Indians, they do not have a family name.

"The [exam] papers are being leaked, the rich are paying for their children to pass, and [we] poor people are being left behind," Rishabh told NPR on Friday. "Where are we supposed to go?"

But young Indians' complaints weren't triggered by the exam leaks alone. The protests coincided with a controversial comment by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant describing unemployed youth as "cockroaches" in May, a comment he later said was misquoted. The comments are what prompted Dipke to form the 'Cockroach Janta Party.'

The party has since received support from prominent Indians, including author Arundhati Roy, who recently wrote: "Just when hope seemed lost, they came. Young roaches riding in on the rain. The progeny of the unholy union between a judge and a joke."

A Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporter shouts slogans at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on July 23, 2026 during the ongoing protest to demand the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
                
                    
                    SAJJAD HUSSAIN/AFP via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

These protests dramatically swelled in size last week after police forcibly removed a respected educator — who was on hunger strike in solidarity with the students — from the New Delhi protest site, effectively detaining him in a government hospital.

On Friday, the educator, Sonam Wangchuk, announced that he had broken his 26-day fast after receiving assurances that the government would hold authorities to account over the country's failing exam systems.

Even more students held their own protests across the country after police violently cracked down on thousands of protesters who tried to march into parliament on Monday.

Following that outcry, the prime minister Narendra Modi addressed students directly: "Friends, I understand that paper leak is no ordinary subject," he began in Hindi in a post released to Instagram overnight Thursday. He said his government had caught those accused of leaking exam questions and they "are lying in jails."

After Modi issued that statement, student leaders said they would meet with a government representative. They later told protesters they had repeated their demand for the education minister's resignation by the weekend and warned that if he did not, they would call for nationwide marches on Monday.

Supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party wear and display masks during a protest in New Delhi.
                
                    
                    Manish Swarup/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

On Saturday, the students got what they asked for — taking many Indians by surprise.

"This is not a government that backs down very easily," said Vaishnav. "The fact that they were letting [the education minister] go is indeed quite a big deal," he said.

Dhattiwala, the sociologist, said she presumed that the protest leaders may try to continue their momentum in more formal avenues. "There could be a possibility that they might start a youth party," she said, speaking of Dipke and the Cockroach party he led to political success. "Who knows?"

Vaishnav, with the Carnegie Endowment, said even before projecting to the future, "we should stop and remark at how improbable a victory this was," praising the success of the movement and Dipke, a recent graduate of Boston University who returned to India in June to spearhead the movement.

"He sets up an internet meme called a cockroach people's party that goes viral. And he decides to take advantage of that, to come back to his home country and launch a protest to force the sitting education minister to resign. It actually succeeds."

"If you were to rewind the clock a couple of months, I mean, this would have seemed like pure fantasy."

Bilal Kuchay contributed reporting from New Delhi.

Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

Two years after the CFMEU collapsed into chaos, the man charged with investigating its worst branch says a royal commission is still necessary.

The anger rises then recedes. Typically warm and candid, Geoffrey Watson’s wry bemusement with public criticism can sour if he believes the criticism impugns his integrity. So it was in our lengthy conversation this week.

In February, a report prepared by Watson, a silk and former counsel assisting the New South Wales Independent Commission Against Corruption, was released and a mighty storm ensued. Appointed in 2024 by the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union’s then administrator, Mark Irving, to examine the union’s corruption, Watson delivered a 140-page investigation of the Victorian branch, which he titled “Rotting from the Top”.

The report collected evidence of graft, intimidation and the influence of organised crime upon the state’s construction sector – especially within the massive, state-sponsored infrastructure projects known as the Big Build.

“As a lifelong believer in trade unions, it was shocking to see so much crime, so much corruption, such a perversion of values,” Watson wrote. “The CFMEU was no longer on the right side of civil society, it was proudly on the wrong side. The Union was no longer the champion of the working class – the Setka era CFMEU turned to looking after gangsters, standover men, bikies, heroin traffickers, and even killers. By the end of this investigation I have been left with the empty feeling that the Setka-led Victorian branch of the CFMEU was no longer a trade union, it was a crime syndicate.”

Provocatively, Watson also asserted that the scale of corruption was partly helped by political indifference – a kind of wilful blindness. This view was removed from the final draft, a fact we learnt when news of the omissions leaked and lawyers, their curiosity aroused, had the cut sections tabled during Queensland’s commission of inquiry into that state’s branch of the CFMEU.

“It’s appropriate that politicians and public servants should share the responsibility for what has happened – for allowing the CFMEU to run out of control,” Watson wrote. “It is not as though the excesses of the CFMEU have been a secret: the CFMEU revelled in bad publicity … If the press knew, then the public knew. If the public knew, then the Government must have known. More to the point, as the guardian of public money, the Government had a duty to know. It had a duty to monitor delays and costs-blowouts. There is no doubt the Government knew about the rising problem – but it is equally clear that the Government did nothing about it.”

For days after, Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan, who was the state’s infrastructure minister before her promotion three years ago, quivered with indignation. Testy media conferences followed. Allan zeroed in on a figure Watson has used – an estimate, as he qualifies in his report, that the cost of Big Build corruption was likely about $15 billion. The specificity of this figure, and Mark Irving’s private querying of it, had the unfortunate consequence of distracting from the wider findings by offering critics a number to quibble over and use to invite suspicion of Watson’s reliability. “That claim, of any amount, has not been well tested or properly founded,” Allan said in February.

Her police minister, Anthony Carbines, went much further in his criticisms of Watson. “It might be good for a quote, but he’s not much good when it comes to coming up with some facts,” he said. “When his florid ramblings become facts that can be tested in court, all well and good. But if you’ve got evidence, give it to Victoria Police and they’ll take action.”

Watson says he was often in contact with Victoria Police during his investigations – that of course he was – and notes of anger sound when he thinks again of Carbines’ comments. At the time, Watson described the remarks as “Trumpian”, and this week it was made clear that the insult to his integrity still stings.

It was an unusual and unpleasant moment for Watson. His report had attracted the ire of both the Victorian government and the alleged underworld figures and allegedly corrupt former union officials named in it. For a time, they all were joined by the similarity of their denunciations of Watson. Lawsuits have followed, of which Watson cannot speak. “I think Geoffrey would have needed a thorough shower after those years of investigating this putrid mess,” one union source told The Saturday Paper this week. “And they’re still attacking him.”

Watson says he had not appreciated the scale of corruption in Victoria before he began investigating the union in 2024. Then again, why would he? He was a Sydney silk, ordinarily engaged with the prosecution of bent coppers and politicians in that state. “I wondered going into it if it was all a beat-up,” he says. “But on a scale of zero to 10 for corruption, NSW was a two or three. Queensland a five. Victoria was a 1000. Insane. There was trafficking of heroin on sites – and meth, coke. Bikie gangs were fighting each other for control of these sites.”

“I think Geoffrey would have needed a thorough shower after those years of investigating this putrid mess. And they’re still attacking him.”

There’s only one thing for it, Watson says, and his view was echoed by several union sources this week: a royal commission, or something similar, as was instated in Queensland. “If you really want to get to the bottom of all this, then you need a properly empowered public inquiry in the nature of a royal commission,” he says.

Labor’s Big Build, and its entanglement with union corruption and organised crime, will inevitably be invoked in the Victorian election campaign this year. The state will vote in November, when Labor will seek a fourth consecutive term. Union sources are not holding their breath for an inquiry, as proposed by Watson. Allan has made clear that she feels it unnecessary. “There’s no  way the Allan government would call one,” a union source says. “But a commission of inquiry, as happened in Queensland, is what’s needed. Only a serious, independent inquiry will do it.”

In January, the CFMEU’s national secretary, Zach Smith, abruptly resigned. “The reasons I am leaving are personal,” he wrote in a statement. “I cannot continue to serve the union in the way that the members deserve, and taking time away is in the best interests of myself, the people I care about and the union.”

What wasn’t revealed at that time was that he was being investigated by his boss, Mark Irving, for alleged undeclared conflicts of interest regarding romantic relationships with staff.

Irving inherited Smith. The union boss was someone viewed with contemptuous suspicion by whistleblowers within the CFMEU, given his previous closeness to expelled leader John Setka. Nonetheless, Irving was patient with Smith and forgave several missteps – such as when Smith directed a union official to meet with the notorious underworld figure Mick Gatto last year.

Yet Smith’s romantic entanglements, and his less-than-forthcoming disclosures of them and their subsequent conflicts of interest, made his time there untenable. Irving felt personally betrayed, as did many others within the union, who had received from Smith misleading assurances.

Then, in April, Irving resigned. “The Union is changing its personnel,” he said. “It is changing its culture. It is regaining its position in civil society. The rebuild phase requires a different approach … and a different set of skills.”

This was less of a surprise than Smith’s departure. Irving had received a “hospital pass”, in the words of one union source, and inherited a complex and potentially dangerous job. He suffered a heart attack last year and had subsequent surgery, and from early in his tenure was the recipient of several credible death threats. This obliged the deployment of personal security. Sources have told me how Irving learnt to choose tables in restaurants and cafes that provided clear sightlines to the door. “The threats were very, very serious,” one source says. “These were serious people.”

Geoffrey Watson is happy to concede that in his time as corruption investigator, there were disagreements with Irving. They were “always civil”, he says, and not for the first time he stresses Irving’s decency.

“It’s difficult to overstate the difficulty of his job,” Watson says. “And he was earning much less money than he would at the bar. I have great respect for him.”

Nonetheless, in the almost two years of the CFMEU’s government mandated administration, there has been significant staff tumult. Poor appointments were made of people facing serious allegations, who were then sacked or offered generous severance packages, and the departure of Smith means that in under two years the Victorian branch has had four different leaders.

There has been attrition in the administrator’s office also – not only Irving’s departure but also several support staff. None of this surprises one whistleblower. “Look, a lot of Labor or ACTU associated unionists came in to fix the problem,” they say. “But construction is an entirely different culture. They were outsiders to this: people plucked from outside the culture and then dropped into maximum security.”

Irving has been replaced by Michael Crosby, a veteran unionist and former executive of the CFMEU’s NSW branch. Even among the most militant and impatient agitators for reform within the union, there’s begrudging respect for his reputation for integrity and a willingness to confer some benefit of doubt. That said, there remains scepticism of the appointment of another man with very little experience in construction.

“The next phase” begins, as Mark Irving said, but union sources told me they have no idea what that means. Irving did oversee the dismissal of hundreds of people, but many of those departures came with generous severance packages – a fact that angers whistleblowers, not least those who have suffered from their blacklisting for speaking out.

“After almost two years of administration, what’s the scorecard?” asks one union source. “There’s not much. We’ve had some clowns appointed to positions, which turned bad. The embattled chancellor’s conservative party suffered its worst result in postwar German history as the far-right AfD won its second regional election in two weeks.

BERLIN — Germany’s embattled Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservatives suffered a second major defeat to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in a regional vote Sunday — a result Merz conceded was a “disaster.”But the chancellor moved to quickly quell a rising storm of speculation that he would move to step aside following the loss, which comes only two weeks after another historic defeat to the AfD in a regional contest. He appeared before cameras just minutes after the polls closed Sunday to say he would continue to push through his reform agenda and act as an anchor of stability in turbulent times.“These reforms are the antidote to the poison of authoritarianism,” he said. “What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience. I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country.”The AfD won around 38% of the vote in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — the second-best result in its history, just ahead of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) on 35%, according to preliminary results.

Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered its worst result in a state or national election since the end of World War II, by the end of election night coming in at 4.9%, according to a preliminary count, just below the vote threshold required to make it into the state parliament.

The failure to meet that threshold deals an even more painful blow to the chancellor, who is already struggling to maintain support among his party’s rank and file.

AfD leaders hailed their victory — party national co-leader Tino Chrupalla called the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result a “sensation” — while also putting the pressure on a profoundly weakened Merz to step aside and abandon his party’s policy of maintaining a “firewall” around the far right.“Friedrich Merz is the wrong chancellor for the CDU and is dragging the CDU down with him,” national co-leader Alice Weidel told German public television. “So the CDU must ask itself, above all else, does it want to continue with this chancellor and with these left-wing policies?”

Merz took the unusual step of convening CDU leaders at the party’s Berlin headquarters on Sunday night in an effort to rally their support ahead of what he knew would be another humiliating election defeat. Merz’s approval ratings are among the lowest ever recorded for a German chancellor at this point in their tenure, prompting internal CDU discussions about a possible change at the top—Kanzlertausch.

“Of course, the mood isn’t exactly lighthearted,” Ines Claus, a CDU politician who took part in the leadership meeting, told ARD. “If you ask me now whether one might prefer to just pull the covers over one’s head, well, that might be the case. But that’s not what responsibility is about; stability is what’s required now.”

Ahead of the election, one CDU official told POLITICO that “all hell breaks loose” in the party if the conservatives fail to make it into Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state parliament — an outcome that remained distinctly possible as of 10 p.m. on election night.

Just 1% of voters — and 1% of CDU supporters — said Chancellor Merz had helped his party’s election performance in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to a poll by public broadcaster ZDF.“We can’t sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania,” Merz said after the polls closed Sunday. “It’s a disaster.”The CDU also saw its support decline in a separate regional vote in Berlin, finishing second with around 19%, according to a preliminary count, behind the Left party, a far-left force which won 25.5% and is now poised to take over the capital’s mayoralty from Merz’s conservatives in coalition with center-left parties.

Merz has staked his chancellorship on a reform agenda he argues will boost Germany’s competitiveness and restore growth to the EU’s largest economy, and has urged voters to be patient as the reforms kick in.

But as Germany’s export-oriented growth model continues to suffer amid increased competition from China and U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff wars, German voters don’t appear to be giving him the benefit of the doubt.

The chancellor’s agenda includes raising the retirement age to shore up the pension system, cutting some health-insurance benefits to curb rising premiums and making it harder for workers to take sick leave in an effort to boost growth.

Many of those reforms impose clear costs on ordinary voters, giving the far right and far left ample opportunity to exploit public discontent.

Despite the AfD’s victory in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the party has no chance of governing in the state in part due to a late, come-from-behind surge for the SPD under state premier Manuela Schwesig, who cast herself in the election as a bulwark against the far right by employing the slogan “Frau gegen Blau” — “Woman against Blue,” a reference to the AfD’s party color.Schwesig is now likely to lead a new coalition government in the state with a coalition of left-wing parties.CDU leaders blamed Schwesig’s approach for effectively turning the election in her state into a two-party race that has greatly weakened Merz’s conservatives. “The CDU fought hard, but in the end, it was crushed in the escalating confrontation between the SPD and the AfD,” Merz said.But Schwesig blamed Merz and the CDU for failing to connect with voters and was able to gain on the AfD late in the race in great part because she attacked Merz as out of touch with ordinary people and his reform drive as punishing some of the most vulnerable.“The issue of the cost of living is a very significant one, and it’s important for the federal government to take a stand in favor of greater economic development to create jobs, but also to provide relief,” she told a public television broadcaster after the vote.

Still, trying to stabilize the situation, Philipp Amthor, a CDU politician from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the chancellery’s federal-state affairs chief, said it was time to end the Kanzlertausch discussion.

“We have seen that what we have experienced over the past two weeks since the state election in Saxony-Anhalt has done more harm than good — namely, ongoing discussions about personnel that have completely overshadowed the discussion of the issues at hand,” he said.

“In that regard, it is right to put an end to these personnel discussions now and refocus on the issues.”

This story has been updated.

But leading German economists warned of more trouble ahead, including rapidly rising debt levels.

Berlin’s Europe minister rebuked the European Council president’s remarks to POLITICO.

Chancellor insists his reforms are needed to revive the economy and competitiveness, but the proposals are turning off voters.

The chancellor is clinging to power, promising a political reset to unite the CDU’s rank and file behind his leadership.

Gippsland coastal communities have been told to monitor conditions as firefighters battle an out-of-control bushfire at Seacombe, about 42 kilometres east of Sale.

The CFA issued a Watch and Act warning on Sunday afternoon, "strongly" recommending residents in Golden Beach, Paradise Beach and Seacombe prepare to leave after a fire broke out on the Longford-Loch Sport Road.

It later added Dutson Downs to the Watch and Act warning.

In its 8:30pm update, the CFA said the threat had reduced, but residents should "monitor conditions and be ready to act" because "the situation can change at any time".

People were also advised not to travel to the area, and that it was "not safe to return".

Residents of Loch Sport were warned not to travel south along Longford-Loch Sport Road, while those west of the fire were told not to travel on that road toward Loch Sport, and instead to travel toward Yarram or Sale.

A CFA firefighter near an out-of-control bushfire at Seacombe. (Supplied: Candice Dockett)

A CFA spokesperson said crews responded to reports of smoke about 1:20pm on the Longford-Loch Sport Road in Seacombe.

The fire, located south-west of the coastal town of Loch Sport, is burning in a south-easterly direction towards Paradise Beach.

By 8:30pm Sunday, 28 CFA vehicles were on scene fighting the blaze, while air attack support had also been requested.

The cause of the fire is yet to be determined.

Firefighters were called out to a blaze on the Longford-Loch Sport Road on Sunday afternoon. (Supplied: CFA)

On Sunday afternoon, authorities said they had closed the Longford-Loch Sport Road at the Seacombe turn-off so that people could not enter the area, but said they were still free to leave.

They encouraged people to monitor the situation, including increases to wind speed or a change in wind direction, and to note that smoke or poor visibility can mean the situation is worsening.

A column of smoke rises on the horizon after the fire broke out. (Supplied: Gerard Walsh)

Earlier, a CFA spokesperson advised people in the affected communities to leave as soon as they were ready, "as roads will become busy".

"Those affected can travel to Yarram or Sale, or friends or family away from the fire," they said.

People are still being encouraged to leave the area if the situation changes or they feel unsafe.

As of 9:30pm, CFA crews were continuing to fight the blaze, and residents were advised to monitor warnings via the Vic Emergency site.
