car_finance_delay:
Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, regulators have announced.

Average payments of about Â£829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

However, legal challenges to the scheme mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed.

The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.

Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024.

The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - just over 40% of the total number during the period.

In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.

The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much.

Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for at least 35% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan.

Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders.

Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of Â£829 per mis-sold agreement.

The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit Â£9.1bn.

How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered.

For some customers - especially if their contact details have changed - it could take many months before compensation is paid.

Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything.

The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company.

The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts.

Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation.

The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain, external.

Under its plans:

lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much â but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge

those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster

people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027

those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed

those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim

Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees.

FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme  was "free to use" for consumers.

Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027.

But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme.

Consumer Voice said the scheme left "too many people short-changed". The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance.

The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, either in December or February next year.

It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes.

The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme. Without a scheme in place, the FCA has estimated that up to 19 million complaints would need to be handled individually, taking three years and costing lenders Â£6bn more.

It said it would "defend the scheme robustly as lawful and the best way to resolve such a widespread, long running and complex issue".

Ultimately, the industry is expected to cover the full costs of any compensation scheme, including any administrative costs.

Lenders - including some of the UK's biggest banks and specialist motor finance firms - have already set aside billions of pounds for potential payouts.

The body that represents the lending industry, the Finance and Leasing Association, said it had "concerns" about the programme but that it was choosing not to raise a legal challenge.

Santander, Barclays and Lloyds also accepted the scheme, despite raising concerns that the level of redress is disproportionate to those who suffered harm.

Even if drivers are entitled to compensation from these lenders they will need to wait.

There were some concessions made to lenders in a scaled-down final compensation plan from the FCA.

The Supreme Court considered three test cases which influenced the FCA's decision and, ultimately, limited how broad the compensation programme could have been.

It focused on whether the car dealers had a duty to act on behalf of their customers, rather than in their own interests. The test case which was upheld was that of Marcus Johnson, who bought his first car - a Suzuki Swift - in 2017.

In his case, the Supreme Court said the terms of his finance deal were unfair due of the size of the commission payment, and the fact he appeared to have been misled over the relationship between the finance firm and the dealer.

Northern Territory Police have upgraded the charges against three men who allegedly beat 48-year-old Darwin man Martin Wiberg to death in a "vicious attack" at the Casuarina bus stop earlier this year to murder.

Police initially arrested four men aged between 19 and 30 after they allegedly knocked Mr Wiberg to the ground and stomped on his head on March 12, rendering him unconscious.

Paramedics rushed Mr Wiberg to hospital in a critical condition, where he allegedly died from his injuries two months later.

Martin Wiberg has been remembered as a "beautiful, kind, caring man" with a "heart of gold". (Supplied)

In a statement released today, an NT Police spokesperson said three of the four men, who were originally charged with aggravated assault, had had their charges upgraded.

The other man, aged 19, was released without charge.

"The Major Crime Squad has continued to investigate the incident and subsequently submitted a brief to the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) seeking to upgrade the charges from aggravated assault to murder," they said.

NT Police have upgraded the charges against three men over Mr Wiberg's death at the Casuarina bus stop. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Mr Wiberg's loved ones have remembered the animal lover and karaoke enthusiast as a "beautiful, kind, caring man" with a "heart of gold".

Friends of Martin Wiberg are remembering him as a "very gentle soul".

Detective Senior Sergeant Paul Morrissey said today the 48-year-old's family remained "at the forefront of investigators' minds".

"Our thoughts remain with the family and loved ones of this man as they continue to endure an unimaginable loss," he said.

Two of the men, aged 26 and 31, are due to face the Darwin Local Court tomorrow, while the remaining 19-year-old is due to appear on August 12.

California is recalling more cannabis products after a worker died at a massive marijuana farm that has since been shut down by state regulators.

At least four cannabis products have been pulled over potential contamination, with two of the recalls confirmed to be connected to the Lake County farm where 46-year-old Yufang Lan worked.

State officials believe Lan died following an “occupational pesticide exposure” at Joel Michaely Farms, according to an affidavit obtained by MJBizDaily through a public records request.

Lan died in intensive care Aug. 27, six days after an unidentified man brought her to a local hospital. She was suffering cardiac arrest, according to law enforcement.

The California Department of Cannabis Control shut down the farm Sept. 8 and suspended its license after investigators uncovered alleged violations involving untagged plants, unaccounted-for inventory, failures to use the state’s tracking system and violations of environmental and pesticide laws.

The agency has recalled four products deemed “adulterated” because they were “produced under unsanitary conditions and the methods, facilities, or controls used to cultivate the cannabis did not conform with pesticide statutes and regulations.”

The recalled products are:

The DCC confirmed the Iced and Martini’s recalls are connected to Joel Michaely Farms. The agency has not confirmed whether the other two products came from the farm.

And the scope of the operation was enormous.

Lake County planning records show the farm was approved for nearly 1 million square feet of cannabis canopy.

When investigators executed a search warrant Aug. 31, they allegedly found 55,069 cannabis plants, 6,000 pounds of processed cannabis, “illegal chemicals” and “approximately 20,000 gallons of contaminated liquid requiring specialized disposal.”

Officials said all of the cannabis was destroyed.

Investigators also found evidence of banned and unapproved chemicals throughout the property.

DCC Special Investigator Jaime Musuda said in a Sept. 8 affidavit that the farm consisted of “two outdoor cultivation areas” and “112 hoophouse structures.”

In roughly 20 of the hoophouses, investigators found “cans of fumigant pesticide ‘Real-Kill Indoor Fogger’” positioned several feet apart.

Outside, investigators discovered “several different bottles of illicit foreign labeled pesticides” along with “three pesticides unapproved for use” on cannabis, according to the affidavit.

Those included Eagle 20, which contains myclobutanil; Sanmite SC, which contains pyridaben; and Altus, which contains flupyradifurone.

The investigation also raised questions about the conditions faced by workers at the sprawling farm.

Musuda said about 10 to 15 workers lived on the property in cramped, unsanitary conditions with “moldy walls.” It remains unclear whether Lan was among them.

The workers all spoke Mandarin, according to the affidavit, and none had been paid because the farm had yet to turn a profit, the onsite cultivation manager told Musuda, “which could take years.”

More recalls could follow as California officials continue investigating the operation.

cbc_nuclear_risk:
When Tim Hodgson, Canada’s natural resources minister, announced the federal government’s plan to dramatically expand the nuclear energy industry, he cited a project in the U.K. as a model.

That plant, Sizewell C on the Suffolk coast of England, is set to cost 38.2 billion pounds ($72.3 billion Cdn). But a key detail is that private investors are taking a 55 per cent stake in the project by sharing the construction costs.

Hodgson wants to emulate that model to achieve his government's lofty target of building up to 10 new reactors in Canada.

The prospect isn't far-fetched: one of Sizewell C’s investors is La Caisse, the public pension fund of Quebec, which has taken a 20 per cent stake in the reactor through an investment of $3.2 billion Cdn.

But attracting this kind of investment isn't easy, especially for risk-averse pension funds.

Nuclear energy in Western countries has developed a reputation for going eye-wateringly over budget. Hinkley Point C, the newest nuclear plant in the U.K., began construction in 2017 with an initial budget of $34 billion. It is now estimated to cost more than $64 billion.

Another recent project, Olkiluoto 3 in Finland, began construction in 2005 and took until 2022 to complete. Its cost ballooned from $5.1 billion to $17.8 billion.

WATCH | New nuclear strategy to boost jobs, economy:

Canada's nuclear strategy will lead 'to at least a doubling' of industry jobs: minister

"There's a reason why the nuclear industry has had really very flat growth over the last couple of decades. It's not about governments deciding not to build nuclear; in fact, there's been a ton of government support for nuclear projects," said Adam Scott, executive director of Shift Action, a Canadian initiative to push financial institutions and pensions to align their investments with green energy and climate action.

"It's that the projects have gone over budget and been incredibly expensive at such a scale that it has limited the ability to keep building these types of projects."

"If you want to have private sector investors, they need some de-risking," said Yrjo Koskinen, professor of sustainable finance at the University of Calgary.

That means that convincing private investors — such as pension funds, investment firms, energy and infrastructure companies — to invest in nuclear plants, they need some protection from the risks of huge cost overruns or long construction delays.

Koskinen says someone has to pay for covering that risk, and it will likely be taxpayers or electricity consumers.

Pension funds in particular need a reduction in risk, because of their duty to protect their members’ retirements.

Sizewell C in the U.K relies on a new funding scheme called the regulated asset base (RAB) model. Under the RAB, private investors such as La Caisse start getting paid back during the construction phase of the project, and don’t have to wait until the plant is actually operational and selling electricity.

Investors are paid through a levy on every British ratepayer — a one-pound charge on their monthly electricity bill — meaning investors see returns even if there are construction delays.

The RAB model also limits the risk to private investors if the project's costs balloon.

It works like this: Sizewell C is currently estimated to cost 38.5 billion pounds ($78.9 billion). If costs rise to an upper limit of 47.7 billion pounds ($90.3 billion), all the investors — public and private — will share the cost overruns equally. If costs go over that limit, the private investors won’t be forced to fund the overruns and the government may have to cover them.

The prospect of taxpayers being on the hook has left some locals critical of the deal.

"I think the thing that really sticks in our throats is that the way it's set up, the investors cannot lose," said Alison Downes of Stop Sizewell C, a campaign group in Suffolk, England, that opposes the project due to financial and environmental concerns.

"It puts risk onto energy bill payers, who are the people least in the world able to influence the outcome of a big construction project like Sizewell C."

In addition to being protected from major cost overruns, investors get attractive returns. The U.K.’s National Audit Office estimates investors will see returns of 11 to 13 per cent after construction is completed.

The British government says the Sizewell C plant will lower electricity bills by producing cheap energy — possibly into the next century. But the auditor’s report also said that the cost to consumers will not be outweighed by the benefits until at least 2064.

Critics of this technology point to the issue of nuclear waste. Like Canada, the U.K. does not yet have a facility for the long-term storage of nuclear waste. All the waste generated until now has been stored on site, at the nuclear plants themselves. (Both Canada and the U.K. are planning an underground storage site for permanent disposal of the waste.)

Critics also frequently point out that solar and wind energy, along with battery storage, are rapidly falling in cost and becoming more efficient. In recent public procurements conducted by Ontario’s energy system operator, renewables and battery storage won out with lower rates than previous procurements.

But Canada isn’t alone in also doubling down on nuclear. The new Hinkley and Sizewell plants combined will provide about 14 per cent of the U.K.’s electricity. The Trump administration is changing nuclear safety rules and providing loans to help build new plants in the U.S. France is undergoing a $110-billion Cdn nuclear expansion plan that could build six new reactors. Even Japan, still recovering from the memory of the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster, is planning to refurbish existing plants and build new ones.

It’s a global boom this country wants to join.

"Canada has a really strong track record of nuclear deployment, particularly in Ontario. There's a 50-year history of delivering and running these plants," said David Pickup, director of the electricity program at the Pembina Institute, an energy think-tank.

"We're encouraged by that sort of vision of a global nuclear industry that Canada would be a big part of, while cautioning that that shouldn't come on the backs of Canadians at home."

Ontario gets almost half of its electricity from nuclear, via massive plants like Darlington, Pickering and Bruce. All of the plants have CANDU reactors, a Canadian nuclear design developed in the 1950s that was exported around the world.

But experts are doubtful that nuclear plants can be built without cost overruns — at least for the first few reactors that Canada builds, before it regains the experience it used to have.

"Canada had a sort of a heyday from 1970 until about 1991-92, when there wasn't a year we weren't building a nuclear reactor somewhere. And what that meant is that we developed a workforce that was very skilled, very trained, very good at their jobs," said Warren Mabee, professor of energy and environmental policy at Queen’s University in Kingston, Ont.

"It's really hard to build nuclear when you haven't been doing it for a while."

Despite the financial and logistical challenges, experiences in other countries show that large energy projects are often seen positively, even after massive costs.

The reactor in Finland came online just as Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022 and started cutting off energy supplies to the rest of Europe.

Without the new reactor, the Finnish people may have faced the skyrocketing energy prices suffered by other countries in the region. Instead, Finland now has some of the cheapest electricity in Europe.

"So in that sense, thank goodness Finland has this new reactor," Koskinen said. "But of course, when it was commissioned, nobody knew about that."

Reporter

Inayat Singh covers the environment and climate change at CBC News. He is based in Toronto and has previously reported from Winnipeg. Email: inayat.singh@cbc.ca

census-midterms-representation:
Republican turnout is key to pushing back on Democrats’ systematic rigging of the electoral process through the census.

Illegal aliens cannot legally vote in federal elections, but their presence in the country still helps determine how much power Democrats and Republicans have in Washington. By counting them when allocating congressional seats and electoral votes, the federal government allows illegal aliens to fundamentally shape Congress and, as a result, our laws. But President Donald Trump is locked in a fight to keep illegal aliens out of the census count, and the upcoming midterms represent an important crossroads in that fight.

The Trump administration proposed in September that the process for calculating the census must exclude noncitizens. The rule would remove illegal aliens due to their “lack of sufficient tie and allegiance to the United States.”

Noncitizens — and illegal aliens — don’t get to vote in federal elections, since that’s a right of citizens only. And yet they significantly impact elections through apportionment and the electoral college. Every decade the Census Bureau will calculate how many congressional seats a state gets as well as how many electoral votes the state gets based on its population. The population has included illegal aliens — a benefit for Democrats, according to RealClearPolitics.

Had the Census Bureau excluded the estimated 18.6 million illegal aliens from the census in 2020, it would have shifted “eight House seats, mostly from blue to red and purple states.”

“Removing all 41 million non-citizens would shift a stunning 22 seats the same way,” Hayden Ludwig wrote for RealClearPolitics. “In either case, these are districts that should represent U.S. citizens; instead, they’re brimming with non-citizens, and Democratic Party politicians prefer it this way.”

In fact, “Democrats also control seven of the 10 House districts with the most non-citizens; the other three are held by Republicans, either born in Cuba or who are children of Cuban immigrants,” Ludwig continues. Notably, Democrats facilitated a mass invasion of illegal aliens under the Biden administration, which then flocked to blue states like New York, California, Massachusetts, and other hot spots.

Trump previously tried to level the playing field back in 2019 by adding a citizenship question to the census questionnaire. The Supreme Court ultimately stopped his attempt but did not rule that asking immigration status would be unconstitutional. In fact, “The Enumeration Clause [Article I Section 2] does not provide a basis to set aside the Secretary’s decision,” the justices ruled.

As Ludwig explained, the Trump administration originally used the “wrong arguments” and “still came within one vote of winning that fight.” Further, Trump also issued a memo in 2020 excluding illegal aliens from the population used for apportionment, and the Supreme Court dismissed a challenge to the memo (which was ultimately rescinded by the Biden administration).

But this is why the midterms matter, because Trump’s latest effort will likely face legal challenges and there’s a clear role for Congress. Many Americans frustrated by high gas prices feel tempted to sit out the midterms, either to punish do-nothing Republican leadership in the Senate or to punish Trump. But efforts like this exemplify how much of the work the Trump administration is doing behind the scenes can have a significant effect on American governance. And while most of the administration’s efforts to fix census errors have been limited to administrative rule-making and court proceedings, there are ways that Congress could work for or against the effort depending on the midterm results.

A Republican Congress could also help codify any changes to census procedures into federal law, especially if Trump continues to face roadblocks in the courts. That matters because even if Trump is successful vis a vis executive action, a future administration could simply undo it. A Rep
ceuta-migration-debate:
In Ceuta, the small Spanish territory at the tip of North Africa where more than 72,000 people crossed from Morocco last week by swimming around the border, asylum seekers wait to learn what comes next.

Dozens were seen resting on a small beach on the outskirts of town this week, as the enclave's few shelters were full, mostly with women and children, according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.

Aid groups that were largely absent when exhausted swimmers first stumbled ashore now distribute food and water to those who were not forced to return to Morocco. (Moroccan nationals cannot claim asylum in Spain under an agreement designating Morocco a safe third country.)

While humanitarian organizations respond to the aftermath on the ground, the debate across Europe has largely been about how to prevent another mass crossing.

European lawmakers debated the Ceuta crossings and migration policy in Brussels on Wednesday, after last week's events triggered one of the bloc's sharpest political disputes over migration in years.

Within hours of the crossings last week, member states of the European Union rushed to blame Spain, saying decisions by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's government had encouraged migrants to attempt the journey.

Ceuta grapples with child migrants as Spain approves millions to deal with crisis

Spain’s mass border breach fuels anti-migrant backlash

Italy temporarily suspended passport-free Schengen travel arrangements with Spain, even though they do not apply to Ceuta. And 22 of the European Union's 27 member states called for stronger external border controls.

Ceuta faces humanitarian challenge after surge of migrants

European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen called the crossings "unacceptable," and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz demanded Morocco "take back illegal migrants immediately."

Wednesday's meeting shifted the rhetoric of the past week somewhat, with interior ministers releasing a statement in solidarity with Spain and condemning attempts to divide the bloc.

But the sentiment remains. Over the weekend, new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Dover, where asylum seekers land after crossing the Channel from France on boats. His visit came after Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage said that if elected, he would employ the Royal Navy to return migrants crossing the Channel back to France.

The reactions to Ceuta are a reflection not only of disagreements over migration policy but domestic political calculations, said Davide Colombi, a migration researcher at the Centre for European Policy Studies.

"Member states' governments are still acting according to their own national electorate," Colombi said, rather than in the interest of Europe. When they blamed Spain for the events in Ceuta, "they acted in their own defence rather than in co-operation."

For José Javier Olivas, an associate professor of political science at Spain's UNED university, the significance of Ceuta lies in how it has been discussed.

He says politicians across Europe rapidly adopted language portraying the crossing as an "invasion," framing it as a security threat rather than a humanitarian emergency.

"They have managed to impose the terms in which we discuss about the issue," Olivas said, arguing the far right's greatest victory was shifting the conversation away from the people still stranded in Ceuta.

Spain has increasingly found itself out of step with much of Europe on migration. Earlier this year, Prime Minister Sánchez expanded a program allowing 500,000 undocumented migrants, many of them from Latin America, already living in Spain to regularize their legal status.

Meanwhile, countries like Italy, Denmark and the Netherlands have emphasized migrant returns and tougher border enforcement. Colombi described Spain as "going in a very different direction" from many of its European partners.

Exactly what prompted tens of thousands of people to attempt the Ceuta crossing last week remains disputed.

Researchers point to a combination of misleading online claims, confusion over a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling affecting return procedures for migrants arriving by sea and questions over Morocco's border enforcement.

Colombi said there was evidence of widespread misinformation encouraging people to believe anyone reaching Ceuta would be allowed to remain in Spain, while adding that Morocco's precise role remains unclear.

In the days before the crossing, videos circulated widely on social media claiming migrants who reached Ceuta would not be deported. Other posts falsely suggested Spain's regularization program was about to close, creating a sense of urgency for people hoping to reach Europe.

Most of those videos have since been removed.

European leaders are now focused on reinforcing borders instead of debating the fate of thousands of asylum seekers still awaiting legal assistance, shelter or asylum decisions, Olivas said.

"Very few people are talking about the fact that there are thousands of people still in the streets in Ceuta who don't have water, who don't have food, who don't know what's going to happen to them," he said.

Many of the remaining crossers are from other parts of Africa, having spent years travelling north in search of protection in Europe. In photographs taken by news agencies, some hold handmade signs reading "Asilo."

One Yemeni man who fled his country's civil war five years ago told El Pais he lost his brother in the sea near Ceuta. More than 80 people drowned or were crushed in last week's rush across the border, according to official figures.

Meanwhile, roughly 1,100 unaccompanied minors remain in Ceuta because they cannot be summarily deported, according to local authorities.

Many are staying in makeshift accommodation or sleeping rough as charities and neighbourhood groups struggle to care for children, pregnant women and others left stranded.

Verity is a reporter for CBC in Montreal. She previously worked for the Globe and Mail, Toronto Star and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal.

Article text size: This control adjusts article text size. For broader accessibility options, please use your browser or device text scaling settings.

Two years after the CFMEU collapsed into chaos, the man charged with investigating its worst branch says a royal commission is still necessary.

The anger rises then recedes. Typically warm and candid, Geoffrey Watson’s wry bemusement with public criticism can sour if he believes the criticism impugns his integrity. So it was in our lengthy conversation this week.

In February, a report prepared by Watson, a silk and former counsel assisting the New South Wales Independent Commission Against Corruption, was released and a mighty storm ensued. Appointed in 2024 by the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union’s then administrator, Mark Irving, to examine the union’s corruption, Watson delivered a 140-page investigation of the Victorian branch, which he titled “Rotting from the Top”.

The report collected evidence of graft, intimidation and the influence of organised crime upon the state’s construction sector – especially within the massive, state-sponsored infrastructure projects known as the Big Build.

“As a lifelong believer in trade unions, it was shocking to see so much crime, so much corruption, such a perversion of values,” Watson wrote. “The CFMEU was no longer on the right side of civil society, it was proudly on the wrong side. The Union was no longer the champion of the working class – the Setka era CFMEU turned to looking after gangsters, standover men, bikies, heroin traffickers, and even killers. By the end of this investigation I have been left with the empty feeling that the Setka-led Victorian branch of the CFMEU was no longer a trade union, it was a crime syndicate.”

Provocatively, Watson also asserted that the scale of corruption was partly helped by political indifference – a kind of wilful blindness. This view was removed from the final draft, a fact we learnt when news of the omissions leaked and lawyers, their curiosity aroused, had the cut sections tabled during Queensland’s commission of inquiry into that state’s branch of the CFMEU.

“It’s appropriate that politicians and public servants should share the responsibility for what has happened – for allowing the CFMEU to run out of control,” Watson wrote. “It is not as though the excesses of the CFMEU have been a secret: the CFMEU revelled in bad publicity … If the press knew, then the public knew. If the public knew, then the Government must have known. More to the point, as the guardian of public money, the Government had a duty to know. It had a duty to monitor delays and costs-blowouts. There is no doubt the Government knew about the rising problem – but it is equally clear that the Government did nothing about it.”

For days after, Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan, who was the state’s infrastructure minister before her promotion three years ago, quivered with indignation. Testy media conferences followed. Allan zeroed in on a figure Watson has used – an estimate, as he qualifies in his report, that the cost of Big Build corruption was likely about $15 billion. The specificity of this figure, and Mark Irving’s private querying of it, had the unfortunate consequence of distracting from the wider findings by offering critics a number to quibble over and use to invite suspicion of Watson’s reliability. “That claim, of any amount, has not been well tested or properly founded,” Allan said in February.

Her police minister, Anthony Carbines, went much further in his criticisms of Watson. “It might be good for a quote, but he’s not much good when it comes to coming up with some facts,” he said. “When his florid ramblings become facts that can be tested in court, all well and good. But if you’ve got evidence, give it to Victoria Police and they’ll take action.”

Watson says he was often in contact with Victoria Police during his investigations – that of course he was – and notes of anger sound when he thinks again of Carbines’ comments. At the time, Watson described the remarks as “Trumpian”, and this week it was made clear that the insult to his integrity still stings.

It was an unusual and unpleasant moment for Watson. His report had attracted the ire of both the Victorian government and the alleged underworld figures and allegedly corrupt former union officials named in it. For a time, they all were joined by the similarity of their denunciations of Watson. Lawsuits have followed, of which Watson cannot speak. “I think Geoffrey would have needed a thorough shower after those years of investigating this putrid mess,” one union source told The Saturday Paper this week. “And they’re still attacking him.”

Watson says he had not appreciated the scale of corruption in Victoria before he began investigating the union in 2024. Then again, why would he? He was a Sydney silk, ordinarily engaged with the prosecution of bent coppers and politicians in that state. “I wondered going into it if it was all a beat-up,” he says. “But on a scale of zero to 10 for corruption, NSW was a two or three. Queensland a five. Victoria was a 1000. Insane. There was trafficking of heroin on sites – and meth, coke. Bikie gangs were fighting each other for control of these sites.”

“I think Geoffrey would have needed a thorough shower after those years of investigating this putrid mess. And they’re still attacking him.”

There’s only one thing for it, Watson says, and his view was echoed by several union sources this week: a royal commission, or something similar, as was instated in Queensland. “If you really want to get to the bottom of all this, then you need a properly empowered public inquiry in the nature of a royal commission,” he says.

Labor’s Big Build, and its entanglement with union corruption and organised crime, will inevitably be invoked in the Victorian election campaign this year. The state will vote in November, when Labor will seek a fourth consecutive term. Union sources are not holding their breath for an inquiry, as proposed by Watson. Allan has made clear that she feels it unnecessary. “There’s no  way the Allan government would call one,” a union source says. “But a commission of inquiry, as happened in Queensland, is what’s needed. Only a serious, independent inquiry will do it.”

In January, the CFMEU’s national secretary, Zach Smith, abruptly resigned. “The reasons I am leaving are personal,” he wrote in a statement. “I cannot continue to serve the union in the way that the members deserve, and taking time away is in the best interests of myself, the people I care about and the union.”

What wasn’t revealed at that time was that he was being investigated by his boss, Mark Irving, for alleged undeclared conflicts of interest regarding romantic relationships with staff.

Irving inherited Smith. The union boss was someone viewed with contemptuous suspicion by whistleblowers within the CFMEU, given his previous closeness to expelled leader John Setka. Nonetheless, Irving was patient with Smith and forgave several missteps – such as when Smith directed a union official to meet with the notorious underworld figure Mick Gatto last year.

Yet Smith’s romantic entanglements, and his less-than-forthcoming disclosures of them and their subsequent conflicts of interest, made his time there untenable. Irving felt personally betrayed, as did many others within the union, who had received from Smith misleading assurances.

Then, in April, Irving resigned. “The Union is changing its personnel,” he said. “It is changing its culture. It is regaining its position in civil society. The rebuild phase requires a different approach … and a different set of skills.”

This was less of a surprise than Smith’s departure. Irving had received a “hospital pass”, in the words of one union source, and inherited a complex and potentially dangerous job. He suffered a heart attack last year and had subsequent surgery, and from early in his tenure was the recipient of several credible death threats. This obliged the deployment of personal security. Sources have told me how Irving learnt to choose tables in restaurants and cafes that provided clear sightlines to the door. “The threats were very, very serious,” one source says. “These were serious people.”

Geoffrey Watson is happy to concede that in his time as corruption investigator, there were disagreements with Irving. They were “always civil”, he says, and not for the first time he stresses Irving’s decency.

“It’s difficult to overstate the difficulty of his job,” Watson says. “And he was earning much less money than he would at the bar. I have great respect for him.”

Nonetheless, in the almost two years of the CFMEU’s government mandated administration, there has been significant staff tumult. Poor appointments were made of people facing serious allegations, who were then sacked or offered generous severance packages, and the departure of Smith means that in under two years the Victorian branch has had four different leaders.

There has been attrition in the administrator’s office also – not only Irving’s departure but also several support staff. None of this surprises one whistleblower. “Look, a lot of Labor or ACTU associated unionists came in to fix the problem,” they say. “But construction is an entirely different culture. They were outsiders to this: people plucked from outside the culture and then dropped into maximum security.”

Irving has been replaced by Michael Crosby, a veteran unionist and former executive of the CFMEU’s NSW branch. Even among the most militant and impatient agitators for reform within the union, there’s begrudging respect for his reputation for integrity and a willingness to confer some benefit of doubt. That said, there remains scepticism of the appointment of another man with very little experience in construction.

“The next phase” begins, as Mark Irving said, but union sources told me they have no idea what that means. A lawsuit alleging a Champaign doctor botched an abortion was settled last month.

Dr. Keith Reisinger-Kindle was accused of leaving part of a fetus inside a woman and puncturing  her uterus while performing an abortion  at Champaign-based Equity Clinic in April 2023. When she started experiencing extreme cramping, Reisinger-Kindle allegedly told her to take Tylenol and laxatives.

The woman sued Reisinger-Kindle and Equity Clinic in March 2025. They reached a settlement on July 8, according to the News Gazette newspaper in central Illinois.

The woman’s lawyer at the Chicago firm McNabola & Associates declined to comment. Reisinger-Kindle’s lawyers at Pretzel & Stouffer did not respond to a request for comment.

The woman, a mother of four, was about 22 weeks along when she sought an abortion from Reisinger-Kindle, according to her suit. Two days after the procedure, she was still experiencing cramps, so she went to the emergency room.

That’s when doctors found parts of a fetus in her right pelvis and surgically removed them. Doctors also found a hole in her uterus about the size of a quarter, according to the suit. Reisinger-Kindle allegedly refused to answer questions or share information with one of the surgeons who operated on the woman.

In July 2025, Reisinger-Kindle was disciplined by the state and fined $5,000. He also had to complete 20 hours of continuing medical education for failing to properly evaluate a patient.

Clinicians at an Irish treatment center have warned that Chemsex is increasingly presenting as a treatment issue in Ireland, noting substantial levels of recreational and sexualized drug use among gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men.

Chemsex is defined as the intentional use of specific drugs before or during sex to facilitate, enhance, or prolong sexual experiences. Irish research has shown that LGBTQI+ people can face specific barriers in mental health care, including fear of misunderstanding and lower confidence in practitioners' knowledge of LGBTQI+ identities.

According to Smarmore Castle, a private rehab clinic in Co Louth, research has documented that LGBTQI+ communities have faced experiences of stigma and discrimination that can make it harder to seek help.

Those experiences have been linked to higher rates of distress, self-harm, suicidality, eating disorders and other trauma-related conditions.

Chemsex often requires care that is informed by sexual health and mental health, and by the need to create space for people to talk about their experiences openly, without feeling judged or misunderstood.

"Chemsex rarely arrives in the consulting room as a simple drug issue," says Stephen Murray, a therapist at Smarmore Castle.

"People may be struggling with dependency, but also with anxiety, secrecy, low mood, relationship difficulties, sexual health concerns, or a sense that parts of their lives have become increasingly difficult to talk about."

"Effective treatment starts with understanding the whole person rather than focusing solely on the substance use," Murray added.

"Too many of the people we see tell us they've previously felt judged, misunderstood, or unable to be fully honest about their experiences when seeking support."

"When people are concerned about how they will be perceived, they may delay reaching out for help altogether. Creating a non-judgemental environment where people feel respected, heard and understood is fundamental to effective treatment."

Chen Xi stared at the table. At the impossible thing sitting there.

Her brows slowly knit together, lips parting just slightly as her thoughts tangled into knots she couldn’t undo.

'A coincidence?'

Her fingers curled under her chin as she leaned forward.

'A fateful encounter?'

Her eyes narrowed. Then widened.

'Or am I still dreaming?'

She blinked once. Twice.

Then her posture straightened abruptly, as if struck by lightning.

'Wait…'

Her hand slid from her chin to hover midair, trembling with realization.

'Have I somehow become an oracle?!'

She sucked in a breath, eyes gleaming.

'Or… did I attain enlightenment in my sleep?'

Her gaze lifted slightly, as though already looking down at the world from some unseen peak.

A slow smile spread across her face.

'Doesn’t that make me… a living legend?'

Her chin tilted up. Her shoulders squared.

The smile sharpened into something dangerously close to pride.

'Aren’t I amazing?'

Her thoughts spiraled higher, leaping from one absurd possibility to an even greater one, each more unbelievable than the last.

Completely unaware—

That she was not alone in stillness.

Xu Kai stood a few steps away, watching her. Silently.

His gaze traced every shift in her expression, the subtle furrow of concentration, the widening of her eyes, the flicker of shock, the bloom of awe… then more awe… then unmistakable pride.

He exhaled through his nose and shook his head faintly.

“She has lost it.”

He made no move to interrupt her.

Instead, he turned away and walked toward the table.

His steps were light. Unhurried. The kind that made no sound unless one listened for it, and Chen Xi was far too busy ascending to legendhood to notice.

He pulled out a chair and sat. The wood barely creaked.

Reaching for his chopsticks, he picked up a piece of chicken. Steam curled faintly from it.

Without hesitation, he brought it to his mouth. Chewed. Paused.

A smile tugged at his lips.

He always enjoyed his cooking.

It was simple, dependable. Something that never betrayed him. Whenever he ate food he made himself, something in him loosened, like a knot quietly unraveling.

A small, steady source of happiness.

He took another bite, slower this time.

In his past life, that had been enough.

There had been no one else. No one to cook for him. No one to wait for him.

Growing up, the house had been quiet more often than not. His parents were rarely home, and so he learned early, if he didn’t take care of himself, no one would.

Cooking. Cleaning. Washing.

He had done it all. Because he had to.

Even later, when he started working, nothing changed. His days were swallowed by work, his time devoured whole. Relationships… never had the chance to take root.

Not because he couldn’t. But because there was simply no space for them.

Xu Kai’s smile softened, tinged with something quieter.

'Strange.'

Thinking about that life now, in this unfamiliar world… it didn’t feel as heavy as it once did.

If anything, it felt distant. Almost… reassuring.

He lifted another piece of chicken and ate.

Then paused. His brows drew together slightly.

He chewed again, slower.

He had eaten chicken more times than he could count.

But—

This was different.

He picked up another piece.

The flavor was richer. Deeper. There was something else woven into it, something he couldn’t quite name.

A faint warmth spread across his tongue, then down his throat.

Like a current.

Like—

“Huh!”

The sharp sound cut through the room.

Chen Xi jolted, her body stiffening as if someone had yanked her back from the heavens.

Her head snapped toward the table. Toward him.

Xu Kai glanced up, completely unsurprised.

“Welcome back to reality.”

Chen Xi blinked.

Once. Twice.

Her gaze moved from his face… to the food… back to his face… then back to the food again.

Her expression was blank for a moment, as if her mind had simply stopped.

Processing. Trying to catch up.

“Master…” she said slowly, her voice uncertain. “…are you eating?”

Xu Kai looked at her, then at the plate in front of him, then back at her again.

“It’s exactly as you are seeing,” he replied calmly. “Yes.”

Chen Xi froze.

Her entire face twisted into a single, silent question.

'How?'

Her brows furrowed deeper. Her lips pressed together.

Her eyes darted around the room, as if retracing invisible steps.

'How did he get there without me noticing?'

'How did he start eating… and I didn’t hear a thing?'

'How did he go from standing right beside me… to sitting there… halfway done with the food?'

Her head tilted slightly, like a machine struggling to compute.

'How did everything happen?'

She stared at him. Then at the plate. Then at him again.

And the more she looked—

The less sense it made.

And—

Chen Xi’s stunned silence snapped like a stretched thread.

“Why are you eating without me?!”

Her voice rang through the room, sharp and indignant. She took a step forward, eyes blazing, finger already half-raised in accusation.

Xu Kai didn’t even flinch.

He calmly set down his chopsticks, glanced at her, and spoke as if explaining something painfully obvious.

“I saw you thinking about something,” he said. “Or… well, trying to think. It was written all over your face.”

A faint pause.

“So I didn’t interrupt. Didn’t want to ruin your… daydream.” His lips twitched. “And, by the way, you spent quite a long time.”

Chen Xi froze mid-step.

Her raised hand slowly lowered.

'That’s—'

She blinked, her anger faltering as realization crept in.

'So that’s what happened…'

For a brief moment, she looked almost embarrassed.

Then her chin lifted again.

“But that doesn’t change anything!” she declared, straightening her back and placing a hand on her hip. “It is improper to leave a guest standing while you eat first!”

Xu Kai rolled his eyes without hesitation.

“You’re not a guest.”

Chen Xi scoffed, the sound loud and dramatic.

“I may not be a guest to the house,” she shot back, leaning forward slightly, her finger now pointed directly at him, “but you cooked and invited me to eat. That makes me your dining guest. And as such, it is only proper for you to treat me well!”

Her lips curved into a smug smile.

'Perfect. Let’s see how you counter that, Master.'

Xu Kai didn’t even need a second.

“Did I ever say I was proper?”

Chen Xi deflated instantly. Her shoulders dropped. Her mouth opened… then closed.

She had lost. Again.

“…Master, you are the worst.”

Xu Kai ignored her completely, picking his chopsticks back up as if she hadn’t spoken at all.

“Come eat,” he said casually. “Your food is getting cold.”

“It’s already cold.”

“It’s getting colder.”

Chen Xi clicked her tongue but didn’t argue further. Instead, she walked over and dropped into the seat across from him.

Then she saw it properly. Her eyes widened.

The table was filled, plate after plate, arranged in neat abundance. Steaming dishes, rich colors, the scent of seasoning hanging thick in the air.

For a moment, she just stared.

“Master…” she said slowly, her gaze sweeping across the spread. “How did you cook this much?”

Xu Kai shrugged lightly.

“I’ll admit, it took a while,” he said. “I had to get used to the kitchen first. Then I went through the cooking book to find meals we had ingredients for. Since I couldn’t go out.”

Chen Xi hummed thoughtfully, nodding along.

“Then let’s go out next time!” she said suddenly, her tone brightening. She leaned forward, enthusiasm lighting up her face. “I can show you the path I usually take to the nearest city near Lud Forest. And around the city too!”

Xu Kai glanced at her, then gave a small nod.

“Sure. That would be great.”

Chen Xi smiled, satisfied, as if she had just accomplished something significant.

Then her attention snapped back to the food.

“Wow…”

She quickly wiped at the corner of her mouth before any drool could betray her, grabbed her chopsticks, and dove in.

A piece of chicken. A bite of rice.

She chewed. Slowly at first.

Then her eyes closed. Her shoulders relaxed, and a soft, almost blissful expression spread across her face as she savored the taste.

“Mhm… this is good,” she murmured, more to herself than anyone else.

Her chopsticks didn’t stop moving.

“Master, how did you cook something this good?” she asked, already reaching for another dish, her cheeks puffed slightly as she spoke through a mouthful.

Xu Kai watched her for a moment before answering.

“I told you,” he said. “I just followed the instructions in the cooking book. Nothing special.”

Chen Xi’s head snapped up.

“Nothing special?!” she repeated, incredulous. She pointed her chopsticks at the dishes. “This is from a mid-stage cooking book! Sure, the rice and chicken might be from the beginner section, but the rest aren’t!”

She shook her head, eyes shining.

“This is amazing!”

Xu Kai chuckled softly, leaning back slightly as he watched her devour the meal.

A moment ago, she had been sulking.

Now—

She looked like someone who had forgotten the world existed beyond the table.

He didn’t mind. If anything, he felt… satisfied.

Then suddenly—

Chen Xi stopped.

Her chopsticks hovered mid-air. Her chewing slowed… then ceased.

“Master,” she said.

Her tone had changed.

Xu Kai’s gaze sharpened slightly.

“You said you made this food using the instructions from the cooking book?”

“Yes.”

A pause.

Chen Xi lowered her chopsticks slowly, placing them against the edge of her bowl with deliberate care.

“But…” she began, her brows drawing together as her eyes locked onto him, “that’s impossible.”

The air shifted.

“Someone with no experience in cooking,” she continued, her voice quieter now but far more focused, “someone who doesn’t even know how to properly handle cooking tools… can’t just follow a book once and make something like this without mistakes.”

Xu Kai stilled.

Her eyes narrowed slightly.

“And earlier,” she added, leaning forward just a fraction, “when I asked you how you did it… you froze.”

Her gaze sharpened, piercing.

“Why?”

For a law-abiding man who wants to comply with the rules of the city he has called home for the last quarter century, Robert Schwartz was taken aback this spring when he saw a sign on the High Line Canal trail in Cherry Hills Village prohibiting electric bicycles.

There are, in fact, at least two “No e-bike” signs along the heavily used trail inside the affluent Arapahoe County city — a diagonal red slash drawn across a stick figure riding a bike with an electric plug attached.

Schwartz, a retired geriatrician who knows a thing or two about the value of exercise for older folks like himself, first noticed one of the signs at the Dahlia Street High Line trailhead in April. He was left to wonder how many seniors might be skipping their daily ride for fear of getting nabbed by the e-bike police.

“If you want to obey the law and don’t want to get in trouble, a sign staring you in the face telling you you can’t do this is limiting,” said Schwartz, 78.

He said he’s tried to get the attention of city leaders to reconsider the ban but hasn’t heard back.

“Older people are limited in the kind of exercise they can get that is free from pain and discomfort,” Schwartz said. “What is not terribly impactful for a 30-year-old, 40-year-old or 50-year-old can be very detrimental to someone who is 75 years old, 85 years old or older. E-bikes assist you in pedaling.”

The High Line Canal is a 71-mile ditch, mostly owned by Denver Water, that runs through 11 jurisdictions from Waterton Canyon in Douglas County to Aurora.

The High Line Canal Conservancy calls the accompanying trail “one of the longest continuous urban trails in the country.” And for the vast majority of its length, e-bikes are permitted, including in Greenwood Village and Denver, between which Cherry Hills Village lies.

But in the city of 6,400, where the houses are big and the lots even bigger, they are not. That presents a continuity conundrum for users entering the several miles of the High Line Canal trail that lie inside Cherry Hills Village.

E-bikes also aren’t allowed in Waterton Canyon, where the U.S. Forest Service oversees portions of the trail. The federal agency considers the path at the western terminus of the canal trail a “non-motorized path,” Denver Water spokesman Travis Thompson said.

There are exceptions for those with disabilities, he said.

Cherry Hills Village has for years forbidden any motorized vehicles on its trails, said spokeswoman Denise White. 				
					
				
“The citywide rule reflects safety considerations on trails shared by pedestrians, bicyclists, children, pets and equestrians,” she said. “Because e-bikes have motors, all classes of e-bikes fall within that prohibition.”

There is an exception for e-bikes used by “an individual with a disability for mobility assistance,” White said.

E-bikes generally come in three flavors, with Class 1 models requiring the rider to pedal to get the electric boost while Class 2 models provide power regardless of pedaling. Both classes of bike top out at 20 mph. Class 3 e-bikes also require pedal power to trigger electric help. They can go as fast as 28 mph.

The number of people riding e-bikes is steadily rising and efforts to corral their use will likely face increasing pushback.

According to Mordor Intelligence, U.S. e-bike sales reached nearly $3.8 billion last year. That number is expected to reach slightly more than $4 billion this year, with projections of nearly $5.8 billion in e-bike sales in 2031. 
Last week, the Colorado Energy Office announced it was resurrecting its popular e-bike rebate program, offering $1,000 discounts toward the purchase of a new e-bike to more than 2,800 income-qualified residents over the next year.

Pete Piccolo, executive director at Bicycle Colorado, said bans on e-bikes “disproportionately impact older riders and people with disabilities who rely on e-bikes for transportation or recreation.”

“E-bikes are an accessible, environmentally friendly way that many Coloradans get to work, run errands and spend time outdoors with family,” he said. “We believe there are numerous other strategies to improve safety and address fast, unpredictable riders on a shared trail, other than a ban.”

One of those is enforcing a speed limit regardless of vehicle type, he said.

“Trail conflicts are real,” Piccolo said, but the heart of the issue lies in “speed and behavior, not the type of bike someone rides.”

“A posted limit applies to everyone on the trail, whether they are riding a traditional bike or an e-bike,” he said. “A ban excludes a category of rider regardless of how they actually ride.”

The posted speed limit on Cherry Hills Village’s portion of the High Line Canal trail is 15 mph. Richard Spritz, a resident for nearly three decades, said that threshold should be what guides use on the trail.

“Simply have speed limits you enforce,” he said.

Cherry Hills Village police have not cited anyone for illegal use of an e-bike on the High Line Canal trail in the last year, White said, but officers often give a warning for a first offense rather than issuing a ticket.

Spritz, a pediatrician, treats the opposite end of the age spectrum than Schwartz, his fellow villager, once did. But he knows from his own advance in years — he’s 75 — that e-bikes give a rider like him “the juice to just get over the hump.”

“It keeps people mobile,” he said.

Relief could be coming for e-bike lovers in Cherry Hills Village.

White, the city spokeswoman, said the city’s Parks, Trails and Recreation Commission has plans to review e-bike regulations early next year, which could be “the first step in determining whether the commission wishes to recommend any changes to the municipal code for City Council consideration.”

Schwartz hopes a discussion will be held sooner than 2027.

“That six months is a really important time span,” he said. “Being sedentary is terrible for older people. Acting on this faster for older people is important.”

As Illinois joins the country in commemorating 250 years of American history, we’ve been given an opportunity to reflect on the people, places and institutions that have shaped our state — and how our state has helped shape this nation through innovation, culture and civic leadership.

It’s no secret that this milestone is arriving in the middle of significant tension. While so much of our attention is focused on the challenges immediately in front of us — from rising inflation to global conflict — it can be easy to overlook what connects us as Americans, to each other and to our shared history.

Luckily, spaces already exist that are specifically designed to preserve our stories, inspire creativity and help pass Illinois’ legacy on to future generations: museums, libraries, cultural organizations and other public areas that welcome residents and visitors alike.

These institutions capture our most enduring contributions — genre-shaping music, sculptural architecture, great literature, vibrant visual art, provocative theater and more. By protecting and spotlighting these creations, we help the world see Illinois as a whole while ensuring these stories remain accessible for future generations.

The Tribune’s Illinois 250 project recently highlighted many of the innovations and traditions that began here and went on to influence the nation. The contributions that established our city and our state as a center of creativity and cultural expression were nurtured by generations of artists, educators, civic leaders and institutions that made creativity accessible and helped preserve our collective story. People travel from all over the world to experience a fraction of what Chicago has to offer. Those experiences leave visitors with a deeper appreciation for Illinois while reminding residents that the places they pass every day are part of a cultural legacy recognized around the world.

These landmarks are civic assets.

For years, I’ve been advocating to strengthen Chicago’s cultural campus and support the institutions that make our city a global cultural destination — not only because tourism drives economic growth, but because the impact of these spaces matters to Illinois’ own communities and strengthens neighborhoods across our city.

They educate our children. They provide lifelong learning opportunities for residents of every age. They support artists and cultural workers. They create jobs and economic activity. They preserve our history and create opportunities for people to learn from one another. Perhaps most importantly, they help foster a shared sense of identity and belonging.

These places also remind us that history is something we actively preserve, not something that simply survives on its own. Every exhibit, restored landmark, neighborhood library and public performance help connect one generation to the next. They encourage curiosity, spark conversation and provide opportunities for people of every background to better understand one another. At a time when so much seems to divide us, investing in our cultural institutions is also an investment in civic life. They give us spaces where our stories can be explored, challenged and ultimately passed on with greater understanding.

As we reflect on 250 years of American history, we should also think about the legacy we hope to leave behind in Illinois.

Future generations will inherit the institutions we choose to support today. They will learn from the stories we prioritize, the art we celebrate and the cultural spaces we invest in. The decisions we make now will help determine whether those institutions continue to thrive for decades to come.

Chicago’s cultural impact has helped shape our country’s story over the last 250 years. If we want Illinois’ museums, libraries and cultural institutions to help shape the next 250, we must treat them as essential public assets worthy of our continued support.

Ald. Samantha Nugent represents Chicago’s 39th Ward.

The Chicago Board of Elections ruled Tuesday that nearly two dozen school board candidates can’t be disqualified simply because their petition circulators also worked partisan races, removing a significant hurdle for nearly two dozen hopefuls in the election.

The provision known as the dual-circulation rule had been used to challenge the nominating papers of 22 school board candidates. Had the board determined that the law could be applied, it may have wiped most from contention.

“We always hear in these arguments that ballot access is a substantial right in Illinois,” election attorney Ed Mullen told the elections board, arguing on candidates’ behalf. “In this case, it is of greater importance, because this is the first time in history that we’re going to have a fully elected school board.”

The rule says that petition circulators can’t collect signatures for multiple types of candidates in the same election cycle — which includes working for candidates in different parties, or for both independent and partisan candidates.

School board races are nonpartisan, but challengers argued the rule still applied because many candidates used circulators who gathered signatures in the March Democratic primary.

The provision was initially created to prevent candidates who lose partisan primaries from running again in the general election as independents. Attorneys for the candidates contended that it had never been applied to a nonpartisan race.

The objections process is time-consuming and costly: Both the objector and the candidate typically must hire attorneys, as election judges review the validity of contested signatures one by one.

Tuesday’s ruling will be used as guidance for hearing officers as they address individual cases, according to the board. While it doesn’t guarantee candidates’ places on the ballot, it means they can move forward with more standard challenges to their petitions.

Last month, on the final day of the Illinois General Assembly session, lawmakers attempted to clarify that the provision does not apply to school board races in an omnibus election bill. But the change, which was proposed by state Sen. Robert Martwick, did not pass. Martwick is a close ally of the Chicago Teachers Union, but told the Tribune the union was not involved — though it would have benefited a large number of CTU-aligned candidates.

At total of 51 candidates filed to run for 21 seats. Previously, the board was made up of seven mayoral appointees. The board is approaching the end of a two-year transition period, with 10 elected members and 11 mayoral appointees.

The list of candidates for the November election will be finalized Aug. 27.

Maeve Priestley started using a bar to protect the steering wheel of her Honda Civic after her air bag was stolen earlier this year outside her home in Lake View.

Manuel Martinez / WBEZ

Share

Maeve Priestley was overcome with anxiety when she woke up early one morning and discovered the driver’s side window of her Honda Civic had been smashed out.

Priestley, 26, cried outside her Lake View condo building as she assessed the damage and realized an air bag had been ripped out of her steering wheel. She didn’t know what to do, so she called her dad.

“It’s a very violating experience,” says Priestley, a special education teacher. “I felt very panicked.”

She was among the more than 1,200 victims of air bag thefts in Chicago in the first four months of this year. Between 2023 and 2025, there were only 70 such thefts, according to Chicago police data.

Amid this year’s surge, the Chicago Police Department has suspended air bag theft investigations more quickly. And virtually all of the cases have gone unsolved, a Chicago Sun-Times analysis of the data found.

The one man charged with stealing air bags this year has entered into a deferred prosecution agreement, meaning he won’t be convicted if he meets conditions imposed by the court.

A police spokesperson says theft investigations “often take time and can be difficult to solve without video or forensic evidence.”

Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th) says he wants to give police another “tool” to address the spike in thefts. He’s proposed a crackdown on the black market for air bags that the City Council is expected to vote on Wednesday.

His ward, which covers parts of the West and Northwest sides, includes some of the hardest-hit neighborhoods.

Lake View, where Priestley lives, has seen the most air bag thefts. Together with West Town, Logan Square, Belmont Cragin, Humboldt Park and Avondale, just six neighborhoods accounted for 42% of all reported thefts citywide.

“Where I live is super family-friendly,” Priestley says, “so that was just really surprising.”

Anthony Riccio, who retired as the second-ranking Chicago police official, says the rise in air bag thefts likely means criminals have noticed that police aren’t doing much to combat the problem.

Thieves smash car windows, swipe air bags and sell them on the black market for a few hundred bucks. Because thefts happen in minutes, or even seconds, it’s tough to make arrests, according to Riccio.

“Word has gotten out that this is an easy thing to do,” he says. “Minimal tools, super quick, easy turnover, very profitable.”

Anthony Riccio, a former Chicago Police Department first deputy superintendent

Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times

Police have suspended air bag theft investigations quicker as the caseload has grown, records show. Of the more than 1,260 theft cases opened this year, almost 60% had already been suspended.

“Various units,” including the police department’s five detective areas, are tasked with investigating the thefts, according to the police spokesperson, who says cases are only suspended “when all investigative avenues are fully pursued.

“A suspended case will be reopened at any time additional evidence provides leads,” the spokesperson says.

The spokesperson acknowledged that thefts are hard to crack without video or other evidence. But Priestley says the police never asked for photos or videos that might have helped solve her case even though her neighbors have Ring cameras and she took still photos of the crime scene.

Her case was suspended in 26 days, records show.

In addition to the abysmal arrest rate, police have struggled to maintain accurate data tracking air bag thefts, records show. Roughly 4% of the cases analyzed by the Sun-Times were erroneously classified as air bag thefts.

The Sun-Times spoke to more than a dozen representatives for automotive and public safety organizations. No one could offer a clear reason for the rise in air bag thefts.

What’s clear is that Hondas are the primary target. But Lynn Sealey, a Honda spokesperson, says the automaker only receives notice of an air bag theft in “unusual cases.” She says Honda’s primary concern is air bag deployment and safety.

Sair Arapovic, who owns Royce Auto in Bensenville, says Honda’s air bags are actually harder to steal than those installed in some other vehicles. That’s because the air bag compartments have a screw on each side, Arapovic says.

“Most of the air bags are just like a spring system, that all you have to do to remove it is [use] a pry tool that goes on the side of the steering wheel,” he says. “And literally, if you get the right position, it just pops out.”

A Honda with a stolen air bag sits at Royce Auto in Bensenville waiting to be repaired.

Manuel Martinez/WBEZ

Most thieves target cars parked on residential streets, but the circumstances were different in the only theft case that prompted charges this year.

In mid-March, a group allegedly stole air bags from a used car lot in Little Village. They slid the air bags under a fence, then fled in a Volkswagen SUV and hit a forklift that tried to stop them, according to a police report.

An 18-year-old man from Elgin was arrested and charged, the report says. But based on an agreement he made with prosecutors, he won’t be convicted if he stays out of trouble for a year and isn’t caught with a weapon.

No one has been arrested this year in any of the more common theft cases in residential neighborhoods .

Villegas’ proposal would impose higher fines on those caught reselling stolen air bags.

Under the ordinance, junk dealers, pawn shops and auto repair stores must keep receipts proving where they got each of their airbags.

Shops caught buying and selling stolen air bags could face up to a $4,000 fine for the first violation. If a shop is caught multiple times within the span of a year, fines could increase by $2,000 or more.

But Villegas’ “common sense” ordinance doesn’t address how police would actually find those resellers. He says he doesn’t know whether police have bolstered resources to address the increase in thefts.

“All I’m trying to do is provide [police] a tool, so that way we can try to address this huge spike in these air bag thefts,” he says.

Ald. Gilbert Villegas, shown in 2024, is proposing fines for junk dealers, pawn shops and auto repair stores caught reselling stolen airbags.

Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times

The full City Council is expected to vote on the measure Wednesday.

Riccio, the former first deputy police superintendent, says the ordinance is “a step in the right direction.” But he wants to see one key provision to heighten the stakes for auto shops — a so-called presumption of illegal possession clause.

He says the police should visit auto shops and demand documentation of their air bag inventory to check if they’re selling stolen goods. If shops don’t have the proper documentation, authorities would automatically assume the shop sells stolen air bags and would impose penalties.

“They can pass all the ordinances they want in the City Council,” he says. “If there’s not enforcement, essentially it’s not an effective ordinance.”

The 2600 block of North Orchard Street, a sleepy tree-lined stretch of Lincoln Park, is among the blocks that have been hardest hit by air bag thefts.

Parked cars line the 2600 block of North Orchard Street in Lincoln Park, one of the blocks hardest hit by air bag thefts this year.

Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times

Residents have taken note. A handful of Hondas parked near Orchard and Schubert Avenue this month were equipped with bulky metal steering wheel bars. One sedan even had a full metal casing over its wheel.

Jinyoung Koh, 42, says her Honda CR-V was hit in mid-March, along with six other cars in the same day. Koh says she had to pay a $1,000 insurance deductible and that the repairs took months because air bags were on back order.

She was shocked to hear the low arrest numbers:

“What are police officers doing? What kind of actions are they taking? And what are their strategic plans to reduce this crime?”

big_bend_border:
By

Carlos Morales

John Rakowitz waves a 'Don't tread on Big Bend' flag at a rally at Big Bend National Park, a pristine pocket of the West Texas border where the federal government is looking to build patrol roads, vehicle barriers and surveillance systems.
                
                    
                    Carlos Morales/For NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

BIG BEND NATIONAL PARK, Texas – At the foot of Santa Elena Canyon – perhaps the most iconic and photographed stretch of Big Bend National Park – Joan Stutts Escamilla sits in silence by the edge of the Rio Grande.

"It's such a god-given gift," the 70-year-old said, looking up at the canyon's 1,500-foot tall limestone cliffs. "There's just nothing, there's nothing else like this."

But within the last week, federal contractors have moved heavy machinery into the national park, bulldozing through desert shrubs and clearing ecologically sensitive land.

Bright pink ribbons now mark a construction path where willow and mesquite trees once stood.

The $1.7 billion construction plans include a combination of vehicle barriers, winding patrol roads and new surveillance technology.

It's all part of the Trump administration's effort to stop illegal border crossings into the U.S. The Trump administration is bypassing environmental laws for the project. This month a federal judge declined to block construction.

Just north of Big Bend National Park, work crews clear land for a staging site holding excavators, bulldozers and trailers.
                
                    
                    Carlos Morales/for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

In the Big Bend area, the plans have ignited an impassioned coalition of landowners, outdoor enthusiasts and business owners – people across the political spectrum – who all say any work in the national park would forever change the rugged and beloved land often called "Texas' gift to the nation."

"If we lose places like Big Bend, we never get them back," said Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity, a national conservation nonprofit currently suing the federal government over its border barrier projects. "The destruction that will be inflicted here will truly be irreparable."

The Trump administration's initial plans for Big Bend National Park included the construction of 30-foot walls. Following a widespread outcry, contractors will now build patrol roads, vehicle barriers and surveillance systems, according to details shared by Customs and Border Protection.

In a statement to NPR, CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said the work is intended to help border patrol "detect illegal crossings, respond faster, and assist visitors in danger."

But illegal border crossings in the Big Bend Sector – an area covering 517 miles along the U.S.-Mexico border – have dropped significantly.

According to CBP, they made up the fewest number of encounters along the Texas border in fiscal year 2025. Within the national park itself, the number is even lower, according to a local advocacy group.

Commissioner Scott said that what people are seeing within the park right now is related to survey and design work and not construction. The purpose of the new infrastructure, he said, is to secure the park and "protect its legacy."

Joan Stutts Escamilla sits in silence by the edge of the Rio Grande near the iconic limestone cliffs of Santa Elena Canyon. "It's such a god-given gift," said Escamilla.
                
                    
                    Carlos Morales/for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

"We already have effective border security here," said Bernadette Devine, a local educator and former river guide, who is calling on the state's top politicians to help stop the construction.

Republican Sen. John Cornyn last week asked federal officials to meet with locals before moving forward with any additional work here.

Gov. Greg Abbott's office didn't respond to NPR's recent requests for comment on the work within the national park, and instead shared a previous comment on the area. "Rugged, isolated areas like Big Bend are great opportunities to deploy technology to aid in securing the border," the governor's press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris said.

Retired wildlife biologist Raymond Skiles, who spent decades at Big Bend National Park, leads protesters in chanting "No Big Bend Wall."
                
                    
                    Carlos Morales/for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

At Santa Elena Canyon, local river guide Billy Miller speaks into a megaphone – his voice slightly bouncing off the canyon walls.

"The river's being threatened as we speak," Miller told a crowd of nearly 150 people on Wednesday, some standing in the river's waters, others on the banks holding signs that read 'don't bulldoze my church' and 'don't tread on Big Bend.'

"A lot of people might think, 'Well, we saved it from the 30-foot wall, we won the battle," Miller said. "The battle is just now beginning."

While the fight inside the national park is reaching a critical point, the federal government's border security efforts are also progressing outside the park.

Staging sites have been set up in rural West Texas, where the Trump administration is looking to secure private land in border counties to make way for up to 175 miles of steel fencing.

A quiet, two-lane highway – affectionately called 'river road' hugs the Texas-Mexico border – leads to the sprawling 800,000 acres of Big Bend National Park.
                
                    
                    Carlos Morales/for NPR.
