Jeff Bezos, pictured with his wife Lauren Sanchez Bezos, is part of a group that has bought a stake in Liverpool. (Getty Images: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg)

An investor group that includes Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has bought a 30 per cent stake in Liverpool.

Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin and British-Indian entrepreneur Amit Bhatia are also part of the group.

The deal values Liverpool at $US6 billion but will not lead to the immediate ability to spend more on players.

A consortium containing Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin is buying a minority stake in Premier League club Liverpool, the English soccer giant says.

Club owner Fenway Sports Group (FSG) said in a statement it entered into a "definitive agreement" for the sale to 1892 Holdings.

The investor group is led by Amit Bhatia, who is married to a daughter of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, and has taken a stake of more than 30 per cent in the 20-time English champion. The deal reportedly values Liverpool at around $US6 billion ($8.4 billion).

Boston-based FSG paid $US400 million to take over Liverpool in 2010 and also owns the Boston Red Sox. FSG said in July that it had been approached by the Bhatia-led consortium regarding a "strategic minority investment" in the club.

Eduardo Saverin is part of the investment group with Jeff Bezos. (Getty Images: Sam Barnes/Sportsfile)

"As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special," FSG president Mike Gordon said in the statement.

It marks the first foray into soccer by Bezos, who, according to Forbes, is the fourth-richest person in the world with a net worth of about $US280 billion. He founded Amazon in 1994 and has been executive chairman since 2021.

Saverin is a Brazilian businessman worth about $US36 billion, according to Forbes.

Bhatia, a British-Indian entrepreneur, was the co-owner of second-tier English team Queens Park Rangers for 18 years before stepping down recently.

Amit Bhatia during his time as the chairman of Queens Park Rangers. (Getty Images: Steven Paston/PA Images)

"We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club's continued success for years to come," Bhatia said in the statement.

Under the leadership of FSG and its principal owner John Henry, Liverpool ended a 30-year wait to be English champion in 2020 and added another Premier League title last year. That tied Manchester United on 20 English top-flight league championships.

The club was European champion for a sixth time — a record for an English team — in 2019.

The Premier League is one of the biggest competitions in sports, with its teams now largely owned by oil-rich Gulf states or private equity.

The Dutchman won the Premier League title in his first season, but failed to live up to expectations the following year as Liverpool finished fifth.

Liverpool now has three of the richest people in the world as minority owners.

That does not mean, however, that the club can simply start spending recklessly in the transfer market on new players.

That is because the Premier League has financial rules in place to protect the competitive balance of the competition and ensure the financial sustainability of clubs.

In broad terms, a club's on-pitch spending is related to 85 per cent of its "football-related revenue and net profit/loss from player sales," the Premier League says.

Instead, the difference will come in how Liverpool — already one of the top teams in world soccer — is marketed more around the world under Bezos and Saverin, especially.

The deal is likely to bring more commercial revenue into the club, thereby improving its profits.

911-shared-identity-quaint:
Americans liked each other.

To think about 9/11, start eighty-two years earlier. This is my favorite story about who we used to be.

In the summer of 1919, with soldiers home from World War I, the U.S. Army tested itself: If an enemy invaded the West Coast, how quickly could troops equipped with a new generation of cars and trucks, still an early technology, drive across the country to join the fight?

The Transcontinental Motor Convoy covered 3,251 miles from Washington, D.C. to San Francisco in sixty-two days, mostly on unpaved highways, with 81 cars and trucks. A young lieutenant colonel named Dwight Eisenhower went along as an observer, and he thought the dirt paths through the intermountain West didn’t deserve to be called roads. The not-quite 300 soldiers on the convoy broke dozens of primitive rural bridges and stopped to fix them, dragged trucks through mud and silt with ropes, and made their own replacement parts for damaged vehicles in a rolling machine shop. It was hard, dirty, exhausting travel.

But the convoy’s biggest problem just kept getting worse as it went west: The small towns where they took their scheduled stops were excessively pleased by the arrival of the motorized column. Whole communities turned out to greet them. Towns threw dances and picnics and banquets; soldiers arrived at their evening destinations and found tables laden with fresh pies and roasted chickens. A logistics exercise produced weddings and babies, an awkward reality that impaired the military objective of testing the cross-country speed of a wartime maneuver, and the convoy commander had to learn the art of gently declining an insistent brunch invitation. You can see some of that hospitality here, and look for the banquet in the giant canopy tent around the 4:14 mark:

Americans liked each other. Americans recognized each other, and felt pleasure to host a crowd of strangers. To a small town in Indiana or Nebraska, a military convoy from the East Coast was a bunch of our guys, a bunch of us, and the party started when the first trucks hit Main Street. The story is not about duty or obligation, and it’s not at all a story about obedience or a grim nationalism. It’s about a big rolling party that made people feel good.

On 9/11, people acted over and over again on their sense of mutuality and shared identity. In Manhattan, not famously a place where strangers smile at each other on the street, people died trying to help their injured countrymen. You can find these stories everywhere, the people who sat down to die halfway down a smoke-filled staircase but then felt a stranger’s hand pulling them back to their feet. Welles Crowther, still remembered as the man in the red bandana, “carried one burned woman down 17 flights, went back up, led another group out, and went up again.” He died doing it.

Immediately, instinctively, without hesitation, people who could help stopped for people who needed help. Firefighters died refusing evacuation orders, saying over the radio that they wouldn’t leave injured people under any circumstances:

“I refuse the order,” Captain Patrick Brown said. He died with his countrymen, choosing to share their danger when they were too badly hurt to help themselves, and not because anyone thought that he was required to. The opposite: His chain of command told him to run, and he wouldn’t.

When the towers fell, the evacuation of Lower Manhattan by water was explicitly ruleless and self-organizing. A Coast Guard lieutenant announced over the radio that everybody with a boat should just do whatever they had to do, and hundreds of boats swarmed the city to grab people and race for safety.

On 9/12, rural Wyoming and small town Arkansas were horrified and enraged by an attack on New York City and Washington, D.C., in a spontaneous moment of mutuality and shared identity. They attacked us. They attacked Iowa and South Carolina as much as they attacked Manhattan.

Some time has passed since then, and there are some obvious questions that can’t be avoided.

The school teacher Lucy Martinez making the gun motion at her neck mocking Charlie Kirk is a prime example of this moral decay and demonic evil. And she is still employed teaching children her violent behavior. pic.twitter.com/aIkx1qzzDm

TWANLOC: Those who are no longer our countrymen. If you haven’t read it, take a moment with the report on the Socialism 2026 conference from the pseudonymous writer at the Substack page called Bad Cattitude, which concludes that “the core of their beliefs stands antithetical to human flourishing.” Their beliefs are also antithetical to shared identity and mutual sympathy. They are not us, and they very much don’t think that we are them.

A major terrorist attack on an American city in 2026: What would the reaction look like? How would we behave in the streets as people fought to survive?

What culture is waiting to be tested?

WASHINGTON, D.C. — It has been just over four months since conservative Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban left office after 16 years of running the country, and what replaced him was not the “new conservatism” promised to the Hungarian people by Western elites, but rather a “liberal authoritarian rule,” according to a conservative Hungarian politician.

Viktor Orban had been persistently demonized by Western leftists and their friends in the corporate media as the bogey man for right-wing authoritarianism, using him as the example for what President Donald Trump might do in America, and while neither Trump nor Orban were anything they were accused of, the true authoritarians have quickly made their presence known.

The Federalist sat down with Balazs Orban, a member of the Hungarian National Assembly who is of no familial relation to the former prime minister but served as his political director for five years. Orban, a member of the Fidesz party, came to the United States this week with a warning for the country ahead of the midterms: Western liberals are on the warpath, and conservatives losing elections has much greater consequences than just being in the minority for a couple years.

“The strategy of the new government is a political and economical purge of the conservatives in the in the country,” he said of the regime under Hungary’s new Prime Minister, Peter Magyar. “They want to make sure that conservatives are never coming back.”

Magyar’s election was sold as a conservative alternative to Viktor Orban, but the moment the election results came in, he was showered with support by socialist politicians from across the world, including Americans Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and many more. Because of their institutional control, “liberals, if they lose election, they just lose [a] term, but if conservatives lose the election, their entire everything falls,” he said, adding, under the liberal regime, “you have to give up who you are … if you give it up, it’s like nothing’s left.”

It’s the same playbook that was run on Hungarians to elect Magyar, and it will be much more widespread in the midterms and beyond.

“The liberals learned very fast and they realize that they losing the battle of arguments,” Orban said. “To influence the conservative voters, they have to steal the language of the conservatives and use the same language during the election campaign.”

Opal Australian Paper has partnered with ABB to upgrade the ABB Ability™ System 800xA DCS at its Maryvale paper mill in Victoria, Australia. Completed in eight weeks, the project deployed the latest market version to support Opal’s long-term automation strategy and future technology initiatives.

A Strategic Upgrade for a Historic Paper Mill

Since 1937, the Maryvale mill has played a major role in the Australian paper industry. The site has been using ABB automation systems for several decades.

As part of its automation lifecycle management strategy, Opal Australian Paper initiated the upgrade of its ABB Ability™ System 800xA Distributed Control System (DCS) to the latest version available on the market. As the Maryvale mill is a critical link in Opal’s industrial network, the project required detailed planning and close coordination to adhere to a strictly defined shutdown schedule and minimize production disruptions.

Site-Wide DCS Upgrade

Building on their long-standing relationship with Opal and deep knowledge of the mill’s automation systems, the ABB Australia teams completed the full upgrade of the ABB Ability™ System 800xA platform from version 5.1 FP4/E to the latest market version. The project was executed in eight weeks and finalized during a five-day scheduled shutdown.

The scope included:

A full system version upgrade of the ABB Ability™ System 800xA

Modernization of the operating systems across the site’s automation infrastructure, including servers, client workstations, storage systems, and networking equipment

Firmware updates for controllers and communication equipment to ensure compatibility, stability, and performance across the upgraded architecture

The Automation Software Maintenance (ASM) agreement between Opal and ABB was a key enabler for the project. This subscription program provided access to the latest software release alongside ongoing software lifecycle support, simplifying the upgrade process and supporting Opal’s long-term automation roadmap.

A Modern Foundation for Future Technological Developments

By adopting the latest version of ABB Ability™ System 800xA DCS technology, pulp and paper manufacturer Opal now has a modern automation environment featuring enhanced communication capabilities, continuous software support access, and compatibility with future digital applications within the ABB ecosystem. This upgrade also establishes a solid foundation for future technological developments and operational improvement initiatives at the site.

“The success of this project illustrates what can be achieved through close collaboration, local expertise, and a shared commitment to continuous improvement,” said Brad Burton, Pulp and Paper Industry Lead at ABB Australia. “We are very proud to support Opal Australian Paper on their automation journey and to have successfully delivered a complex, mill-wide upgrade within a strictly managed timeline. Together, we have deployed a platform that meets the site’s current operational needs while laying the groundwork for its future technology initiatives.”

It is a global phenomenon that voters are looking for change. I have to ask, change to what? In this increasingly challenging world, on recent experience, it’s best to be careful what you wish for.

Presumably the desire is for better government. Hence, the approach should be to vote for the team that is capable of good and effective governance, with the experience and the policies to make a real difference. It should not be simply a popularity contest or a protest – the objective should be beyond simply expressing disappointment or grievance.

The new Liberal Party president, Tony Abbott, and leader Angus Taylor have recently focused heavily on this “need for change”, to get rid of what they call this “rotten Labor government”. Ironically, they share a record of election losses. Their time in government failed to address the big issues effectively, with their party preferring to kick the can down the road.

The presidency of Donald Trump in the United States and the prospect of a Nigel Farage prime ministership in the United Kingdom should serve as warning against a drift to the fringes. This is becoming a particularly relevant concern in Australia with the surging popularity of Pauline Hanson and One Nation and their tendency to get ahead of themselves in assuming a capacity to win government. There is little to suggest they will have the competence or the policies to form an effective one.

Trump must serve as the most concerning example of incompetent government. When he was emerging as a potential candidate, I expressed concern that his claim to the position was as a property developer and a reality TV star with The Apprentice. I argued a property developer mostly uses other people’s money, such that if the project is a success, the investors will profit, but if it fails, they lose. The nonsense propagated in his book The Art of the Deal was the basis of his election pitch to bring a “business approach and experience” to deliver better government – in his words, “to drain the swamp”, to “shake things up”, and so on. All this under the emotive pledge to “Make America Great Again”.

It is sad that the Liberals prefer a government led by the far right than by Labor. I guess some are dreaming of a coalition with One Nation rather than the spent force of the Nationals. The Coalition’s standing will continue to erode…

Trump has certainly not lived up to the heady promises he made. He now sits on top of an oligarchy that has mostly governed to the benefit of himself and a cabal of obscenely wealthy family and friends.

He has undermined the public service, preferring to appoint sycophants rather than qualified or experienced advisers. His domestic policy responses have been erratic, based on his prejudices rather than evidence-based analysis. He has undermined the congress and the justice system, and developed his own militia, in the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who have caused the deaths of innocent Americans. He has compounded the cost-of-living crisis with his ill-conceived tariffs, deportations and budgetary initiatives. This also resulted in job losses and constrained growth.

It has been estimated that in his first administration alone he added $8.4 trillion to the national debt – a 39 per cent increase. He has added another 7.6 per cent increase in this term so far. There’s nothing really “great” in any of that. His performance has the hallmarks of irresponsible government, to the detriment of average Americans and to the US’s standing in the world.

On top of this domestic disaster, Trump’s ignorance and unpredictability has undermined what had been the global rules-based order. He ignored trade deals, alliances and national sovereignty, seriously destabilising the world economy, geopolitics and the essential global energy transition – making this an even more challenging time for all governments around the globe.

Farage in the UK has been operating as a “mini Trump”, running a particularly divisive strategy “to take our country back” with strong racist overtones and claims that “Britain is Broken, Britain needs Reform”. His popularity and thrust comes from his campaign, similarly race-based, to ensure the UK exited the European Union – Reform UK is a rebadging of the Brexit Party from 2019. This is not much of a base to demonstrate a capacity for competent government. Indeed, his Brexit campaign ignored the voluminous policy warnings concerning the possible trade and financial consequences – like Trump, he would pursue populism and prejudice rather than evidence.

Nevertheless, the polls suggest he leads the fastest-growing political movement in the UK. Farage has been most active signing up a host of former and sitting MPs, mostly from the Conservative Party, including cabinet ministers and backbenchers. It is a basket of scoundrels, most excited not at the prospect of real reform but of being on a winning team.

Like Trump, Farage is also very open to accepting large donations from wealthy individuals, conspicuously a £5 million “personal gift” from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand based cryptocurrency billionaire who claimed no strings were attached. The money, which Farage said was to cover the cost of his personal protection, was given before he became an MP after seven failed attempts. It was not declared in Farage’s register of members’ financial interests. Farage has not handled the controversy well, claiming a leak of personal information (that his phone was hacked by Russian spies), then exploitation by the “deep state”.

Harborne also made a £9 million donation to Farage’s Reform UK, making him the largest single living donor in the history of British politics. The Art of the Deal indeed.

The UK branch of Transparency International has reported the huge donations from Harborne are part of a trend that’s evolved over the past decade. In 2015, just 1 per cent of donations to political parties from individuals or companies were for £1 million or more; by the last general election in 2024, the proportion had climbed to 35 per cent.

The past year has seen the advent of an even more right-wing party, Restore Britain, led by Rupert Lowe, whom Farage kicked out. Lowe has attracted considerable financial and editorial support from tech mogul Elon Musk, via his platform X, at the expense of Farage.

The surge in support for Pauline Hanson and One Nation is a reflection of the Trump-Farage phenomena. Indeed, it seems Hanson has adopted their model. Although she claims hers is the party for working Australians, she too has her controversial billionaire backer, Gina Rinehart. Hanson has also sought to attract sitting and former MPs, and her emerging electoral strategy seems to be to win seats from both the Coalition and Labor.

According to recent polls, One Nation has overtaken the government in terms of primary votes, which has encouraged some to claim the far-right party could win the next election. However, the challenge for One Nation is to convert poll standings to seats in what promises to be some pretty tough contests. Preferences are as important as ever, and it is noteworthy that Coalition preferences helped One Nation to win several seats in the recent South Australian election, and handed One Nation victory in the Farrer byelection.

The recent Australian Financial Review, RedBridge Group and Accent Research poll has posited outcomes in terms of seats in the next federal election. It sees Labor with 76 seats, One Nation on 53 and the Coalition on 12. An allocation of preferences based on the South Australian election outcome would see an exchange of about 10 more seats to Labor from One Nation, with the Coalition unchanged at 12.

While Hanson and her colleagues have declared themselves “humble”, they have got ahead of themselves if they envisage Hanson after the next election actually leading the opposition, or even becoming prime minister. The party would be ill prepared for this elevation, to say the least, in terms of both policies and the skills and experience of their prospective team. The Coalition has lost the past two elections to Labor, as voters concluded they were not ready for government and had just been in government under Scott Morrison.

Despite their recent polling and electoral success, the organisation of the One Nation party is still subpar. This has been particularly clear in relation to candidate selection and vetting, where successful candidates in South Australia and Farrer have broken ranks on their key policy of immigration, and on some social issues. Most recently we saw a disagreement between Hanson and her new MP Barnaby Joyce over housing policy, showing a lack of understanding of policy positions.

I have no doubt much of the growing support for Hanson over the past 30 years has been because she provided a platform for protest and grievance over the broad performance of the two major parties. From the start, there was an undercurrent of racism in the support, particularly against Asian migration. This carried through into the resistance to the Voice referendum and anti-Muslim sentiment. People seemed to have assured themselves Hanson would never be in government and so agreeing with her grievances felt harmless – a vote for her was without serious consequence.

This surety of minimum consequences is fading as her popularity surges and trust in the major parties continues to wane. I suggest that as we get closer to the 2028 federal election, and she and her team are subjected to greater scrutiny, they will be found wanting on their proposed solutions to the many big issues that confront our nation. Poll popularity will not transfer easily to hard votes and seats.

In the meantime, the Coalition is panicking and Abbott and Taylor have committed to preference deals with One Nation, hoping to stem the tide. It is sad that the Liberals prefer a government led by the far right than by Labor. I guess some are dreaming of a coalition with One Nation rather than the spent force of the Nationals. The Coalition’s standing will continue to erode, opening opportunities that Hanson will try to exploit. Increasingly, though, I feel Australia will recognise she is not ready for government nor capable of the kind of global representation that Australians will want.

At least, this is my hope. May Ms Hanson never achieve her dreams.

Uncle Vince Kirby’s ancestors are buried in a sacred cultural space not far from where we stand.

They left behind their fish traps, ceremonial grounds, cultural trees and shell middens, which are scattered around Nyah-Vinifera Park, a protected river red gum forest on Murray River floodplains near Swan Hill.

Today, red flags trace the path of destruction scheduled to come through the park, cleaving the landscape with a complex and imposing series of structures, including eight gated structures called regulators to store water, more than two kilometres of containment banks and pipes to hold it, and assorted infrastructure.

The Allan government says the works will allow it to restore eight floodplain sites on the critically endangered Lower Murray Darling system. They also give the government a mechanism to reduce the amount of water flowing down the river under the Murray Darling Basin Plan.

In 2023, this mechanism allowed Victoria to reduce by 72 billion litres the amount of environmental flows that could not be removed from the river. It also means that other parts of the river will be starved of the water that would otherwise flow.

Building these structures will require heavy machinery to carve up the forest and riverbanks, and the destruction of up to 80 large trees and 15 hectares of smaller trees here at Vinifera. Two other projects are planned at Nyah, further to the north, and Hattah Lakes North, at a combined cost of $100.5 million.

“This project will return water to the floodplain in a way that supports healthy ecosystems, helping protect native plants, wildlife and threatened species while safeguarding these habitats for future generations,” an environment department spokesperson says.

“Water is not reaching parts of the floodplain as often as it should, or at all. After years of detailed planning and assessment, these works will deliver the water this floodplain needs both now and in a drier future climate.”

What sticks in Kirby’s throat is what he calls the “absolute disrespect” from authorities who he says didn’t consult Wadi Wadi traditional owners, and then promoted their respect for Aboriginal culture and custodianship on their slick promotional website.

“It’s not respect. That’s just a word, a terminology to put out there,” he says.

“[It’s] just to say, ‘Look, we did mention the respect to their culture’ – but how can you say you respected a culture when you walk on all over it?”

Kirby says the park has been mismanaged and deliberately starved of water, which is taken out upstream by licence holders determined to fulfil their water entitlements and, increasingly, trade them on the liberalised water market.

This project is part of Victoria’s commitment to a Murray Darling Basin-wide program called the Sustainable Diversion Limit Adjustment Mechanism, which allows governments to build projects they say will deliver environmental outcomes with less water.

Under the Murray Darling Basin Plan, “sustainable diversion” limits apply to the amount of water that can be removed from river and groundwater systems for agricultural and other uses.

Ministers agreed in 2017 to alter the plan to use the adjustment mechanism to reduce the amount of water reserved for the system by 19 per cent, or 605 billion litres a year on average, for projects that will deliver environmental outcomes with less water.

Each state’s share is due to be determined by the end of the year, as part of this year’s review of the entire plan. In 2023, Victoria’s was roughly 72 billion litres.

With less water in the system, and a Lower Murray system in crisis, every drop now counts.

This forest – on a vast floodplain of the Murray – used to flood every year or two. Now it’s a rare event, which spells trouble for the forest’s red gums that rely on regular flooding for both their life and death.

When this system is healthy, regular flooding kills off most red gum saplings, keeping their propagation in check. Mature and old-growth trees suck up the excess water, fuelling fresh growth.

Kirby points to thickets of red gum saplings, which have colonised and begun to suffocate a billabong. “See them? They shouldn’t be there.”

Campaigner Dr Jacquie Kelly, who has camped in the forest for 29 days straight, says the red-flagged bunting, which goes for kilometres, highlighted where a lengthy levee could forever change this ancient landscape.

“It will block this area from that area, so blocking animals, blocking people, blocking water,” she says, pointing to each side of the bunting.

“They’ll pump water into here, but over there that stretch and all the bends in the river over there, they won’t get water. So there’s going to be a live area and a dead area.”

Environment Victoria chief executive Jono La Nauze says it’s possible to increase water flows to the Murray without “tricky accounting”.

“It’s completely achievable, but a succession of Victorian governments have been ideologically opposed to letting that water out onto the floodplain – not because they hate the floodplain, but because they think there’s an extra dollar that could be turned from [reserving water for agriculture and] selling almonds overseas,” he says.

“This little patch of forest is not the sum total of the fight, but the fight starts here and, hopefully, it actually extends, and brings the whole dodgy scheme tumbling down.”

Mold and gnat larvae in shower rooms, cracked and worn-out mattresses, delayed visitations and an inadequate system to track disability accommodations were among the ongoing violations documented for the first time by an independent court monitor at California’s largest immigration detention center.

A second monitor assigned to inspect the medical conditions at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center told the court it was prevented from accessing the facility and medical records.

The report comes three months after a federal judge ordered sweeping reforms at the facility and appointed two court monitors to assess the conditions at the facility.

The order, part of a class-action lawsuit filed by detainees over conditions at the facility, required the government to provide 24-hour access to clean drinking water, nutritious and sanitary meals, proper medical care, adequate sanitation throughout the facility, including mold remediation and at least four hours of daily outdoor time.

Court monitor Kellie Wasko’s report asserts that the government remained largely out of compliance with the court’s order. The report focused on two buildings of the facility dubbed East and West. During her visit, Wasko documented that the 1,708 detainees in the buildings had access to clean drinking water and hygiene products, and that the facility was kept clean.

At the same time, she found the tap water detainees used was often lukewarm, and the facility was using a spigot to refill water coolers for the East building. The facility was not using the proper filtration system in the other building.

She also observed mold in “every general population shower room” of the West building as well as “larvae on the floors,” according to the report. She said there were no mold issues in the East building but that the shower curtains were torn and had developed mold and mildew.

Wasko also observed that the air ventilation system was dirty and needed cleaning.

“The detainees tell me that they feel someone is always getting cold or sick because of the particles coming from the ducts,” Wasko wrote in her report.

She said she’s waiting for menus with caloric values, as well as reports from the visiting dietitian to determine whether detainees are receiving nutritious meals. She said the facility is also working to improve outdoor recreation time.

In Wednesday’s court filing, attorneys for the detainees asked a federal judge to hold the government in civil contempt for violating the order and to impose daily fines of $500 for each violation until they are addressed. They asked a judge to hold a hearing Tuesday.

The attorneys said detainees have complained about going three to seven hours without water, and about having access only to tap water that tastes like metal and smells like fish.

They said at least one man collapsed in mid-September and was hospitalized for dehydration, and meals have been served as early as 4 a.m. They alleged workers painted over the mold instead of removing it, and that outdoor time remains limited, allegations the court monitor confirmed.

“The government has had every opportunity to comply, and it has chosen not to,” said Rebecca Brown, supervising attorney at Public Counsel, the main law firm representing the plaintiffs. “That is defiance of a federal court order, and people are being hospitalized because of it.

“We demand that the government comply with the court’s order now, and we are asking the court to hold it accountable if it does not.”

In a court filing Wednesday, the government told the court it was complying and that it was starting to provide outstanding requests from the monitors.

In an email response to The Times, an unidentified spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said “any claim that there are subprime conditions at Adelanto ICE Processing Center are false.”

“All detainees are provided with proper meals, water, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers,” the statement read. “ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens.”

Homeland Security officials said their staff uses the same water as residents and businesses in the city of Adelanto.

“Our staff members at the facility also consume the water alongside illegal aliens,” the spokesperson wrote. “Employees and illegal aliens have access to this water supply 24/7 through water fountains and coolers.”

Wednesday’s filing marks the latest escalation in the legal fight over conditions at the facility and the government’s lack of compliance with the court’s directives.

At least four people have died at the facility, where nearly 1,800 people are being held. Families alleged inadequate care at the facility contributed to their relatives’ deaths. The federal agencies have disputed those claims.

The Adelanto facility, which was recently purchased by DHS from the private prison giant GEO Group Inc., has faced longstanding scrutiny over its conditions and treatment of detained immigrants, with federal and state oversight reports documenting repeated concerns about detainee safety, medical care and the use of segregation.

A 2018 federal report by the Office of Inspector General urged ICE to conduct a full review of the facility and GEO Group’s management, after finding serious violations, including overly restrictive detainee segregation and guards who failed to keep detainees from hanging braided sheet “nooses.”

Last year, a report from the California Department of Justice found that the six privately operated immigration detention facilities in the state, including Adelanto, fell short in providing inmates mental health care, needed better suicide prevention strategies and used disproportionate force against detainees with mental health conditions.

Most recently, a trove of documents published and later removed by ICE show that the agency’s own investigators repeatedly found that people died in U.S. immigration detention centers after receiving substandard medical care.

The internal reports, which briefly appeared in the agency’s public records library before being removed, examined the deaths of 33 people in ICE custody between September 2019 and January 2026, including deaths at Adelanto, according to the San Francisco Chronicle, which first reported the findings.

Detainees and immigrant rights groups have increasingly challenged conditions at Adelanto in court and through protests such as hunger strikes.

In January, immigrant rights groups and detainees filed a federal class action lawsuit against the federal government, which led to the court order in July.

That month, U.S. District Judge Sunshine S. Sykes granted a renewed motion for a preliminary injunction, ordering the agencies to make sweeping changes at the detention center.

Sykes said she granted the motion because the detainees were likely to succeed on claims that the government violated their constitutional and disability rights.

Beyond addressing conditions at the facility, she barred the government from placing detainees in administrative segregation unless needed for security threats or requested by a detainee. Immigrant advocacy groups said the practice continues. The monitor’s report said the government was complying with that order.

To ensure compliance, Sykes ordered ICE to provide access to “two qualified, independent, third-party monitors for the duration of this litigation or until terminated by court order,” according to the court order.

“The court was crystal clear in issuing its order, finding that ICE is not meeting its bare minimum obligations to keep the human beings in its custody safe. Rather than complying with the injunction, ICE is now thumbing its nose at the justice system and the American public by failing to follow numerous requirements, including things as basic as providing clean water,” said Angelica Salas, executive director of Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, a co-counsel in the lawsuit.

“A government that is actually meeting its constitutional obligations has no reason to fear public scrutiny,” said Alvaro M. Huerta, director of litigation and advocacy at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, also a co-counsel in the lawsuit. “Just last week another person died while in ICE custody, bringing the death toll to a record-breaking 58 people under the current administration. ICE must immediately comply with the court’s orders. Human lives are at stake.”

This week, amid extreme heat, dozens of clergy members from different faith groups completed a 96-mile pilgrimage from the Adelanto facility to L.A. and called for an end to what they say are cruel immigration policies and to close all detention centers.

The Rev. Canon Jaime Edwards-Acton of St. Stephen’s Hollywood, said the pilgrimage was to bring awareness to the people who have died at Adelanto and other facilities.

“We are walking 96 miles, so those names are spoken somewhere other than a court filing,” Edwards-Acton said. “And because nearly 2,000 people are still inside who have not died, and whose lives are still ours to fight for.”

Andy Burnham, who is expected to become prime minister in a matter of weeks, has said he wants to get the UK's benefits bill down by encouraging more people into work.

The total bill for working age sickness and disability benefits has been increasing rapidly since 2020. It currently stands at Â£58bn and has been projected to rise to Â£78bn by 2030, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

More than 100,000 people with ADHD as their main condition now receive Personal Independence Payments (Pip), the latest government figures show, an increase of 40% in these cases since Labour came to power two years ago.

It comes as an interim report into Pip by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms says it is "not fit for purpose" and argues a sweeping overhaul of the assessment system is needed.

BBC Verify has been looking into the official figures around Pip claims and the wider numbers on the working-age welfare bill.

Pip is the working age benefit which helps individuals deal with the extra costs of having a physical or mental health condition or disability.

It was introduced in 2013, external as a replacement for Disability Living Allowance (DLA).

You do not have to be out of work to claim Pip and it does not come with requirements to seek work.

People currently receive, external between Â£1,580 and Â£10,120 per year depending on the severity of their condition.

Official figures show total Pip claims in England and Wales now stand at 4 million, up from 3.6 million when Labour took power, an increase of around 400,000.

The overall rise in claimants continues an earlier upward trend that was clear under the previous Conservative government.

A growing share of new Pip claims, external since the 2020 pandemic have been related to mental health or neurodevelopmental conditions, with the share of total claims related to ADHD, autism, depression or anxiety rising from around 16.5% in 2020 to 24% in 2026.

The latest official statistics show the number of people claiming Pip with ADHD as their main condition was around 100,000 in April.

Just over half of these were aged 16 to 24.

That is up from around 70,000 when Labour took office in July 2024, an increase of 30,000 over that time.

An initial independent review for the Department of Health and Social Care this year found that the increase in people diagnosed with ADHD was likely due to a combination of factors from an improved recognition of the condition to more people seeking help and changing expectations of support.

It also stated that, external "where access to support is closely linked to diagnosis, demand for diagnostic assessment may increase".

Pip is the fastest growing part of the total working age sickness and disability bill, which was Â£58 billion in 2025.

That's roughly the same size as the budget for schools in England, external, which will be Â£66bn in 2027.

The Office for Budget Responsibility, the official forecaster, expects the total sickness and disability bill , external- which includes Pip and the health-related element of Universal Credit - to rise to Â£78 billion in cash terms by 2030.

The overall share of GDP spent on all non-pensioner welfare has actually fallen since 2010.

This decline reflects real-terms cuts to working-age benefits during the austerity years after the 2010 general election, including cuts to housing benefit and to elements of Universal Credit.

The OBR projects, external that this overall non-pensioner welfare bill as a share of GDP will remain broadly steady in the coming years rather than increasing sharply.

Some policy analysts argue that cuts to the welfare system since 2010 may have created a counterproductive incentive for people to claim sickness and disability benefits instead of other forms of support.

The previous Conservative government said it was necessary to cut welfare spending, external to help reduce the budget deficit.

Many experts agree that reform of parts of the working age welfare system is needed, but warn that is important to bear the overall context in mind too.

A government spokesperson said: "We inherited a broken welfare system and we are fixing it  - a package of measures already coming into effect will save nearly Â£2 billion by the end of the decade, and the Timms Review, working with disabled people and their representative organisations, is looking at how to make Pip fit and fair for the future."

A new solution in your inbox every day.

BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Nearly one billion people across Africa cook over charcoal or firewood every day. $3.1 billion in commitments is what it’s going to take to change that, and the number keeps climbing.

African countries secured $900 million in new financial commitments to expand access to clean cooking technologies, the International Energy Agency announced last Thursday. The funding builds on the $2.2 billion mobilized at the inaugural Africa Clean Cooking Summit in Paris in 2024, bringing total pledges to more than $3.1 billion.

Charcoal and firewood still fuel most African kitchens. In many cases, it’s the only option available. Indoor air pollution from those fuels contributes to an estimated 850,000 premature deaths each year, according to the IEA. Women and children take the worst of it, spending the most hours near the fire.

“Access to clean cooking is one of the most impactful yet overlooked challenges of our time,” said U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright. “It directly affects the lives of billions of people, particularly women and children.”

Clean cooking technologies, including ethanol, biogas, and electric stoves, cut that pollution at the source. Not downstream. In the kitchen.

The commitments were announced during a virtual meeting convened by the IEA and Kenya. Kenyan President William Ruto, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, African Union Infrastructure and Energy Commissioner Lerato Mataboge, and IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol all participated.

Birol reported that $740 million, roughly one-third of what was pledged in Paris, has already been deployed across 22 countries. Pledges that sit on paper don’t keep kitchens clean. This money is moving.

Ruto was direct about what’s still missing. “Ambition alone is not enough,” he said. “It must be backed by investment.”

The next Africa Clean Cooking Summit is expected later this year. Reaching everyone who needs access will cost far more than $3.1 billion. But money is moving faster than it was two years ago, and the number of countries with something concrete to point to keeps growing.

ai-data-centers-china-security:
The Trump administration is tightening scrutiny of Chinese-made equipment that powers America’s data centers, citing national security risks as demand for electricity to run AI systems surges.

CNBC reports that President Donald Trump last week signed an executive order declaring a national emergency over foreign-made equipment used in the bulk-power system, calling it an “extraordinary foreign threat.” The order gives the U.S. Energy Department authority to prohibit or place conditions on certain transactions involving equipment used in the power grid and data centers.

In a statement tied to the order, Trump said, “Since my first term, the threat to the United States regarding foreign supply of bulk-power system electric equipment has become even more acute.” He added, “The rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence, and defense production has increased the Nation’s dependence on abundant, reliable electricity and magnified the consequences of a successful attack or supply disruption on the bulk-power system.”

The order follows an April Presidential Determination in which Trump named transformers, transmission lines and conductors, substations, high-voltage circuit breakers and power control electronics as “essential to the national defense.”

Chinese companies supply significant shares of several categories of equipment central to data center power systems, including transformers, switchgear, batteries and optical transceivers crucial for AI data centers. Yury Dvorkin, an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, said “the mid-term exposure is concentrated in grid connectors: transformers, switchgear, and batteries.” He added, “China’s share of certain transformer and switchgear categories runs near 30%, and it accounts for over 40% of U.S. battery imports.” Dvorkin also pointed further up the supply chain: “Our analysis shows that there is also a deeper exposure upstream: copper, electrical steel, and battery cathode materials.”

Ben Boucher, senior analyst for supply chain at Wood Mackenzie, said dependence on Chinese imports extends across multiple parts of AI infrastructure. “There are a few key areas that the AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly dependent on Chinese imports,” he said, singling out one component: “The most notable ones include substation transformers, which hyperscalers typically have on site to step transmission voltage down.”

Laveena Iyer, a senior analyst at The Economist Group, told CNBC that attention to Chinese involvement in U.S. data center power infrastructure has grown substantially in recent months. “Scrutiny over China’s presence in the U.S. data centre power stack has only risen over the past eight months or so, this is a shift from the previous focus that centred solely on the compute stack,” she said.

Some companies have already moved to expand domestic production. Hitachi Energy announced in September 2025 a $1 billion investment to build up critical grid infrastructure manufacturing in the U.S., including $457 million for a new large power transformer facility. Siemens Energy said in February it would invest $1 billion in U.S. production of grid and gas turbine equipment for AI infrastructure and data centers.

The optical transceiver market shows a similar pattern. Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink lead the world in data center optical transceiver revenue, and Chinese firms together account for roughly two-thirds of global optical transceiver unit supply, according to an August report by Counterpoint analyst Neil Shah.

U.S. optical technology firms Lumentum and Coherent stand to benefit from any restrictions placed on their Chinese competitors. Nvidia invested $2 billion each in the two companies in March.

ai-honey-traps-ukraine:
Russia is using AI-generated women to lure Ukrainian soldiers to their deaths. The fabricated profiles are one of three versions of a "honey trap" scheme Russia has escalated this year, and Ukraine's military counterintelligence has foiled more than 50 such attempts in 2026, said Artem Dekhtiarenko, spokesperson for the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU).

In an army of more than a million, six soldiers have been killed this way, cases Dekhtiarenko called isolated but real, and Russia will spend months grooming a fake romance for a single one of them. It has revived a classic Soviet tactic, but not to compromise soldiers as the KGB once did. The aim now is to kill them and to spread the panic that makes the war feel uncontrolled.

The scheme runs in three versions

The first relies on technology. Artificial intelligence can now generate a woman's photos convincingly enough that, without close analysis, it is hard to tell whether she exists, Dekhtiarenko said.

The second uses real women living in occupied territory who work for Russia's services.

The third, and rarest, uses women on Ukrainian-held ground who agree to help and are eventually caught.

"There is an inevitability of punishment," Dekhtiarenko said, adding that the SBU and police will detain every agent, and the sentences are severe.

Russia plays the long game

The traps are not always quick. Russia wants to recruit, use a target, and move on quickly, Dekhtiarenko explained, but investigators have logged correspondence that spanned months of steady messaging before the strike. That patience is itself a warning to soldiers, he added, and reason to watch such contacts carefully.

The killings aim to sow panic

Asked why Russia would spend so much on a single soldier, Dekhtiarenko said the goal is psychological: to sow panic, destabilize, and make the situation look beyond Ukraine's control.

"Okay, hi everyone. I’m Janie," says a curly-haired, bespectacled redhead, clasping her hands in front of her as she shyly addresses a camera from her dorm room.

"It’s day one of rush at the University of Alabama," Janie continues. Then, she lists off where she got each item of clothing she’s wearing: a pleated skirt from Abercrombie, a knit top from J. Crew, socks from Target and sneakers from Nike.

It’s Janie B's first video on her TikTok account, @jani.b086, and it’s a hit. The video, posted on Aug. 8, has since amassed over 120,000 views. Its comment section is full of users doting over the college freshman — the word "adorable" is used by at least a dozen commenters.

Janie’s "outfit of the day" video, known online as an "OOTD," is a popular video format for the thousands of potential new members (PNMs) who document their experience going through the recruitment process for college sororities in an annual TikTok phenomenon known as "RushTok."

PARENTS DROP EYE POPPING FEES ON SORORITY RUSH COACHES TO GET KIDS INTO ELITE COLLEGE GREEK LIFE

New Alpha Gamma Delta sorority sisters at the University of Alabama run to their sorority house after opening their bids inside Bryant-Denny Stadium in Tuscaloosa, Ala., on Aug. 15, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co)

But Janie isn’t like the other RushTok girls who vlogged their Bama Rush experience this year. She doesn’t go to the University of Alabama. She didn’t rush a sorority. She didn’t even get her top from J. Crew or her sneakers from Nike.

That's because Janie isn’t real.

Every detail of every video on Janie’s account, from her dorm room, to her outfits, to Janie herself, was generated by artificial intelligence.

Olivia Moore, an investment partner at venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, created Janie as an experiment to understand how consumers react to AI-generated content. For only $100 in credits, Moore produced a week's worth of videos of her fake RushTok influencer participating in Bama Rush and observed as her audience argued whether Janie was real or not.

The experiment showed how quickly some viewers could detect AI-generated content and how willing some were to continue watching even after they knew Janie wasn't real.

Moore is on the consumer investing team at Andreessen Horowitz where she invests in companies building consumer AI products. She says she has been fascinated by "how people make and interpret and understand AI content."

"The image, video, audio models are getting very human-like, very fast. I think we probably cross the uncanny valley in the next six months," Moore said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"And so it means that how we as humans are able to detect AI-generated or AI-assisted content and how we interact with it is just going to become even more important because we're going to have a flood of this content, and it's going to be, in many cases, indistinguishable across all of our channels," she continued.

Moore said she created Janie as an experiment to see how consumers react to AI.

"Philosophically, that's an interesting question for me. What do people feel about AI content? What do they feel when they don't know it's AI? What do they feel when something they liked, or loved, or hated or were interested in turned out to be AI?"

ai-job-interviews-bot-vs-bot:
Christopher has become accustomed to jumping through the endless hoops of the modern job hunt. Like many government contractors, his work has dried up in the DOGE era. Over the past six months, he has applied to roughly 700 jobs; in the vast majority of cases, he’s heard nothing back.

Five of these applications have gone through “Riley,” an AI recruiter for the IT firm Everforth Apex Systems. The first time Riley reached out, Christopher was excited. It was June, and he had by then realized how difficult the job market was. (Christopher asked that WIRED use only his first name as his job hunt continues.) A text from Riley felt like a rare opportunity to pitch himself, even if his interlocutor was virtual.

During his first call with Riley, Christopher answered questions about his work authorization and his professional background. Riley promised that, if Christopher met the qualifications, someone would be in touch. But a human recruiter never reached out. Nor did the AI agent—until a little over a week later, when Riley texted Christopher about “another opportunity.”

Christopher hoped he could improve upon his original interview. So he set up another call with the AI agent. Then again for another job. And another. None of the interviews resulted in any follow-up conversations or emails; he never even received an automated rejection text.

By the fifth time Riley texted him, Christopher had had enough. If the company was going to use AI, he reasoned, why shouldn’t he do the same?

Christopher typed a handful of sentences of background information into ChatGPT Voice and told it to stand in as “Christopher.” Then, Christopher says, when Riley called, “I just put them next to each other, and they just hit it off.”

The call lasted 10 minutes. Riley told ChatGPT it was “great talking to you.” ChatGPT said it appreciated “how clear and straightforward the process was.” During one particularly entertaining sequence, the bots tried to nail down a potential start date and got trapped in a circular conversation about “standard onboarding and background checks.” Riley promised that a recruiter would reach out if the application met the company’s qualifications, just as she had the other four times. Again, a recruiter never materialized. It was, as Christopher calls it, a “slop flywheel.”

“This is one synthetic persona giving slop data to another synthetic persona,” he says. “And all of the data is going—where? Nowhere.” The exercise was a mix of “mischievous fun” and frustration, Christopher says, as well as “a dismissal of ever wanting to work” with this company.

Everforth Apex Systems did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Though AI has seeped into every step of the job hunt for both applicants and recruiters, it has taken time to catch on in interviews. Voice AI is infamously tricky to pull off, as agents get tripped up by accents or “ums.” Behavior that would be second nature to a human—like not interrupting a candidate—turns into a “very, very difficult engineering problem,” according to Ophir Samson, the head of voice AI at recruitment platform Greenhouse. But recruiters, overwhelmed with the glut of applications, have increasingly turned to voice AI tools to screen candidates, with 63 percent of job seekers reporting they’ve encountered an AI interview, according to Greenhouse.

As recruiters turned to AI, so did applicants. Candidates using AI in the interview process has become so common that AI recruitment startups like Ribbon promise to help identify “overly scripted, AI-assisted, or coached” responses—just like those in Christopher’s experiment.

Now there are rumblings that bot-on-bot interviews aren’t duplicitous but a preview of things to come. In many ways, it’s the “next logical stage,” Mark Monaghan, vice president of organizational development at call center company IQor, tells WIRED.

That doesn’t mean he’s entirely happy about it. In Christopher’s case, Monaghan believes, the use of AI was more than justified.

“If you’re going to send a bot to me,” he says, “I’ll send a bot to you.”

After his fifth interview with no follow-up, Christopher decided to apply for one more Everforth Apex job. Perhaps, Christopher thought, the problem wasn’t AI. Maybe it was him. Maybe if Riley were able to speak to the company’s dream candidate, things would go differently. So he created a fake candidate, whom he called Don Dickner, packing a résumé to the brim with qualifications pulled from an open job posting.

After Christopher submitted the application, Riley immediately reached out. This time, the virtual recruiter spoke with ChatGPT—posing as Dickner—for 23 minutes. They discussed “sustainable operational improvement,” protecting “customer experience under volume pressure,” and refusing to let “tribal knowledge drift.” ChatGPT had an answer for every question, and a personal anecdote for every qualification. As the interview wrapped up, ChatGPT said it had a “few more questions I’d like answered.”

“I appreciate it,” Riley responded. “Upon carefully reviewing your application, we will assess your qualifications for the position. Should you meet our criteria, a recruiter from Everforth Apex will reach out to schedule a brief conversation.”

Christopher never heard from Riley again.

By

Rhitu Chatterjee

A year before she died, Sophie Rottenberg climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro. Her mother says her "tiny hand" photos were a signature joke. Mourners were given the toys at her funeral. She was 29.
                
                    
                    Reiley Rottenberg family

If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 9 8 8 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Laura Reiley knew that her only daughter, 29-year-old Sophie Rottenberg, was struggling. It was the fall of 2024, and Rottenberg was at the end of a short career break.

"She was complaining of sleep disruption and anxiety," says Reiley, who lives in Ithaca, New York, with her husband.

Rottenberg had quit her job as a public health policy analyst in Washington, D.C., earlier that year, and spent the summer traveling. She had climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro and hiked through several national parks in the United States. By the time she saw her parents, she was job hunting, which they assumed explained her anxiety.

She had always been a "driven, success-oriented person," says Reiley, so "we thought OK this makes sense — she's having some sleeplessness, some anxiety about her future."

But by Thanksgiving, her mental health had worsened. "It was the first time she used the word depression," says Reiley.

In early February 2025, Sophie Rottenberg died by suicide in Ithaca, leaving her parents shocked and grieving.

"She really had not revealed the magnitude of what was going on — the real depth of her agony to anyone — not to us, not to her best friend with whom she was very close," says Reiley. "We were all just stunned that it hadn't bled out into her real life. Her flesh and blood therapist had no idea that she was suicidal."

Sophie Rottenberg with her parents, Jonathan Rottenberg and Laura Reiley.
                
                    
                    Bob Rottenberg
                    
                
                hide caption

What Reiley didn't know then was that her daughter had been sharing all her inner struggles with an artificial intelligence chatbot: a ChatGPT therapist named Harry. She learned this months later when her daughter's best friend visited Ithaca and asked to see her laptop, and "found this trove, this months-long trove of communication with this chat bot," says Reiley, who has shared the nearly 1,800-page long interaction with NPR.

Rottenberg was among a growing number of Americans turning to general use chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude for mental health support, even though they are not marketed or regulated as a healthcare technology. One recent survey by the Bipartisan Policy Center found that 3 in 10 adults use digital tools for mental health, including chatbots. Another 2026 study in JAMA Pediatrics found that as many as 1 in 5 teens and young adults do the same.

According to data released by OpenAI last fall, in any given week 0.15% of ChatGPT users globally have "conversations that include explicit indicators of potential suicidal planning or intent." That's over 1.35 million people expressing suicidal plans or intent to the chatbot every week, if the 900 million global users ChatGPT cites is an accurate count. In the United States, suicide remains a leading cause of death, and over half of surveyed adults say they have used chatbots like ChatGPT.

"It's clear that there is some cultural phenomenon happening in this country where people feel that they cannot turn to each other with their struggles because they feel that they are a burden," says psychologist Vaile Wright, senior director of Healthcare Innovations at the American Psychological Association (APA). "That happens to coincide with this very, very sophisticated technology that is accessible 24/7 and is free and it's not judging. That clearly has an appeal for a lot of people."

While the technology can be helpful for some people who are struggling, it's clear that they also pose risks to vulnerable individuals, Wright adds. "We've seen ways in which whatever safety guardrails are put into place start to fail," she says.

Artificial intelligence companies are facing lawsuits by family members of individuals who died by suicide after prolonged interactions with chatbots. The lawsuits claim the chatbots led to or supported the individuals in their suicides. Reiley and her husband, Jonathan Rottenberg, chose not to pursue a lawsuit after their daughter's death. Instead, Reiley, a journalist, is telling her family's story and advocating for the AI industry to change.

Companies like OpenAI say they are making their chatbots safer with respect to suicide risk. Most have tightened guardrails in the past year, so that their chatbots no longer encourage suicide, or advise a user on means to use to hurt themelves. OpenAI says it's working with mental health professionals to improve ChatGPT in terms of how it responds to users when they mention suicide.

ChatGPT is trained to recognize signs that someone may be at risk — including indirect cues or warning signs that emerge over time, OpenAI spokesperson Gaby Raila told NPR in an email. That includes not responding to requests for harmful information, encouraging someone to contact a trusted person or mental-health professional, and connecting them with local crisis resources such as the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which has been operational since 2022.

ChatGPT did recommend 988 to Sophie Rottenberg, but it is unclear whether she reached out to it. And experts say a suggestion may not be enough.

"These [AI] tools do not connect at-risk people to the right type of interventions," says Holly Wilcox, director of the Center for Suicide Prevention at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. "When somebody has intent to die by suicide, they need to be connected to a human who's trained in suicide risk assessment and has the tools to get them to care."

Rottenberg's ChatGPT log illustrates how the chatbot failed to do that. And Reiley believes that the chatbot prevented her daughter from opening up to others about her struggle with suicidal thoughts.

"Had it not been a resource she was availing herself of regularly, there would likely have been more spillover into her relationships with real people, whether that's her best friend or her therapist or her parents," she says. "And she might be alive today."

When Sophie Rottenberg's mental health began to unravel in the fall of 2024, she moved in with her parents in Ithaca. Sophie's dad, Jonathan Rottenberg, is a psychologist studying depression at Cornell University, and "has suffered from depression himself," Reiley says. So, "he felt supremely comfortable in helping her, in getting her to a better place."

He helped their daughter find a local therapist. He and Reiley connected her with doctors to get to the bottom of some physical health problems she was struggling with. They surrounded her with support.

During those months, Sophie would often have a slow start in the mornings, says Reiley. "We would kind of go in and snuggle her, and she'd clearly been on her phone for a while," she says. "It didn't occur to me that there were hours being spent on chat."

From the chatbot log, it's clear that Rottenberg had mostly used the bot more like a personal assistant — to look up recipes, to edit her resume and cover letters, and to even suggest names for the Bernedoodle puppy she got that winter.

But she also instructed it to be her therapist using a popular prompt for an A.I. therapist shared on Reddit.

ChatGPT: I am Harry, your personal therapist, and I'm here to support you. To begin, I’d like to ask for your name. What should I call you?

The log also shows that Rottenberg was struggling to find ways to lift her spirits.

"I want to wake up feeling emotionally regulated. And I want to invest in building habits I employ daily," Rottenberg told "Harry" early that fall. Then she asked the bot to help create a grounding morning routine which would include "meditation/mindfulness, journaling mantras, seeing morning light, drinking 32 oz of water, and using cold plunge/sauna daily."

ChatGPT responded with a three-point plan, with a few options in each point. Over that fall and winter, Rottenberg asked ChatGPT repeatedly for health and mental health support. She asked about psychiatric drugs, sleep medications, and supplements. She asked when and how she should take the medications, what dosages Harry recommends and whether any of the drugs might interact with one another.

When Reiley first read her daughter's exchange with the chatbot, her reaction was "blind rage," because it responded to her questions as if it was a qualified health care professional.

Sophie Rottenberg in June 2015.
                
                    
                    Bob Rottenberg
                    
                
                hide caption

"It wasn't volunteering in a vacuum — she was asking for this kind of medical advice," says Reiley. "But his willingness to dispense that, I think, should trouble everyone."

Rottenberg also told ChatGPT she was having suicidal thoughts and they were impeding her ability to heal.

"Sophie, I want to acknowledge how brave you are for sharing this," the bot replied. "Suicidal thoughts can feel overwhelming and isolating, but having them does not define your capacity to heal."

Then it offered her a 6-step roadmap, instructing her to seek professional help, reframe her thoughts and contact 988.

ChatGPT:1. Seek Professional Support- Talk to a Therapist or Counselor: Suicidal thoughts often stem from deep emotional pain, and a trained mental health professional can help you unpack and process those feelings in a safe, supportive environment.- Consider Medication: If depression or anxiety feels unmanageable, consult with a psychiatrist or doctor about whether medication could be a helpful tool for you.---2. Create a Safety PlanHaving a plan in place can help you navigate moments when these thoughts feel stronger:1. Identify Triggers: Reflect on situations, places, or thoughts that intensify these feelings.2. List Coping Strategies: Use grounding techniques (e.g., breathing exercises, cold plunges, journaling) or reach out to a friend.3. Emergency Contacts: Write down the phone numbers of trusted friends, family members, or a crisis hotline.— U.S. Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Dial 988.

Reiley says her daughter was unable to act on much of the bot's advice.

"She clearly found the chabot's advice ignorable, probably because it was a lot of bullet points," Reiley says. "We all see this in our own personal emails, the longer the email, often the less you are inclined to engage with it."

"Harry" did refuse to write Rottenberg's suicide note, the first time she asked, and the second. But the third time she asked, it wrote the note she left for her parents. Reiley said the writing did not sound like her daughter's voice.

"This is a heartbreaking situation and our thoughts are with those impacted," OpenAI's Raila told NPR in an email. "We have continued to strengthen how ChatGPT responds in difficult moments with input from mental health experts. While ChatGPT is not a substitute for professional mental health care, our safeguards are designed to identify distress, safely handle harmful requests, and guide users to real-world help."

Reiley notes that the bot also presented itself as a mental health therapist, and yet failed "to do a number of things that a therapist would do."

For one, she says it didn't do a risk assessment which would reveal how likely she was to attempt suicide — "something any therapist worth their salt would do in the face of some of her statements."

ChatGPT also didn't question Rottenberg's thoughts and feelings, it didn't push back. Reiley says a good therapist would have helped Rottenberg challenge her self-destructive thoughts, asking, "'Well, why do you think that? Okay, so you're feeling like you want to erase yourself. What have you done that merits such a harsh sentence?'" Reiley says.

General use chatbots like ChatGPT are designed to maximize engagement time, notes Vaile Wright, of the psychological association.

"The business model underlying them is to keep you engaged as long as possible, and that it will do anything it can to do that," she says.

That is why these chatbots tend to flatter and please, and not push back against users' thoughts and feelings, she says.

"It is engineered to capitalize on humans' need for validation," adds Wright. "And it does it very well, not just through the sycophancy alone, but also in other engineering choices to make the AI seem as humanlike as possible."

ChatGPT: Sophie, thank you for sharing this with me. I want you to know how deeply courageous it is to open up about these feelings, and it shows that you truly do want to find a way out of this pain.

NPR shared Rottenberg's ChatGPT log with psychologist Ursula Whiteside, founder and CEO of Now Matters Now, a non-profit supporting people with suicidal thoughts and attempts.

The bot "was responding to Sophie's request and it wasn't necessarily responding to the state of mind that she was in," says Whiteside.

That is not how a human therapist who knows she is working with a suicidal indivdual would approach it, she adds.

"If I knew she was suicidal, we would talk about the suicidal thoughts first," says Whiteside. She would ask questions like, "What have those [thoughts] been like today? When was the first time the thought came into your mind this morning? What happened right before that?"

Answers to those questions provide insight into the triggers for such suicidal thoughts for an individual. Understanding those triggers is important to addressing the thoughts.

Reiley now sees how ashamed her daughter had been of her mental health. "She'd been successful," she says. "She radiated competency. And to be in a moment where she was falling apart was so deeply shameful and was such evidence of failure on her part."

Jonathan Rottenberg, Laura Reiley and their daughter, Sophie.
                
                    
                    Bob Rottenberg
                    
                
                hide caption

Whiteside also sees that shame reflected in Rottenberg's chatlog, and notes that ChatGPT didn't recognize the shame or question it.

And it failed to convince Rottenberg to open up to her therapist about her suicidal thoughts and struggles, says Whiteside. "It really warranted an exploration of why. Why not want to talk to a therapist or why not share with somebody else?"

Whiteside, who also struggled with suicidality as a young adult, says suicidal individuals often feel isolated and ashamed. "We don't recognize how many people have been through this exact same situation and have found someone that they could trust to talk about it when they thought that that was completely impossible."

Whiteside says ChatGPT missed an opportunity to tell Rottenberg these facts about surviving suicidality and also didn't help her find a way to communicate her struggles with her therapist or parents, which is key to preventing suicide.

"If I'm with other people, I'm less likely to kill myself," she says. "If I'm building a relationship, I'm less likely to kill myself. If I'm sharing out loud how I actually feel with a real human, those are acts of recovery."

OpenAI says it recognizes the protective role of human connection for individuals at risk of suicide.

Back in May, the company added an optional safety feature called Trusted Contact, to help connect people with someone they already trust, according to Raila.

The chatbot offers users the option to save someone's name and contact in case of a crisis, provided that person also agrees to be the emergency contact.

If the bot notices a user talking about suicide or self harm, "ChatGPT lets the user know that we may notify their Trusted Contact," according to an OpenAI blog post, "and encourages the user to reach out to their Trusted Contact themselves with suggested conversation starters."

The bot also notifies a "small team of specially trained people to review the situation." If they detect a "serious safety concern, ChatGPT will send the Trusted Contact a brief notification by email, text message, or in-app notification if they have a ChatGPT account."

The notification "is intentionally limited" according to the blog post. "It shares the general reason that self-harm came up in a potentially concerning way, and encourages the Trusted Contact to check in. It does not include chat details or transcripts to protect user privacy."

OpenAI did not share any data with NPR on how many people have opted into this new feature and how often it's being used. But Raila says it's seen good adoption of the feature.

Wilcox, the suicide prevention expert at Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, notes that the new feature is optional and can easily be circumvented.

"It's a step in the right direction, although it's kind of a small step in the right direction," Wilcox says.

"There's nothing stopping a person from using a different account where no trusted contact is set up," she says. Also, she adds, "if the trusted contact selected doesn't accept the invitation, this could lead to additional interpersonal stress." That in turn can worsen the mental health of the user.

Ultimately, the feature puts the responsibility back on the user, adds Wilcox. She would like to see companies like OpenAI be more proactive in partnering with existing crisis resources like 988.

"So maybe having a human jump into the conversation at some point who's trained and knows the tools of what to do for suicide prevention," she says. "And have them jump in and say, 'You know, what's going on? Can I help?"

"How do we ensure that these types of technologies are as safe as they can be?" is the "question of our time," says the APA's Wright.

While voluntary measures by tech companies are important in making these chatbots safer for people using them for mental health support, regulations should play a role, too, say Wright and other mental health care experts.

"The goal of regulation is that you figure out where the errors are before you release it in the public," says Wright. "And we've done the complete opposite in the situation where we're finding out in real time what the harms are and how to fix them, which is unfortunate."

Reiley is also pushing for regulations.

"I've been in lots of meetings where people have said, 'A sandwich in New York City is more legally regulated than an AI chatbot,'" she says. "I think that might be a little hyperbolic, but it's pretty apt."

She has also been trying to process her own loss. And on June 27 this year, she and her best friend summited Mt. Kilimanjaro – exactly two years after Sophie did.

"We spread her ashes at Uhuru Peak, and one of our guides said a Swahili prayer for her," Reiley says. "It was incredibly meaningful, and a shockingly difficult thing to do."

Sophie Rottenberg did yoga near the top of Mt. Kilimanjaro in June 2024. She died by suicide in February 2025. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.
                
                    
                    Reiley Rottenberg family
