The Justice Department has activated a special court that's never before been used to argue for the removal of a woman accused of supporting the Islamic State.

Prosecutors detailed some of the government's case in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, the first such proceeding since Congress created the Alien Terrorist Removal Court in 1996. Authorities want to deport Nazira Haji Zada, originally from Afghanistan and now a lawful permanent resident who resides in Fort Worth, Texas.

Much of the evidence against Zada, 47, remains classified. But under prodding from Senior U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen, prosecutors said the FBI had developed information that she's a supporter of the Islamic State who worked with her son-in-law to "radicalize" other family members.

"In this case, the United States is alleging that Ms. Haji Zada is an alien terrorist...and that the U.S. has classified evidence to prove that," prosecutor Hayden O'Byrne said.

The Justice Department already brought criminal charges against her son and son-in-law for trying to attack the 2024 elections on behalf of the Islamic State, a terror organization. Both men were sentenced to time in prison and will be deported after serving their sentences.

But rather than charge Zada in the criminal justice system, leaders at the Justice Department launched first-of-their kind civil proceedings. The Alien Terrorist Removal Court allows the government to use a lower standard of proof to remove someone from American soil than in a criminal proceeding, which requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt. Congress created the court to make it easier for the DOJ to use classified evidence to deport people.

Federal agents arrested Zada earlier this week and she will remain in custody for now. Zada interjected at the start of the hearing, interrupting the courtroom clerk; her remarks were not translated. She said little else during the 40-minute proceeding, which she listened to with the help of a pair of interpreters.

Her court-appointed public defenders signaled they will challenge the legality of the untested court and its procedures.

"This entire scheme is in violation of due process and is unconstitutional," said public defender Matthew Farley. "The lack of process and due process provided to the respondent in these proceedings is woefully inadequate."

Judge Ericksen, who normally serves as a judge in the Minnesota district court, said the infrastructure for the new court is still coming into focus. She told an audience filled with government workers and reporters that it at times may seem "inelegant." Court officials have built a web site for the institution, which has been dormant for three decades, and are working on an electronic filing system where people can find relevant court papers.

"The court's committed to exactness, carefulness, circumspection and fealty to the Constitution and the rule of law," Judge Ericksen said.

Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche approved the government application before it went to the judge earlier this month.

"The allegations in this case show the matriarch of an ISIS-sympathizing family aiding in a plot to launch a mass casualty attack on American voters on Election Day," Blanche said in a statement.

"The Department's application in this court makes clear that terrorists have no place in the United States of America."

Matthias Jaissle was appointed by Al-Ahli on 29 July 2023, only 24 hours after ASM had signed for them.

The newly promoted club then saw the new manager and winger help guide them to third place in the Saudi Pro league, in the only season Matthias Jaissle and Allan Saint-Maximin spent together.

amazon_deforestation_hits_13_year_low:
Elizabeth Jacyshyn-Owen | Posted on August 10, 2026 |

Photo: James Cheung/Unsplash (CC0)

In today’s edition: deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level in 13 years; harvesting rainwater from rooftops could help cities stay cooler during heatwaves; and Bogotá increases the proportion of cycling journeys taken by women.

According to new satellite data, deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level in 13 years, continuing a decline that began after President Lula da Silva returned to office in 2023. The drop has coincided with renewed environmental enforcement under Lula, with Brazil pledging to eliminate illegal deforestation by 2030.

Source: Mongabay

New research from Ecuador indicates that rainforests are able to recover much faster after deforestation than previously thought. In fact, after approximately thirty years, local biodiversity appears to largely return to its original level. (Archive)

Source: Earth

Ramón Pucha and his family have spent years recreating their own piece of jungle with rescued species on a 32-hectare farm known as El Picaflor in the Indigenous Quichua community of Alto Ila, 128 km southeast of the capital, Quito. The family even shares the fruits of their labor, selling or gifting a percentage of the plants to neighbours committed to forest regeneration. (Archive)

Source: Euronews

Germany is on track to leave polluting coal behind “much sooner” than originally planned as part of its clean energy transition. New data from the Energy Institute show wind and solar generated 44% of the country’s electricity in 2025, overtaking fossil fuels for the first time.

Source: Euronews

Harvesting rainwater from rooftops could help cities stay cooler during heatwaves while also reducing the need for air conditioning. Researchers at the University of Manchester have tested a system using stored rainwater to spray on rooftops during extreme heat periods, creating a cooling effect through evaporation.

Source: Euronews

A promising new vaccine could help prevent one of the world’s leading causes of diarrhoeal deaths. Called WRSs2, the vaccine was 89% effective at preventing shigellosis in a clinical trial, acting as a new option for tackling a disease that still kills hundreds of thousands of people each year.

Source: NPR

Indianapolis International Airport is installing solar canopies over its car parks to help power the terminal itself. The projects are part of a push to build airport microgrids, alongside an existing 187-acre solar farm that generates enough electricity to power around 3,000 homes.

Source: WTHR13 News

Białystok in northeastern Poland is turning discarded beverage cartons into durable public benches, with four new seats made from composite boards containing 70% shredded cartons and 30% polyethylene film.

Source: TVP World

With less than a third of cycling journeys taken by women, Colombia’s capital, Bogotá, is installing bike lanes, teaching cycling and making sure “stereotypes are left behind”.

Source: The Guardian

In Topeka, Kansas, a women-led initiative is approaching care for people in and beyond the criminal justice system from a new angle. Longtime local Patti Mellard founded the Rotary Club of Community Action Against Human Trafficking to focus on prevention, survivor support and advocacy, with the intention of helping vulnerable women rebuild their lives on release from prison.

Source: Reasons To Be Cheerful

A female Amur tiger called Umit has been released into the wild in Kazakhstan, the first such release since the Turan tiger disappeared from the country more than 70 years ago. The conservation programme hopes to bring back tigers to their historic native range across Central Asia.

Source: Euronews

Fifteen years ago, Jantho Pine Forest Nature Reserve in Sumatra had no orangutans. Today, the Indonesian reserve is home to a growing wild population, thanks to a pioneering conservation programme that has rescued, rehabilitated and returned orangutans to the forest.

Source: Mongabay

americas_obsession_with_mental_illness:
Thank You For Sharing exposes how the mental health industry thrives off of telling people that their worst behaviors can be excused because of ‘illness.’

Our culture has an unhealthy obsession with mental illness, and the Lindsay Clancy trial is just the latest reminder. Children and adults alike build their entire personalities around their perceived illnesses, whether by going to therapy five days a week or identifying as transgender. Thank You For Sharing, the newest film from director Sonia Zawitkowski, argues that this alleged crisis is predominantly artificial.

The documentary tracks how we invented and gradually expanded the concept of mental health. It exposes how the modern field of medicine, originally centered around soldiers suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder, has spiralled into an industry that encourages children to take wrong-sex hormones, get hooked on SSRIs, and rebuild their identities around their perceived illness.

For decades, the corporate media have pushed the narrative that we are caught in a mental health crisis. As Thank You For Sharing argues, the problem isn’t that mental health doesn’t get enough attention but that it gets far too much attention. The industry is extremely predatory, seeking out vulnerable people and coaxing them into believing they need treatment.

In a recent report from the Department of Health and Human Services, titled “Wolves in White Coats,” the Trump administration exposed how doctors and other medical professionals encourage young people to pursue transgender procedures. Doctors diagnose their young patients with gender dysphoria, setting them on a path to “transition” that will cost them hundreds of thousands of dollars over the course of their lives. The cost of long-term cross-sex hormones, puberty blockers, and surgeries can cost more than $600,000. Throughout Thank You For Sharing, doctors and longtime industry professionals pull back the curtain on the mental health cash cow, revealing how diagnoses such as depression and ADHD became much more common once the insurance-health care racket realized the massive profits from affirming “mental illness.”

What Thank You For Sharing addresses best is how Americans’ fixation on mental health has been building for a long time. Part of the blame for our current situation falls on the experts, who developed the field of psychiatry but had very little scientific data backing their diagnostic process. During the second half of the 20th century, when pharmaceutical companies became more profitable, the rates of diagnoses began to climb.

In 1950, nearly 580,000 people, or 0.38 percent of the U.S. population, were receiving long-term hospital care for mental illness. By 2022, the number of inpatient hospitalizations for mental health and substance abuse, which often go hand in hand, reached 1.65 million, or 0.5 percent of the population. But measuring only the serious cases doesn’t give the full picture of Americans’ obsession. A whopping 72 percent of Gen Z believe they have a mental illness, with more than 40 percent having received official diagnoses and 60 percent taking pharmaceutical drugs “to help manage their mental health.”

The documentary points out how what is considered to be mental illness has expanded over the past century. Doctors and patients alike testify about how fast many therapists and psychiatrists are to pathologize normal human behavior. One industry expert explains that the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders cited only about 100 different disorders during its first publication. Today, it lists more than 300. In addition, the supposed symptoms have broadened, allowing for almost any human behavior to fit some criteria for “mental illness.” In the past decade, the DSM has added “illnesses” such as “prolonged grief disorder” and “unspecified mood disorder.” Another recent addition, “stimulant-induced mild neurocognitive disorder,” simply refers to how people who use drugs for a long time are more prone to forgetfulness.

Perhaps Thank You For Sharing’s greatest strength is its willingness to call out doctors and health “experts” who have made a fortune convincing people they are ill. In 2025 alone, the U.S. spent about $118 billion on mental health. That number is expected to rise to $159 billion by 2030. More than 14,500 mental health companies currently operate in the U.S., employing more than 750,000 workers.

In the documentary, several people reflect on how their perceived mental illness entitled them to victimhood status. This is a trend we see with transgender influencers like Dylan Mulvaney and celebrities like Demi Lovato. Thank You For Sharing shines a light into how public sympathy for neurological disorders gives people permission to behave erratically. It briefly touches on how social media sites such as Tumblr and TikTok have glamorized mental illness. The glorification of mental health has had terrible effects on American youths raised in the tech age; this deserves further investigation.

What Thank You For Sharing doesn’t predict is how the mental health field has affected the public’s perception of horrific crimes such as murder. The Lindsay Clancy case is an extreme instance of someone using mental illness as a get-out-of-jail-free card. Although Clancy has admitted to strangling and killing her three children, she has claimed “temporary psychosis” as a reason to avoid consequences. Clancy’s trial has drawn support from thousands of other women, who have expressed sympathy for the violent killer because of her mental health.

Thank You For Sharing exposes how the mental health industry thrives off of telling people that all of their worst behaviors can be excused because of “illness.” It explains how a victimhood mentality has eroded our country and our culture. The neuroticism around mental health has enabled children to chop off healthy body parts, prompted the masses to sympathize with a child killer, and coaxed millions of people into thinking they are broken.

andy-burnham-influencers:
Young Labour supporters whose TikToks took them to Downing Street

Andy Burnham is a past master at using social media to create a political brand - and it seems he has no plans to let up now that he is prime minister.

One Downing Street source told the BBC they planned to take a "more social first" and "authentic to Andy" approach, with "less high production, polished" content than might have been seen from a prime minister in the past.

This means we can expect more clips of Burnham in casual mode, chatting into a handheld phone or answering questions on policy in an apparently spontaneous fashion on X, Instagram or TikTok.

There will also be a focus on collaborations with social media creators.

In an earlier age, political leaders liked to court TV stars and other celebrities to help get their message out.

Now the Holy Grail is online influencers, who are seen as more authentic, and trusted, by hard-to-reach voters who don't watch much TV or read newspapers.

Sir Keir Starmer's government had already begun experimenting with giving access to influencers, with ministers appearing on some of the more popular channels.

Downing Street also held receptions for influencers and during Tim Allan's tenure as director of communications content creators were invited to Downing Street press conferences.

Some critics saw this is a way of avoiding serious scrutiny of polices in favour of softball questions from non-specialists.

But Burnham's advisers see collaborations with influencers as a way of getting the government's message to audiences it might not normally reach.

A Downing Street source said "the vast majority" of the public will not see or interact with content that is coming from government or the prime minister's social media channels.

Andy Burnham appeared on influencer Max Klymenko's 'career ladder' on his first day as PM

In the hours before and after becoming prime minister, Burnham co-authored two posts on TikTok and Instagram, including a running video with Sir Mo Farah.

Young TikTokers were also invited to Downing Street to thank them for their work on his Makerfield by-election campaign.

One of the social channels Sir Keir Starmer appeared on was run by Ukrainian online personality Max Klymenko, who won TikTok Creator of the year for his viral "The Career Ladder" series, where he quizzes people about their job history.

Klymenko was first approached by Burnham's team around two months ago to collaborate on content.

His team filmed the video quizzing the former Greater Manchester mayor on his first job, before he entered politics, a week ago, then planned to post it on his first day as prime minister to capitalise on the buzz.

The creator's core audience are aged 18 to 24, according to his team, while the majority of people who watch his content are aged between 25 and 30.

A member of his team pointed out this is far younger than the audience for a traditional TV interview, while his cumulative subscriber and follower count across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook is more than 16.3 million accounts.

While there is some paid-for content on his pages, Klymenko said no payment or contract was exchanged with Burnham's team and they did not request changes to the content before it was posted.

Meanwhile, Sir Mo Farah's uploads, running while discussing sport, education and mental health with Burnham, went to his three million followers across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, a far bigger reach than the prime minister's personal channels.

Andy Burnham Went Online, and Got Into No 10

Ros Atkins reports on how the new PM uses social media to get his message across.

Available now

The strategy is the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, who ran Burnham's digital communications during the by-election, and who the BBC can confirm has been kept on for a new role in Burnham's administration.

She began her career in social media aged 17 by starting a "Milifandom" campaign on social media for Ed Miliband over a decade ago.

In more recent years, she has worked in digital communications for the Labour Party, and for Keir Starmer in Number10 before quitting last year.

Tomlinson has been credited with how Burnham connected with voters across platforms in recent months.

The new PM has rationed interviews with traditional media since returning to Parliament, in favour of vlogs, a question and answer session on Reddit and X posts clapping back at political opponents.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch took to Reddit to urge him to "come out from hiding, face a proper press conference and submit yourself to scrutiny and some tough questions".

Burnham responded to it by saying it had only been two weeks since he faced questions from "74,000 members of the public of Makerfield".

Sir Mo Farah put Andy Burnham through his paces on his social media channels

Another key strand of Burnham's campaigning strategy has been connecting with and organising grassroots social media activists.

Among the politicians and staffers invited to stand outside Number 10 to watch Burnham become prime minister on Monday were teenage TikTokers whose video edits have brought him to a new social media audience.

Between them, Will, Lottie, Megan, Ellen and Poppy, all aged between 17 and 19  have racked up millions of likes on TikTok, and across platforms share memes, trends and nostalgic edits of New Labour footage, including of Burnham's time in office.

The Labour activists were invited to canvass with him and make edits of his time on the Makerfield by-election campaign trail in a language and style that resonates with people online.

One way they got thousands of likes was by getting him to sign and pose with red pre-made cocktails popular with Gen Z.

Megan Cassidy, 19, from Havering, started making Labour content a year ago and said it was "surreal" to have found herself at Downing Street: "I really felt like I was witnessing history around me".

The young Labour activists said they were given access to Burnham and footage of him by his team, but are not paid and can choose to edit the material how they like.

They saw it as an opportunity to gain ground from social media savvy parties like Reform, whose leader Nigel Farage has an exponentially bigger following on social media, and the Greens who have experienced large growth in recent months.

It helped that Burnham was "natural" and happy to spontaneously appear in content, they told the BBC.

"I do think he gets it, absolutely compared to other politicians, compared to Starmer for example, I think he's a lot more charismatic," said Megan.

Get the FREE App

Angus Taylor has branded the government’s backdown on capital gains taxes for small businesses “half-arsed” as the topic is set to dominate business in Canberra this week.

The Opposition Leader diminished the government’s limited reductions on capital gains taxes for new businesses, days after Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers announced start-ups with turnover up to $10m will get a 50 per cent tax discount; up from $2m.

The initial CGT tweak, delivered in last month’s budget, has been widely panned by tech founders, and the federal opposition has described it as a “war on ambition”.

Speaking after the turnover threshold was lifted, Mr Taylor said the carve-outs were “half-arsed” and the tax as a whole was an “abject failure”.

“This is abject failure, and they are layering failure upon failure,” he told Sky News’ Sunday Agenda.

“And now we see a half-arsed carve-out from this government that is an admission of failure.

“Well, why not just get rid of the whole thing? Scrap it and start again. We need a budget that is right for the times, right for the country and right for prosperity.”

The fine print on the carve-outs will become clearer after consultation.

But a narrow range of “innovative” start-ups, such as technology and biotechnology firms, will be eligible for a 50 per cent discount on capital gains. The tax is likely to apply to founders, employees granted shares and other early-stage investors.

Criticism of the budget announcement has included fears the taxes will drive entrepreneurial Australians overseas.

About 60 per cent of all capital gains income is shared by just 0.2 per cent of tax filers, tax office figures show. Revealed by Mr Chalmers this week, 99 per cent of Australian tax filers account for only 13 per cent of all capital gains income in the 2023/24 year.

Mr Taylor said those figures were “ridiculous”.

“That’s irrelevant. What matters is what happens over someone’s lifetime, not over a very short period of time, so it’s a ridiculous analysis,” he said.

“What’s clear is that these taxes are going to hurt aspiration in this country.

“They are an assault on aspiration, on ambition, on investment, on risk-taking, on growth, on rising standards of living, on all the things that we know drive prosperity.”

The federal budget also included a $10bn package to cut a host of red tape for businesses.

In an earlier, prerecorded interview with Sky News, the Prime Minister said it was important to remember capital gains taxes were paid when an asset was sold.

“This isn’t an ongoing tax on a week-to-week basis,” he said.

Consultation with start-ups is also ongoing.

Mr Albanese said just because taxes were higher when an owner sold their business, that did not reduce incentive to grow the business itself.

“The aspiration is the same as for every worker; more income, to aspire to be better off in life,” he said.

“And what we’re doing is better aligning income from work, with income from assets.

“When most people go into small business, they don’t go in so they can start a small business today and sell it tomorrow.”

Many small businesses were also run by generations of the same family, he said.

“This is removing an anomaly, really, that was there that saw from 1999 - what we saw was additional investment, funnelled into housing, that’s had a real impact on property, that has meant that young Australians are simply priced out of housing.”

An under-the-radar Australian skincare brand beloved by beauty journalists, industry insiders and a fiercely loyal fan base has just announced a restock of its latest launch, after the pre-sale sold out in under 24 hours.

AEON Skincare, whose cult face oil Liquid Magic boasts over 470 five-star reviews, thrilled its customers when it released a vitamin C serum specifically formulated for 'skin that hates traditional vitamin C'.

While many vitamin C products are notoriously harsh on sensitive skin types, and often have an offputting smell, AEON's C Bomb Brightening Serum promises that its formulation of four brightening actives can help to improve the appearance of dullness, dark spots and uneven skin tone, without the associated irritation.

The gentle, lightweight cream is powered by four hardworking actives, including ascorbyl tetraisopalmitate, a stable, oil-soluble form of vitamin C. AEON says it is less prone to oxidising than traditional vitamin C, so it stays effective for longer, while helping to visibly brighten skin and even out tone.

The formula also includes alpha-arbutin and kojic acid, two brightening ingredients that work to fade the look of dark spots, post-breakout marks and discolouration over time, and antioxidant-rich bilberry extract, which helps protect skin from environmental stressors that can leave it looking dull, for a fresher, more radiant-looking complexion.

An under-the-radar Australian skincare brand beloved by beauty journalists, industry insiders and a fiercely loyal fan base has just announced a restock of it's latest launch, after the pre-sale sold out in under 24 hours

AEON Skincare's cult face oil Liquid Magic boasts over 470 five star reviews (pictured, customer review before and after images using Liquid Magic)

One five-star reviewer on the website shared: 'This has been the best Vit C I have ever used! It has the most beautiful scent (as to be expected with any AEON product) and applies beautifully. I've been using it for almost a week now and I've had zero reaction which I'm so thankful for as all the Vit C's I've used in the past haven't agreed with my skin. Can't wait to see the longer term effects of using it as the new regular in my skin routine.'

'I have never used a c product I enjoy or one that actually delivers what it promises. C-Bomb is now the exception. Smells divine! (No weird ham smell here) and the texture is glorious,' another shopper raved, rating the product 'five stars and more'.

'I am in love, have used for a week and now cannot be without it, next purchase will be a subscription for sure,' they continued, also declaring: 'At this point I will most likely purchase anything released with blind faith due to EVERY. SINGLE. PRODUCT. BEING. BEYOND. AMAZING!'

AEON's latest launch, C Bomb Brightening Serum, promises that its formulation of four brightening actives can help to improve the appearance of dullness, dark spots and uneven skin tone, without the associated irritation

Less than two years old, the brand has gained its insider cult status primarily through word of mouth. As a former beauty writer, Ms Sophia's Instagram following trusted her expertise on products they should spend their money on, and it was these followers who snapped up her first launch, Liquid Magic (then named Skin Flash), when she released 500 for pre-sale orders in February 2025.

Selling out of this first batch within 48 hours, and then selling out again, led to bigger batch productions, a warehouse space and new product development.

Today, AEON boasts six products, hundreds of five-star reviews, and reports an impressive 40 per cent return customer rate.

Liquid Magic has sold over 10,000 units, and boasts a 4.95-star rating from 488 reviews on AEON's website. It's an oil-serum hybrid that blends 14 nourishing botanical oils and extracts, including marula, seabuckthorn and strawberry seed, with bakuchiol, a plant-based ingredient often called a gentler alternative to retinol.

Designed to visibly brighten, firm and even out skin tone, it promises to leave the complexion looking plump and glowing rather than greasy.

In a consumer study of 208 participants, 97 per cent reported increased radiance and 91 per cent saw an improvement in skin tone.

Other bestsellers include Venom 32 Mini Peel which boasts 113 five-star ratings, and Hespera Hybrid Cleanser, with 129 five-star ratings.

Getting initial customers as a startup can be one of the most grueling challenges in business. Even when companies manage to snag some early interest, there’s no guarantee those customers will stick around.

At TechCrunch Disrupt last week, Elia Wallen, founder and CEO of travel startup Engine, Gamma founder and CEO Grant Lee, and Crystal Huang, general partner at Google Ventures, shared tips on how to attract and retain customers.

In the current era — when young AI companies like Cluely and Instinct are building big audiences not just through their products but also through their founders’ colorful online presences — social media can seem like a magic bullet for reaching early customers. But founders who want heighten their business strategy with modern marketing, have to be strategic, according to Lee.

Gamma, which sells AI-powered presentation software, managed to scale its business exponentially with a social media strategy that deployed influencers through its Ambassadors (or “Gambassador”) program. The company adopted the plan before influencer-based marketing was a tried-and-true strategy for smaller companies, eventually reaching a multi-billion dollar valuation.

But simply giving influencers a platform and telling them to promote your brand online doesn’t automatically translate to sales, said Lee. There’s more to it than that.

“If you have a product that can serve many different segments or use cases, then you want to basically have creators that can target each one of those,” Lee said. “If you have folks that are in consulting versus people that do all their marketing and create all the decks for their CMO, there’s all these different segments you might want to go after.”

Lee said sometimes founders seem to treat creator marketing or influencer marketing as a sort of set it and forget it thing.

“I think you’re better served by really spending a lot of time with these creators, because if they’re not able to understand how to articulate the value of your product, it doesn’t matter how much money you spend, it’s just going to fall flat,” Lee added.

The effectiveness of social media depends largely on the type of business. Other ways of reaching customers can be just (if not more) effective.

Wallen would know. His company Engine, which manages lodging and travel bookings for midsize businesses, bootstrapped its way to $150 million in bookings before taking on any outside funding. They also had no visible social media strategy at all. For Wallen, traditional sales tactics can be far more useful than a positive TikTok video.

“We did events and we smiled and dialed,” said Wallen. “We still have a lot of people picking up the phone. A lot of people who didn’t grow up with that or don’t understand it think that it’s outdated or it doesn’t work but it does. It’s a hard thing. There are a lot of companies that just refuse to do it or don’t know how to do it well. But they’re missing out on a very big offline client base.” He added: “The phone still works.”

Wallen also shared an in-person tactic that his company deployed during its scrappy early days: hiring a magician named David to perform tricks for prospective clients at events and encourage them to visit the Engine’s booth. In short, old-fashioned personal engagement can work just as well, if not better, than the latest social media tricks.

Huang, who has managed droves of startups and shepherded them to success, said that once you have a customer, a lot of value can be derived from looking at how they use the product.

“Can you look into usage data and figure out if it’s recurring, if it’s increasing, if they are referring their friends?” Huang said. “It can come across in early usage and retention information as well. And then also, do you see some super fans, right, who even want to work at the company, promote the company, be attached to the brand?” She added: “You need to have ways to create evangelists who are really passionate about the product.”

Product-market fit — when a startup’s product sells well — has become even harder to find in this AI era. Despite startups achieving record-fast growth, not all customers are sticky and products can be replicated more easily than ever.

Anu Bharadwaj, a partner at Iconiq; Rajeev Dham, a partner at Sapphire Ventures; and Rahul Vohra, the founder of Superhuman Mail, discussed the new rules for product-market fit last week at TechCrunch Disrupt.

“It’s never been easier to gain a bunch of pilots because lots of companies across the board are open to trying new things,” Bharadwaj said to the audience. “But going from pilot to production is really the hard thing.”

Right now, she said, a lot of founders pitch revenue metrics to investors without specifying which revenue they are talking about. “Is it true ARR or is it run rate?” she said. “There’s many ways to obfuscate the whole thing.”

Lately, much chatter on X has focused on AI founders inflating ARR numbers (which could mean “annualized run rate” or the more solid “annual recurring revenue”) to make it seem like their companies are doing better than they are. A common gimmick is counting pilot customers, who might only use the product for a couple of months, in the annualized run rate revenue number, implying that income is expected to continue for the entire year.

It should be obvious, but Bharadwaj pointed out, “It’s definitely in your long-term interest that you be very honest and upfront about what quality of revenue this is.”

She said companies need to separate hype from reality when looking at the quality of their revenue. It’s a red flag, for example, if only a few customers make up much of a company’s revenue or if the customers can easily go to another vendor for a better price. “Churn rate and retention [are] really dependent on that,” she continued.

That’s why Vohra advises startups to track customer engagement and dollar retention, especially for consumer products. “Figure out what benchmark [is] good, great, and excellent for your space,” he said.

For example, at Superhuman, he said that the company tracked ARR but also had their own internal metric called “delighted ARR,” which, he said, “was the ARR only from customers who are super engaged with the product.” He said that metric helped them see how sticky the customers were and how long they were likely to stay around.

“Those users are now still users, those companies are now still customers,” he continued. “We obsessed over serving that particular category of our user base and our customer base.”

The panelists also discussed green flags that indicate a startup has indeed found product-market fit. For Vohra, he said  talk to customers to understand what value they find in the product and how they would feel if they could no longer use it. Then be honest with yourself when measuring those responses.

“If you’re 15%, 14%, 13%, or below, consider a complete pivot. Take the codebase, take the team, build something entirely new. “But if you’re 20%, you can totally optimize your way from 20% to 40%,” Vohra said.

Actually, Dham said, it’s important for a founder not to confuse having a vision with having a good business.

At the seed level especially, Barudvaj said that it’s fine to pivot. She doesn’t even look for product-market fit at that stage, but “does the founder have a thesis that seems plausible and do they have the agility to duck and wave as the situation changes?” she said.

Dham added that he values founders even more these days who have made numerous pivots because it shows they’ve had to make very hard decisions in this ever-shifting moment.

Product-market fit, therefore, is something founders will always have to redefine and re-earn. “Even at a billion in revenue, these companies are re-earning their product-market fit,” he said. “You constantly have to be innovating on products.”

Kate Hudson spoke to Fox News Digital on the red carpet at the 28th Costume Designers Guild Awards and reflected on the advice that she would give her younger self.

Kate Hudson isn't quite ready to leave her Hawaiian getaway behind.

The 47-year-old actress shared a series of vacation throwbacks on Instagram, including photos from a recent trip to Hawaii for a friend's wedding.

In one photo, Hudson showed off her toned figure in a bright red bandeau bikini while relaxing on the beach with her fiancé, Danny Fujikawa.

KATE HUDSON SHOWS OFF FIT BODY IN MULTIPLE STRING BIKINIS DURING FAMILY VACATION IN GREECE

Kate Hudson enjoys beach time in Hawaii with fiancé Danny Fujikawa. (Kate Hudson/Instagram)

The "Song Sung Blue" star wore dark sunglasses and a gold necklace, with her blonde hair pulled back as she sat beside Fujikawa, who went shirtless in patterned swim trunks and a baseball cap.

"M​​entally still here," Hudson captioned the Instagram carousel.

KATE HUDSON TURNS HEADS IN BOLD YELLOW DRESS WITH REVEALING CUTOUTS WHILE ON THE RED CARPET

Another photo captured Hudson soaking up the sun alongside a friend as the two lounged on separate white towels spread across the sand.

Hudson wore the same red bikini while her friend opted for a black two-piece. Both accessorized with dark sunglasses as they enjoyed the sunny weather.

Kate Hudson soaked up the sun in a red bikini while lounging on the beach with a friend during her Hawaiian getaway. (Kate Hudson/Instagram)

The actress's followers were quick to react to the vacation photos, with several praising her appearance.

"I feel like all the women I grew up with and watched on tv, who are around the same age as me, are absolutely glowing in their 40s-50s era," one person commented.

"There's a confidence, a freedom and a beauty that comes with this stage of life. You're glowing, Kate."

GOLDIE HAWN CREDITS ‘FREEDOM’ FOR KEEPING 43-YEAR RELATIONSHIP WITH KURT RUSSELL STRONG

Another wrote, "Without sounding creepy, all I want is to hang out with Kate Hudson for a day! she is just a ray of sunshine!"

The beach getaway also included a glamorous evening celebrating a friend's wedding.

In another photo, Hudson traded her bikini for a strapless, floor-length gown covered in shimmering embellishments as she posed with a friend wearing a white feather-trimmed dress.

The two smiled for the camera while holding drinks at an outdoor reception decorated with elaborate white floral arrangements.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Kate Hudson celebrates a friend's wedding in Hawaii, sharing a glimpse of her look for the special occasion. (Kate Hudson/Instagram)

Hudson also shared a playful glimpse of her travels in a photo taken aboard a private jet.

The actress posed in a flowing leopard-print dress and sunglasses while standing near the aircraft's cabin entrance.

While Hudson was celebrating someone else's wedding in Hawaii, she has been candid about the challenges of planning her own.

Kate Hudson posed aboard a private jet in a flowing leopard-print dress. (Kate Hudson/Instagram)

The actress has been engaged to Fujikawa since September 2021, but the couple has yet to walk down the aisle.

During a September appearance on the "Sibling Revelry" podcast, which she co-hosts with her brother, Oliver Hudson, the actress admitted that the size of their family has made wedding planning complicated.

"I still am not married. I'm just engaged," Hudson said during a conversation with actresses Joey and Hunter King.

"And I keep thinking about wedding. You know, like, what are we going to do? And then every time we started thinking about who we have to invite, and Danny's like, ‘I just want a small wedding.’

"Our family alone is like 50 people."

Hudson also acknowledged the expense of planning a wedding while discussing the elaborate celebrations some couples organize.

"That's part of why I don't want to get married," she said. "I'm like, 'It's too expensive. I just want like hors d'oeuvres.'"

Hudson and Fujikawa began dating in 2016 after knowing each other for years through mutual friends. They welcomed their daughter, Rani Rose, in October 2018.

The actress is also mom to sons Ryder Robinson, whom she shares with ex-husband Chris Robinson, and Bingham Bellamy, whom she shares with former fiancé Matt Bellamy.

Kate Hudson is the daughter of actress Goldie Hawn and musician Bill Hudson. (Getty Images for Academy Museum)

Although it seems like she's torn over the idea of a wedding, Hudson has made it clear that Fujikawa is the one for her.

In a 2019 interview with Women's Health, she described him as a supportive partner who shares her commitment to family.

"I've got the best man," she said. "It's the first time I feel like I have a real teammate in this."

venezuelan-protests-2026:
Thousands of Venezuelans marched through the streets of Caracas and other cities on Thursday against the nation’s socialist regime to demand presidential elections and the safe return of anti-socialist opposition leader María Corina Machado to the country.

Thursday’s round of protests in Venezuela were organized by Vente Venezuela, the only mainstream center-right party in the country and an organization whose members suffered an extensive persecution campaign during the rule of deposed socialist dictator Nicolás Maduro. Vente is led by Machado, who has found herself unable to return to her country after the administration of President Donald Trump helped her escape from the country in December 2025 to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo, Norway.

The Venezuelan newspaper El Nacional reported that the peaceful protest in Caracas began in the afternoon hours of Thursday near the Central University of Venezuela. Politicians, students, relatives of political prisoners, and civilians marched through toward Plaza Venezuela to demand that Venezuelan regime authorities establish an electoral timetable for a new presidential election in the country, in addition to allowing the safe return of Machado to her country, and the release of all remaining political prisoners.

According to Infobae, Thursday’s protest unfolded with a “notably scarce” presence of Venezuelan security forces — which stands in contrast with the events that occurred during a separate protest this month. In addition to Caracas, simultaneous peaceful demonstrations took place in Valencia, Maracay, San Cristóbal, and Maracaibo. Thursday’s protest in Caracas comes roughly a month after a similar peaceful demonstration took place in the Venezuelan capital.

“They tell us to be patient, that this is just the way things are. And we tell them: We’re going to get organized, and next year we’re going to have presidential elections and get María Corina Machado elected president,” Carlos Fernández, Vente Venezuela’s national youth coordinator, said during the protest.

“We won’t let the guys who destroyed the country stay in power. In 2027, we’re going to have presidential elections, and we’re going to take it upon ourselves to lead this country out of the darkness and into a brighter future,” he continued.

Machado and Vente Venezuela have repeatedly made calls for a free and fair election to take place in Venezuela, proposing July 24, 2027, as potential “Liberation Day.” Venezuelans mark July 24 as a public holiday to commemorate the birthday of their founding father, Simón Bolívar. The prospective date also represents a symbolic counterweight to Maduro’s last sham presidential election, which took place on July 28, 2024 — a date chosen by the socialist regime to mark late dictator Hugo Chávez’s birthday.

El Nacional and other Venezuelan outlets observed that the demonstration also served to commemorate the third anniversary of the Venezuelan opposition’s October 22, 2023, presidential primary election that resulted in an overwhelming victory for Machado, who nevertheless was not allowed by the Venezuelan socialist regime to run against Nicolás Maduro in the 2024 sham presidential election.

Jaime Domínguez, a 77-year-old Venezuelan engineer, spoke with El Nacional during the protest and explained that he lost a major contracting firm when the Venezuelan socialist regime seized a construction project in the town of Ocumare del Tuy, Miranda. Domínguez stressed to the newspaper that his motivation to participate in the demonstration is “the 27 years of disgrace that we have.”

“My demands are democracy, with democracy everything else flows — but this situation of dictatorship, control threats, harassment, and restrictions, added to a currency that lost 14 zeroes, is an economic tragedy,” he said.

Over the past months, representatives of the Venezuelan opposition have engaged in talks with the Venezuelan socialist regime for a democratic transition in the country under the backing of the U.S. State Department.

Speaking with Breitbart News this week, Dinorah Figuera, who leads the opposition delegation in the negotiations, emphasized the need to reconstruct the nation’s Supreme Court, electoral body, political parties, and the release of political prisoners as part of the transition process and the celebration of free and fair elections in Venezuela. As is the case with all Venezuelan institutions, Maduro stacked the Supreme Court and National Electoral Council (CNE) with loyalists throughout his rule. The Venezuelan socialists also hijacked numerous opposition parties, imposing “ad-hoc” leaderships while maintaining the purported notion of the parties still being part of the “opposition.”

“We have to appoint a National Electoral Council that is credible, trustworthy, transparent, that people have in that sense the guarantee that their vote will be respected,” Figuera stressed to Breitbart News.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks alongside Dinorah Figuera, the 2015 Venezuelan National Assembly President, in the Treaty Room at the State Department, Friday, October 9, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta)

“We have initiated technical and plenary forums. In the forum on the National Electoral Council, we are beginning with the organization of political parties,” she continued. “Since there was an unraveling of the right that political parties had to establish themselves and make proposals … people were afraid to participate politically and we are, as we say in Venezuela, picking up the pieces of broken glass.”

This week marked the third round of negotiations between both parties. U.S. State Department spokesman Thomas Pigott detailed on Thursday that the rounds of talks led to further advances towards the selection of new Supreme Court justices.

Figuera met with “acting President” Delcy Rodríguez on Thursday. After the meeting, Rodríguez broadcast a brief address recognizing the efforts of both sides of the negotiating table towards “advancing political safeguards for everyone, for all political parties.” According to Rodríguez, a new round of talks is scheduled to take place in November. Rodríguez’s brother and head of the National Assembly, Jorge Rodríguez, is leading the regime’s delegation in the talks.

While the peaceful protests occurred without any notable incident or acts of repression, Vente Venezuela denounced on social media that the Bolivarian National Police detained seven individuals who were in charge of the three sound trucks used in the Caracas protest, seizing the three vehicles in the process, one of which was seized when the driver was arriving in the Caracas district of Antímano.

“We alert the international community about this attack against Venezuelans who provided their services for the peaceful protest of this October 22,” the message read in part.

“This occurs while Delcy Rodríguez meets with Dinorah Figuera, head of the negotiating commission of the 2015 Assembly, and one day after the agreements on democratic guarantees in the country,” the text continued.

exclusive-tx-gop-candidate-jace-yarborou:
Unfettered illegal immigration causes citizens to often clam up and stop investing in their communities to “fall apart and disintegrate,” Jace Yarborough, the GOP Candidate for Congress in Texas’s 32 Congressional District, said during an appearance on Breitbart News Daily.

“I’ve got massive corridors that come up from the border, I-35 being one of the biggest ones. The point is that there are all kinds of monetary costs and burdens to public programs that we’re seeing more and more of because the work the Trump administration is doing,” he said, laying out what he is seeing in his district in terms of illegal immigration.

“I mean, for decades the Democrats have flooded our communities with these illegal foreign scammers, and we’re seeing millions, billions of dollars in fraud they’re committing, which have, again, like the monetary value can apply to them,” Yarborough said before speaking about an aspect of illegal immigration that “doesn’t really get talked about much.”

“… which is when people in a local community see those around them taking from the community, taking from common spaces and common resources, they clam up, they stop investing in things that aren’t necessarily, you know, that are sort of common and public, and that’s when communities really fall apart and disintegrate,” the GOP hopeful said.

“What I’ve said all along is our communities are strong. Our civilization and country will be strong whenever ordinary citizens have high amounts of trust for the people that they interact with every day, and illegal immigration and fraud and all the things that we’re seeing obviously are terrible for our communities in many ways. But one of them in particular is that it causes us all to turn in, and we stop we stop doing the things that make our communities vibrant and rich and beautiful to live in,” he said.

Yarborough identified himself as someone who has benefited from basic public commodities in the community, as he came from a blue collar family.

“We had to rely on things like local public schools, our local police force, local libraries, sidewalks, right? But all of these things are being completely overrun by people who are here to simply take, take, take, because they don’t have a mindset that was formed by our American culture,” he said.

“We’re the most generous, dynamic, powerful country in the history of the world. These people that we’re shipping in here, that our government has shipped in here, they don’t share those values. They don’t share that perspective. They’re here to take, take, take, and that has really detrimental effects on communities, especially for people in homes like the one I grew up in,” he added, providing some examples, like something as simple as a local park.

“I remember when I was growing up, there there was a gentleman who he sort of took pride in in taking care of a portion of our local park. He mowed and kind of like kept it up, and it was it was a great place to go and just kind of play and hang out. Right now, he didn’t get paid to do that. He wasn’t on the city’s payroll. And I grew up in little bitty towns where these sort of spontaneous organic relationships would pop up and grow, and kids all over the town benefited from the work this gentleman did, and that’s why he loved it, right,” he said.

Between unnecessary regulations and abuse by “third worlders who came to sort of deal their dope and do their crack there or whatever they’re doing” in these parks, this same man would likely opt not to take care of the local park anymore.

“It is simply the case that if you do not have the resources to buffer yourself from common spaces today, then your kind of everyday life is much more, much more difficult,” he added, noting that “civilizations are created by a group of people who love the same things, are drawn to those things together, and therefore get closer together because of it, and are bound up because of it.”

That is missing in the current dynamic promoted by the radical left.

“When we remove those common loves, not only from our own citizens, but certainly we don’t give them to people that immigrate to this country, then things start to fall apart, because we’re not all drawn to the same things. We’re not all ready to give of ourselves to things that we don’t control, like a common community space,” he added.
